chapters.title: The Wonderful World of Science
chapters.summary: In this chapter: wondering about science; science is everywhere; water, materials and scientific questions; finding answers with guesses and tests.

lessons.title: Wondering About Science

activities.prompt: What can you discover when you stay curious?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Wondering About Science
activities.body:
Imagine science as a big adventure. You begin by asking questions and exploring the world around you. As you think, observe and do things, science helps you understand what you see. Your curiosity is the most important quality for science.

Now, notice a tiny grain of sand. Then turn your eyes towards a huge mountain. Science can explore both, from the tiniest details to the greatest heights. Each view can open fresh questions in your mind.

Next, lift your gaze to the night sky. Its stars may make you wonder why they shine. New questions can appear, and science gives you ways to explore them. Curiosity helps you keep asking, looking and understanding.

Perhaps you also watch a flower. You may wonder how it knows when to open. Such questions show why curiosity matters so much. As you ask, observe and explore, nature always offers something new and exciting to discover.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is science?
activities.body: Science helps us understand the world by thinking, observing and doing things. It is a big adventure where we ask questions and explore. Curiosity means wanting to ask questions and find out more. It is the most important quality for science. We can explore tiny grains of sand and huge mountains. The night sky may make us wonder why stars shine.
keyPoints: Science helps us understand the world.
Curiosity helps us ask questions and explore.
Science can explore tiny things and huge things.
activities.explanation: Curiosity helps you begin every science adventure.

activities.prompt: A child sees a flower open. The child wonders how it knows when to open.
steps: We ask how the flower knows when to open. Seeing this makes us wonder.
We look closely at the flower. Looking helps us understand the world around us.
We think about what we notice. Science grows through questions and exploring.
So we keep our curiosity and keep exploring. Curiosity is the most important quality for science.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

lessons.title: Science Is Everywhere

activities.prompt: Where might your next science discovery begin?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Science Is Everywhere
activities.body:
Imagine you begin your science tour in the kitchen. You might ask what your food is made of. Science can help you find out. Next, you travel to outer space, where science can be studied.

Your tour then takes you to the playground. Science discoveries can begin here. Many groundbreaking discoveries have come from places we do not expect.

Now picture science as a huge jigsaw puzzle that never ends. Each new discovery adds another piece. New knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out. You see how one discovery can lead to the next.

New discoveries can change how we understand the world. A discovery may show that an old idea was in the wrong place. You picture yourself moving a puzzle piece. Your new understanding helps you ask fresh questions.

Finally, your tour brings you home to Earth. It is our home and the only planet we know that supports life. Earth has many kinds of plants and animals. They survive in different regions. We must protect the environment of our planet.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Science Is Everywhere
activities.body: We can study science in outer space and in our kitchens. A playground can also start new discoveries. Many big discoveries came from places no one expected. Science is like a big jigsaw puzzle. It never ends. Each new discovery adds a piece. New knowledge leads to more questions. Then we find more to learn.
keyPoints: We can study science in many places.
Discoveries can start in places no one expects.
Every discovery adds to science.
activities.explanation: Science is all around us. Each discovery helps us learn more.

The child should keep finding out. Science is like a big puzzle that never ends.

activities.title: Discoveries Change Our View
activities.body: New discoveries can show that an old idea was wrong. They can change how we understand the world. Earth is our home. It is the only planet we know that supports life. We must protect its environment. Earth has many kinds of plants and animals. They live in different regions.
keyPoints: Discoveries can correct old ideas.
We must protect Earth's environment.
Plants and animals live in different regions.
activities.explanation: New discoveries can change what we understand. They help us protect our home.

lessons.title: Water, Materials and Scientific Questions

activities.prompt: How does water change when it gets very cold or very hot?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water and Material Mysteries
activities.body:
You begin with a rainy-day puddle. It makes you curious about rain. You can ask why and how it rains. You also know that you need both food and water to survive.

Now you explore water and its changes. It freezes into ice when it is cooled. It boils and becomes steam when it is heated. You may enjoy cool water in summer and warm water in winter.

These changes lead you to another question. How can we tell how hot something is? Understanding hot and cold helps us know this. Measuring temperature is important during a fever.

Next, you look around your home. Many everyday objects are made from different materials. You wonder whether different objects use different materials. Science helps you work out how to separate them.

Finally, you think about science. Science is not only about memorising facts and figures. It helps you ask questions and find answers. You can keep asking questions and seeking answers.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Water, heat and materials
activities.body: We need food and water to survive. A puddle can make us curious about rain. We can ask why and how it rains. Water becomes ice when cooled and steam when heated. Hot and cold show how hot things are. Measuring how hot something is matters during a fever. Materials are the things used to make objects. Science helps separate materials. Science is not only about memorising facts and figures.
keyPoints: Food and water help us survive.
Cooling and heating change water.
Science helps us ask questions and separate materials.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how questions help us understand water, materials and science.

activities.prompt: Some water is cooled while other water is heated. What changes should be expected, and why?
steps: The cooled water should freeze into ice because cooling makes water change in this way.
The heated water should boil and become steam because heating makes water change in this other way.
The results differ because one part of the water is cooled while the other is heated.
So water changes differently depending on whether it is cooled or heated.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Asking scientific questions
activities.body: A rainy-day puddle can make us curious. We can then ask why and how it rains. We can also ask whether different objects are made from different materials. Science helps us separate materials. Separating means setting different materials apart. Science is not only about memorising facts and figures.
keyPoints: Curiosity can lead us to ask why and how.
Objects can be made from different materials.
Science includes ways to separate materials.
activities.explanation: Good questions help us explore water, materials and science.

activities.prompt: What do we need to survive? (stay alive)

activities.explanation: We need food and water to survive. These are our two basic needs.

activities.prompt: A child sees a puddle on a rainy day. The child wants to know more about rain. Which question should the child ask?

why.Why do we need food and water?: This asks about food and water. It is not about rain.

options: Find out how to separate the materials.
Guess how to separate them without checking.

why.Guess how to separate them without check: This is wrong. Guessing is not science.
This is wrong. Science is not only about remembering facts.

activities.explanation: Science helps us find out how to separate different materials.

lessons.title: Finding Answers with Guesses and Tests

activities.prompt: How can you find out why your pen stops writing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Pen Problem
activities.body:
You might not notice when you are finding an answer. Finding answers is something you have already been doing. You use this skill whenever you wonder what has happened.

Now imagine that your pen stops writing. You have a problem to investigate. First, you ask yourself why the pen has stopped writing. One possible answer is that the ink has finished.

Next, you open the pen to check whether the ink has finished. If you find an empty ink refill, your guess was correct. The empty refill gives you the answer you needed.

However, if the ink is not finished, you need another possible answer. You might guess that the ink has dried up. You test this new guess by trying something else.

The pen problem shows you how science works. You ask, make a guess, and then test it. A test helps you find out whether your answer is right.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How We Find Answers
activities.body: We often find answers without noticing it. A pen has stopped writing. This is a problem to solve. First, ask why it stopped writing. One possible answer is that the ink has run out. Open the pen to check. An empty refill tells us our guess was right. If not, try another answer. The ink might have dried up. Test this new guess.
keyPoints: We often find answers without noticing.
We ask why a problem has happened.
We check a guess and try another if needed.
activities.explanation: Nice work! The pen shows how guessing, checking and trying again help us find answers.

activities.prompt: A pen has stopped writing. What could be wrong?
steps: A pen stops writing. This is a problem to look into.
We ask why. We make a guess: the ink has finished.
We open the pen to test our guess. An empty refill means our guess was right.
If the ink is not finished, we make a new guess. Maybe the ink has dried up. We test this new guess. This is how science works.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: We often find answers without knowing we are doing it.
activities.explanation: Yes! We already find answers, often without knowing it.

activities.prompt: The pen has stopped writing. What should we ask first?
options: Why did the pen stop writing?
Which pen should we buy?
How should we clean the pen?
What should we write next?
activities.explanation: Good choice! We first ask why the pen has stopped writing.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the right step in the pen test.
pairs: Why did the pen stop writing?
activities.explanation: Good! Each clue matches a step in the pen test.

activities.prompt: An empty ink refill tells us that our guess was ______.
activities.hint: Open the pen and check the refill.
activities.explanation: Exactly! An empty ink refill tells us that our guess was correct.

activities.prompt: The ink is not finished. What should we do next?
options: Keep the first guess and stop checking.
Choose an answer without testing it.
Stop investigating the pen.
Try another possible answer and test it.
activities.explanation: Well done! If the ink is not finished, we need another possible answer.

activities.prompt: An empty ink refill shows that the dried-up guess was correct.
activities.explanation: Good check! The empty refill supports the guess that the ink has finished.

activities.prompt: Put the pen investigation steps in the correct order.
items: Ask why the pen stopped writing
Guess that the ink has finished
Open the pen to check
If the refill is empty, the guess is right
If the ink is not finished, try another guess and test it
activities.explanation: Excellent! The steps go from a question to guesses, checks, and another test.

activities.prompt: How does the pen problem show how science works?
options: It uses guessing instead of checking.
It always takes the first possible answer.
It checks a guess and tries again when needed.
It finds answers without noticing any problem.
activities.explanation: Great thinking! The problem uses a guess, a check, and another test.

activities.prompt: A pen stops writing while a child is doing homework. The child opens it and sees that the ink refill is empty. What should the child conclude?
options: The ink has now finished.
The ink might have dried up.
The pen needs another test.
The pen is working very well.

Drying up is a different guess, not the one this check confirms.
The empty refill has already checked the correct guess.
A stopped pen shows a problem, not that the pen is working well.

activities.explanation: An empty refill shows that the ink-finished guess was right.

activities.prompt: Which order shows how science works in the pen problem?
options: Ask, guess, test, then guess again.
Test first, then make no guess.
Make one guess and never check it.
Ask, but do not test the answer.

The pen problem starts with asking why, before a guess.
One guess that is never checked does not show science.
Asking why but not testing leaves the guess unchecked.

activities.explanation: Science starts by asking why, making a guess, and testing it.

lessons.title: The Scientific Method

activities.prompt: What could you discover on a little science adventure?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Scientific Method Tour
activities.body:
You notice something interesting or puzzling. Observation makes you wonder and think of a question. You turn that wonder into a clear question. Your curiosity begins the scientific method.

Next, you guess a possible answer. You test that guess through experiments or further observations. Testing comes after your guess.

The scientific method helps you work through a problem. Scientists follow it to solve problems and discover new things. Anyone who follows it works like a scientist.

Ordinary life can include this method too. A cook may use it while wondering why dal has spilled. A bicycle repairer may look for the reason that a tyre is flat.

You can use the method in science and in everyday life. It helps people solve problems or find new things. When you follow its steps, you work like a scientist.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How scientists solve problems
activities.body: Scientists solve problems in steps. First, you notice something. It is interesting or puzzling. This makes you wonder. You think of a question. Then you make the question clear. You guess a possible answer. Next, you test your guess. Use experiments or more observations. This helps people solve problems. It also helps them find new things.
keyPoints: Noticing something makes us wonder and ask a question.
We make the question clear. We guess a possible answer.
We test the guess with experiments or more observations.
activities.explanation: Scientists turn wonder into clear questions and tested guesses.

activities.title: Test a guess with a pendulum

tasks.say: I guess a short string swings quickly. Set it to 10 cm and watch.
tasks.then: The short pendulum swings quickly.

tasks.say: Now set the string to 100 cm and test your guess again.
tasks.then: The longer string swings more slowly.

activities.takeaway: By observing, guessing, and changing one thing to test the guess, we can find the answer.
activities.explanation: By observing, guessing, and changing one thing to test the guess, we can find the answer.

activities.prompt: Why is a bicycle tyre flat?
steps: A bicycle repairer sees a flat tyre. This is something puzzling. It starts the scientific method.
The repairer wonders about it. Then the wonder becomes a clear question: Why is the tyre flat?
Next, the repairer guesses a possible answer.
The repairer tests the guess with an experiment or more observation.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The starting point
activities.prompt: The scientific method starts by observing something interesting or hard to explain.
activities.explanation: Observing something interesting or hard to explain starts the scientific method.

activities.title: Make the wonder clear
activities.prompt: Scientists make a clear ______ from their wonder.
activities.hint: We make our wonder clear before guessing.
activities.explanation: We make a clear question before we guess an answer.

activities.title: Match the steps
activities.prompt: Match each scientific method step to its description.
pairs: Observe something interesting or hard to explain
Turn your wondering into a clear question
activities.explanation: The method goes from observing, to a clear question, to a guess, to testing.

activities.title: What the method can do
activities.prompt: What can the scientific method help people do?
options: Stop after guessing
Skip the clear question
Solve problems or find new things

activities.explanation: Scientists follow it to solve problems and discover new things.

activities.title: Put the method in order
activities.prompt: Put these scientific method steps in the right order.
items: Observe something interesting or puzzling
Turn the wonder into a clear question
Guess a possible answer
Test the guess through experiments or further observations
activities.explanation: The order goes from seeing and asking to guessing and testing.

activities.title: Only for science?
activities.prompt: The scientific method is only for science. It is not for daily life.
activities.explanation: The method is useful in daily life too, not only in science.

activities.prompt: A cook sees dal on the floor. What should the cook do next?
options: Ask why the dal spilled.
Guess the cause without asking.
Test the floor before wondering.
Decide the cause without checking.

This skips making a clear question first.
This tests too early. The wonder and question come first.
This decides the cause, but nothing was tested.

activities.explanation: This turns the cook's wonder into a clear question. The method needs this.

activities.prompt: A child finds a toy in a strange place. Which step of the scientific method comes next?
options: Ask a clear question about why it is there.
Decide the cause without wondering.
Test a cause before you look at the toy.
Choose a cause and skip testing.

This skips wondering and asking a question.
Testing cannot come before looking and asking a question.
Skipping the test means the guess is not checked.

activities.explanation: A clear question comes after looking. It shows the child's wonder.

lessons.title: A Scientific Journey Together

activities.prompt: What could we discover if we started our science journey together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey of Wonder
activities.body:
You begin your science journey with a simple wonder. Something around you catches your attention. You pause and observe your surroundings carefully. Curiosity leads you to ask how and why questions.

Curiosity is the first and foremost quality for learning science. You use the scientific method in daily-life situations. You apply it to some extent, just as all of us do. Your learning journey starts with this useful habit.

Learning science develops your ability to find solutions. Your questions lead you towards many unknown things waiting for you to explore. You keep observing carefully. Curiosity keeps guiding your learning.

Science helps you solve bigger problems and mysteries of the universe. Scientific work is rarely done by one person alone. Scientists often work together in large teams. Perhaps your classmates join your exploration.

Together, you share the work of exploration. Science should be a joyful journey of exploration. You keep asking how and why. Many unknown things wait for your curiosity.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Science Is a Shared Journey
activities.body: We often use the scientific method in daily life. We all use it a little. Curiosity is the most important quality for learning science. Curiosity means wanting to know things. It helps us ask how and why questions. We should observe (watch carefully) our surroundings. We should explore the many things we do not know. Scientists rarely work alone. So teamwork matters. Science helps us find solutions and solve big problems. It also helps us explore the mysteries of the universe. Science should be a joyful journey.
keyPoints: Use the scientific method in daily life.
Be curious and ask how and why questions.
Observe, explore, solve, and work together.
Enjoy science as a joyful journey.
activities.explanation: Curiosity, careful watching and teamwork make science a shared journey.

activities.prompt: You notice a mark on a wall and wonder what made it.
steps: Observe the wall carefully, because we should study our surroundings closely.
Ask how and why it happened, because curiosity leads us to ask useful questions.
Explore the question with others, because scientific work is rarely done by one person alone.
Keep learning together with joy, because science helps us find solutions and many unknowns are waiting to be explored.

options: In everyday life
Only for big mysteries
Only for science teams

activities.prompt: We should ______ the things around us carefully.

activities.prompt: Curiosity is the first and foremost quality for learning science.
activities.explanation: Curiosity is the first and foremost quality for learning science.

activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.

Avoid asking questions

activities.prompt: Which choice shows the best way to think about science?
options: Stop asking how and why questions
Keep every mystery a secret
Stay curious, explore, and enjoy science

activities.explanation: Curiosity guides our questions. Exploring should be fun. Science work often needs teamwork.

activities.prompt: Four students notice different things about one question. No student knows everything. What should they do next?
options: Share notes and study together.
Keep notes apart and study alone.
Pick one clue and ignore the rest.
Wait for one student to find it all.

Working alone means they do not share ideas.
Ignoring clues wastes what the group has found.
Waiting for one person does not use team work.

activities.explanation: Working together is right. Science is often done by big teams.

activities.prompt: A class asks a how-and-why question. The class explores it as a team. What might happen?
options: They may find answers and more to explore.
They will have no more questions about science.
They will solve every mystery in the universe.
They will lose the fun of exploring together.

why.They will have no more questions about s: This wrongly thinks one answer ends all questions.
why.They will solve every mystery in the uni: This wrongly says one class can answer every mystery.
why.They will lose the fun of exploring toge: This wrongly thinks teamwork takes away the fun.

activities.explanation: Learning science helps us find answers. Many unknown things are still left to explore.

activities.prompt: A student says: 'I worked alone once. So science never needs a team.' Which reply is best?
options: Scientists often work in big teams.
If one person starts, the work must stay alone.
Teamwork only matters after all answers are found.
One person always knows the whole answer.

why.If one person starts, the work must stay: This mixes up one person working alone with a rule for all science.
why.Teamwork only matters after all answers: This says teamwork comes too late in science work.
why.One person always knows the whole answer: This thinks one person's effort gives all the science knowledge.

activities.explanation: This is right. Science is rarely done by one person alone.

activities.context: A student looks closely at grains of sand. The student then watches a huge mountain and asks how it is so large. While looking at the night sky, the student wonders why the stars shine. Later, the student notices a flower opening and wonders how it knows when to open. These questions make the student want to observe, explore, and investigate. The student thinks of science as a big adventure, with always something new and exciting to discover in nature.
activities.prompt: After noticing the sand grains and the mountain, what should the student do next to continue exploring the questions?
options: Observe the sand and mountain closely, then explore the questions they raise.
Stop looking at nature because the questions have already been answered.
Look only at the mountain and treat the sand as unimportant.
Wait for nature to provide answers without observing or thinking.

why.Stop looking at nature because the quest: Mistake: Curiosity makes the student keep asking and exploring questions.
why.Look only at the mountain and treat the: Mistake: Science can explore tiny grains of sand as well as huge mountains.
why.Wait for nature to provide answers witho: Mistake: Science involves thinking, observing, and doing things rather than only waiting.

activities.explanation: Correct: Close observation and exploration help the student continue investigating.

activities.context: A student looks closely at grains of sand. The student then watches a huge mountain and asks how it is so large. While looking at the night sky, the student wonders why the stars shine. Later, the student notices a flower opening and wonders how it knows when to open. activities.prompt: If the student notices another flower opening, what best shows a curious scientist?
options: Observe the flower and ask what makes it open at that time.
Leave it alone because nature does not need to be explored.
Study only the mountain because huge things are more useful to science.
Stop asking questions because the student has already seen a flower open.

why.Leave it alone because nature does not n: Mistake: Curiosity encourages exploration of things in nature.
why.Study only the mountain because huge thi: Mistake: Science can explore tiny objects as well as huge mountains.
why.Stop asking questions because the studen: Mistake: Seeing one example does not remove the reason to keep asking questions.

activities.explanation: Correct: The student observes carefully and asks a new question about the flower.

activities.prompt: Explain why curiosity is the most important quality for science.
activities.answer: Curiosity is the most important quality because science is a big adventure in which we ask questions and explore. It helps us notice tiny grains of sand and huge mountains, wonder why the stars shine, and find something new and exciting in nature. Curiosity keeps us ready to observe and understand the world.
points: States that curiosity is the most important quality
Explains that science involves asking questions and exploring
Uses examples such as sand, mountains, or stars
Connects curiosity with observing and discovering new things

activities.context: While helping her family prepare dishes from different parts of India, Meera wondered what the food was made of. Science could help her find out, just as science can be studied in outer space and in our kitchens. During a visit to the playground, she learned that discoveries can begin there too. She also understood that many groundbreaking discoveries come from unexpected places. Each new discovery added another piece to the endless science puzzle and led to more questions.
activities.prompt: After Meera uses new knowledge to explain one dish, what would be a likely next step in her learning?
options: She may use the new knowledge to decide what to investigate next.
She may treat the science puzzle as completely solved.
She may stop investigating because one explanation is enough.
She may expect discoveries only when she goes into outer space.

why.She may treat the science puzzle as comp: One discovery does not complete the science puzzle.
why.She may stop investigating because one e: One answer is a beginning, not an end to learning.
why.She may expect discoveries only when she: Science discoveries can begin in many places, including playgrounds.

activities.explanation: New knowledge leads to further questions and things to find out.

activities.context: While helping her family prepare dishes from different parts of India, Meera wondered what the food was made of. activities.prompt: If a discovery shows that an old idea was in the wrong place, what could result?
options: People may understand how the world works in a different way.
The old idea would become more secure.
The science puzzle would have to stop growing.
The discovery would matter only for the old idea and nothing else.

A discovery showing an error would not strengthen the old idea.
why.The science puzzle would have to stop gr: Each discovery adds another piece rather than stopping the puzzle.
why.The discovery would matter only for the: A changed understanding can affect much more than one old idea.

activities.explanation: New discoveries can change our understanding of the world.

activities.prompt: How does the science-puzzle idea explain why learning does not really end?
activities.answer: Science is like a huge jigsaw puzzle that never ends. Each new discovery adds another piece, so our knowledge grows. New knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out. This continuing process shows why learning can keep leading us toward further discoveries.
points: Science is compared with a never-ending jigsaw puzzle.
Every discovery adds another piece to knowledge.
New knowledge produces more questions and further investigation.

activities.context: On a rainy day, a child watched water gather in a puddle and wondered why and how it rains. At home, the child cooled a cup of water and noticed that it froze into ice. Later, the child heated water until it boiled and became steam. The child checked how hot a forehead felt during a fever. In the kitchen, the child wondered whether spoons and cups were made from different materials and asked how science could help separate them.
activities.prompt: Why was checking how hot the forehead felt useful during the child's fever?
options: It helps determine how hot the forehead is.
It helps identify the material of the forehead.
It helps measure the amount of water in the puddle.
It helps measure how much the forehead weighs.

why.It helps identify the material of the fo: Identifying a material is a different kind of question.
why.It helps measure the amount of water in: The puddle's water is not connected to measuring the forehead.
why.It helps measure how much the forehead w: Weighing the forehead does not measure its hotness.

activities.explanation: Understanding hot and cold helps us know how hot something is.

activities.context: On a rainy day, a child watched water gather in a puddle and wondered why and how it rains. At home, the child cooled a cup of water and noticed that it froze into ice. Later, the child heated water until it boiled and became steam. The child checked how hot a forehead felt during a fever. In the kitchen, the child wondered whether spoons and cups were made from different materials and asked how science could help separate them.
activities.prompt: What should the child do next to find out how the materials in the spoons and cups could be separated?
options: Try to find a scientific way to separate the materials.
Guess without asking any scientific questions.
Assume that every object is made from the same material.
Memorise facts without investigating them.

why.Guess without asking any scientific ques: A guess does not show how the materials can be separated.
why.Assume that every object is made from th: Different everyday objects can be made from different materials.
why.Memorise facts without investigating the: Science is not only about memorising facts and figures.

activities.prompt: Explain how cooling and heating change water.
activities.answer: Cooling water causes it to freeze into ice. Heating water causes it to boil and become steam. Therefore, cooling and heating lead to different changes in water.

Heating makes water boil.

activities.context: A student noticed that a pen had stopped writing. The student first wondered why this had happened. One possible answer was that the ink had finished. The pen was opened, and the empty ink refill showed that this guess was correct. The student then saw that this small investigation was an example of how science works.
activities.prompt: If the ink refill were not finished, what should the student do next?
options: Form another possible explanation and test it.
Keep the first explanation even though the check did not support it.
Close the pen and decide that no answer can be found.
Open the pen repeatedly without considering another explanation.

why.Keep the first explanation even though t: The empty-refill check would not support the first explanation.
why.Close the pen and decide that no answer: Science involves testing possible answers rather than giving up.
why.Open the pen repeatedly without consider: Repeated opening would not test a different possible answer.

activities.explanation: This follows the next step when the first guess is not correct.

activities.context: A student noticed that a pen had stopped writing. The student first wondered why this had happened. One possible answer was that the ink had finished. The pen was opened, and the empty ink refill showed that this guess was correct. The student then saw that this small investigation was an example of how science works.
activities.prompt: After the refill is found to be empty, what does this tell the student about the first possible answer?
options: It is supported and can be accepted as correct.
It is disproved, so another possible answer is needed.
It is neither supported nor disproved.
It shows that the dried-up guess was correct.

why.It is disproved, so another possible ans: The opposite conclusion does not agree with the result of the check.
The result gives support to the first explanation.
why.It shows that the dried-up guess was cor: The empty refill supports the ink-finished explanation, not the dried-up explanation.

activities.explanation: An empty refill supports the explanation that the ink had finished.

activities.prompt: Why does testing a guess help someone find an answer?
activities.answer: A guess is only one possible answer to a problem. Testing it gives evidence for or against it. In the pen case, opening the pen checked whether the ink had finished. The empty refill supported that guess, while ink that was not finished would lead to another possible answer and another test.
points: A guess is one possible answer.
A test checks whether the guess is supported.
The empty refill supported the ink-finished guess.
An unfinished refill would require another possible answer.

Stop because a possible answer may already be correct.
Think about the spill again without checking the guess.
Make another guess without testing either answer.

why.Stop because a possible answer may alrea: A possible answer is not certain, so it should not be accepted without checking.
why.Think about the spill again without chec: Thinking again does not test the proposed explanation.
why.Make another guess without testing eithe: Another guess also needs to be checked.

activities.context: A cook sees dal spilled on the kitchen floor and finds it puzzling. The cook wonders what caused the spill and turns this wondering into the clear question of why the dal spilled. why.It shows that only scientists can use th: Anyone who follows the method works like a scientist.

activities.answer: The cook observes the spilled dal and wonders what caused it. Wondering becomes a clear question, followed by a possible answer. why.Wait for someone else to explore the que: Waiting alone does not help the student explore.

activities.context: When a light in the classroom is switched off, the room becomes dark. A student wonders why the switch works this way and watches carefully instead of accepting the first idea. options: It helps the student explore, learn, and find solutions

activities.answer: Trying alone may provide only one person’s ideas and observations. Working with a team allows people to share ideas, observe carefully, and ask how and why questions together. lessons.title: Seeing Diversity Around Us

activities.prompt: What wonders might you discover on a quiet nature walk?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Walk Full of Life
activities.body:
You begin your nature walk by looking closely at what lives nearby. You see grasses, bushes and large trees. The walk helps you experience the beauty and variety of plants and animals. You observe living creatures without disturbing them.

Listen carefully, and each bird offers its own unique chirp. Look at leaves, too. Their shapes differ. Their arrangements on stems or branches also differ.

Stop beside flowers and compare their colours, shapes and scents. Notice how flowers can look or smell different from each other. Now watch where animals live. Some stay on land, while others live in trees. Frogs can live both on land and in water. You see animals living in different places.

As the walk continues, you notice the variety of plants and animals around you. This variety forms part of the region's biodiversity. You see that plants and animals depend on one another. The walk has helped you experience nature's beauty and variety.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Many Kinds of Nature
activities.body: A nature walk helps you see many plants and animals. Watch them, but do not bother them. You can see grass, bushes and big trees. Each bird sings in its own way. Leaves and flowers look different. Frogs can live on land and in water. The variety of life in a place is called biodiversity. Plants and animals need each other.
keyPoints: Watch living things without bothering them.
Leaves and flowers look different.
Plants and animals need each other.
activities.explanation: Nature has many differences. We should always be kind to living things.

activities.prompt: During a nature walk, a student sees grasses, bushes, large trees, flowers, birds, and a frog. What should the student notice, and how should the student behave?
steps: The student should notice the grasses, bushes, and large trees because the walk shows that plant life is not all alike.
The student should compare the leaves and flowers because leaves differ in shape and arrangement, while flowers differ in colour, shape, and scent.

The student should watch the animals quietly and note where they live because some live on land, some live in trees, and frogs can live in both land and water, while all living creatures should not be disturbed.
The varied plant and animal life is part of the region's biodiversity, and the student should remember that plants and animals depend on one another.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You see a living thing on a walk. What should you do?
options: Bother it to watch it move
Watch it without bothering it
Pick it up for a short time
Make noise next to it
activities.explanation: Living things should be watched without bothering them.

activities.prompt: A frog can live on ______ and in water.
activities.hint: Think about the two places a frog can live.
activities.explanation: Frogs can live on land and in water.

activities.prompt: Match each living thing with its feature or home.
pairs: Shape and arrangement on stems or branches
Living on land and in water
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a living thing with a feature or home.

activities.prompt: Put these plants from smallest to largest.
items: Grasses
Bushes
Large trees
activities.explanation: Grasses are smallest. Bushes are bigger. Large trees are biggest.

activities.prompt: You see many kinds of plants and animals in one area. What is this called?
options: Dependence
Chirp
Arrangement
Biodiversity
activities.explanation: The many kinds of plants and animals in an area make up its biodiversity.

activities.prompt: A frog moves from the edge of a pond onto wet ground. Which guess makes sense?
options: It can live in both places, because frogs live on land and in water.
It can live only in the pond, because frogs must always swim.
It can live only on land, because frogs cannot stay in water.
It cannot live in either place, because frogs must live in trees.

why.It can live only in the pond, because fr: This answer is wrong. It thinks a frog must always be in water.
why.It can live only on land, because frogs: This answer is wrong. It thinks a frog cannot go into water.
why.It cannot live in either place, because: This answer is wrong. It mixes up a frog with an animal that lives in trees.

activities.explanation: This is right. Frogs can live on land and in water.

activities.prompt: A student wants to compare how the leaves are arranged on two branches. What is the best way?
options: Look at both branches and compare leaf shapes and arrangement.
Pick one leaf from each branch and hide the stems.
Count only the flowers on both branches. Ignore the leaves.
Touch the leaves so their shapes and places are clearer.

why.Pick one leaf from each branch and hide: This is wrong. One leaf cannot show how all the leaves are arranged.
This is wrong. Flowers are not leaves.
why.Touch the leaves so their shapes and pla: This is wrong. Touching the plant does not help us observe it.

activities.explanation: This is right. Leaves can be different in shape and in arrangement on stems or branches.

activities.prompt: Two flowers look alike at first. Which observation best checks how they differ?
options: Compare their colours, their shapes, and their scents.
Compare only their colours because colour shows every difference.
Compare only their shapes because flowers never vary in scent.
Compare their scents alone because flowers do not vary in shape.

why.Compare only their colours because colou: This mistake comes from checking one feature and ignoring the others.
why.Compare only their shapes because flower: This mistake comes from thinking shape is the only feature that can differ.
why.Compare their scents alone because flowe: This mistake comes from thinking scent is the only feature that can differ.

activities.explanation: This is right because flowers can differ in colour, shape, and scent.

activities.prompt: A class hears two birds. They cannot see the birds. What can the class expect?
options: Each bird may have its own special chirp.
Both birds must make the same chirp.
Only the bird in the tree can chirp.
Birds on the ground never chirp.

This mistake comes from thinking all birds make the same sound.
This mistake comes from thinking only birds in trees can chirp.
This mistake comes from thinking birds on the ground never chirp.

activities.explanation: This is right. Each bird has its own special chirp.

lessons.title: Grouping Plants and Animals

activities.prompt: What can we learn by grouping the plants and animals around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Grouping Plants and Animals
activities.body:
You begin a gentle tour of the plant and animal groups around you. Why are living things placed in different groups? We will look at the features that guide these groupings.

Plants can be grouped by height. Plant stems vary in thickness, height and hardness. You may see trees, which are tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems. Flowers also guide grouping. Their presence or absence helps you sort plants.

Shrubs have hard woody stems that branch close to the ground. Herbs are usually small plants with soft and green stems. Climbers have weak stems and need support to climb and grow. Creepers grow along the ground.

Animals may be grouped by food, place, colour and movement. As you look around, ask what an animal eats. Notice where it stays. Check its colour. Watch its movement.

Grouping makes plants and animals easier to understand and study. By noticing similarities and differences, you can compare each group. Sorting plants and animals gives you a clearer way to learn about them.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Different Features Make Groups
activities.body: We can group plants and animals by similarities and differences. Different groups may use different features. Plants can be grouped by height. They can also be grouped by whether they have flowers. Animals may be grouped by food, place, colour and movement. Grouping helps people study plants and animals more easily.
keyPoints: Groups can use similarities and differences.
Plants may be grouped by height or flowers.
Animals may be grouped by food, place, colour and movement.
activities.explanation: Different features help us make useful groups.

activities.prompt: Three plants are mixed together. One is tall. Its stem is hard, thick, brown and woody. One has weak stems. It needs support. One grows along the ground. How should you group them?
steps: Group the plants by their stems and how they grow. Different groups may look at different parts.
Put the tall plant with trees. It has a hard, thick, brown, woody stem like a tree.
Put the plant with weak stems with climbers. Weak stems need support to climb.
Put the plant that grows on the ground with creepers. This makes the groups clear and easy to study.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Plant Groups and Their Stems
activities.body: Plant stems vary in thickness, height and hardness. Trees are tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems. Shrubs have hard woody stems that branch close to the ground. Herbs are usually small plants with soft and green stems. Climbers have weak stems and need support. Creepers grow along the ground.
keyPoints: Trees have hard, thick, brown and woody stems.
Herbs are usually small with soft and green stems.
Climbers need support, while creepers grow along the ground.
activities.explanation: Stem and growth features help us recognise plant groups.

activities.prompt: Which feature can be used to group plants?
options: Height
Food
Movement
Colour
activities.explanation: Plant height can be used as a basis for grouping plants.

activities.prompt: Trees are tall plants with hard, thick, brown and ______ stems.
activities.hint: This word describes the hard stems of trees.
activities.explanation: Trees are tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems.

activities.prompt: Animals may be grouped by food, place, colour and movement.
activities.explanation: These are all features used for grouping animals.

activities.prompt: Match each plant group with its feature.
pairs: Tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems
Hard woody stems with branches near the ground
Usually small plants with soft green stems
Weak stems that need help to climb and grow
activities.explanation: Each plant group has a special stem or growth feature.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order.
items: Pick features to group by
Group things by what is alike and what is different
Understand the groups and study them more easily
activities.explanation: Features can help us group things. Groups make study easier.

activities.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a plant group with its stem feature?
options: Climbers — weak stems needing support
Trees — soft green stems
Herbs — stems branching close to the ground
Creepers — hard, thick, brown stems
activities.explanation: Climbers have weak stems and need support to climb and grow.

activities.prompt: One plant has a tall, hard, thick, brown stem. Another plant has a small, soft, green stem. Why are they in different groups?
options: Their stems differ in height, thickness, hardness and colour.
Their stems are the same, so the groups must match.
Only flowers can tell these two plants apart.
Their heights match, so stem features do not matter.

why.Their stems are the same, so the groups: This wrongly says both plants have the same stems.
why.Only flowers can tell these two plants a: This wrongly says only flowers can tell them apart.
why.Their heights match, so stem features do: This wrongly says matching height makes stems useless.

activities.explanation: The two plants have very different stems.

activities.prompt: A weak-stemmed plant is placed near a support so it can reach upward. What is the likely result, and why?
options: It climbs the support, because it needs support.
It creeps along the ground, because weak stems stay low.
It grows a thick woody stem, because support makes stems hard.
It stays the same height, because weak stems cannot grow.

why.It creeps along the ground, because weak: This mistake confuses a climber with a creeper.
why.It grows a thick woody stem, because sup: This mistake assumes support can make a weak stem hard and woody.
why.It stays the same height, because weak s: This mistake assumes a weak stem cannot grow at all.

activities.explanation: This is right because weak stems need support to climb and grow.

activities.prompt: Two plants are the same height. One has flowers. One has no flowers. A child says, 'They must be in the same group.' Is this fair?
options: No; their flowers can set them apart.
Yes; same height decides every group.
No; every plant group needs different heights.
Yes; flowers never matter for groups.

This mistake thinks height is the only rule for grouping.
why.No; every plant group needs different he: This mistake thinks every group must differ in every way.
This mistake believes flowers are never useful.

activities.explanation: This is right because flowers can group plants, even if they are the same height.

activities.prompt: One class groups animals by food. Another class groups them by where they live. Why can both ways be good?
options: Animal groups can use different useful features.
Only one feature can be used for animal groups.
Food cannot be used if place is also used.
Both classes must group animals by how they move.

why.Only one feature can be used for animal: This mistake thinks all groups must use one feature.
why.Food cannot be used if place is also use: This mistake thinks two features cannot be used together.
why.Both classes must group animals by how t: This mistake thinks movement is the only useful feature.

activities.explanation: This is right. Animal groups can use food, place, colour, or movement.

activities.prompt: A plant has hard, woody stems. They branch close to the ground. Which change would make the stems like a tree, not a shrub?
options: The stem gets tall and thick.
The stems keep branching near the ground.
The stems get small, soft, and green.
The stem gets weak and bends easily.

why.The stems keep branching near the ground: This mistake keeps the stem of a shrub.
This mistake changes the stem to fit herbs.
This mistake changes the stem to fit climbers.

activities.explanation: This is right because trees have tall, thick, woody stems.

activities.prompt: A class sorts many plants and animals into groups. What shows that sorting helped them study?
options: They can compare members in each group more clearly.
They can forget all differences between members.
They can put all members into one big group.
They can stop studying members in each group.

why.They can forget all differences between: This mistake thinks grouping removes all differences inside groups.
why.They can put all members into one big gr: This mistake thinks grouping should put everything into one group.
why.They can stop studying members in each g: This mistake thinks stopping the study shows better understanding.

activities.explanation: This is right. Grouping makes plants and animals easier to understand and study.

lessons.sceneCaption: A side-by-side comparison shows two similar plants with differently shaped bracts.

sceneCredit.creator: Christian Fischer

funFacts: Lotus flowers grow in muddy water, but their petals stay clean and dry.
Bamboo is not a tree. It is a giant grass.
Penguins cannot fly, but they are great swimmers in the sea.

lessons.title: Leaves, Roots and Seeds

activities.prompt: What might leaves, roots and seeds reveal together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Leaves, Roots and Seeds
activities.body:
You begin your plant tour by looking closely at leaves. You may notice thin lines on the leaves of many plants. This arrangement of veins is called venation.

Some leaves have a net-like pattern of veins. This pattern is called reticulate venation. Other leaves have veins that run side by side. This arrangement shows parallel venation.

Now turn your attention from leaves to roots. The main root of a plant is called a taproot. A bunch of similar-sized thin roots is called fibrous roots. Plants with reticulate venation generally have taproots. Plants with parallel venation generally have fibrous roots.

Your tour now reaches a chickpea seed. Each part of the seed is called a cotyledon. Plants whose seeds have two cotyledons are called dicotyledons. A maize seed has one thin cotyledon. Plants with seeds like those of maize are called monocotyledons. Dicotyledons generally have reticulate venation and taproot systems. Now you can compare a plant's leaves, roots and seeds.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Patterns in Leaves, Roots and Seeds
activities.body: Many plant leaves have thin lines. The pattern of these lines is called venation. A net-like pattern is called reticulate venation. Veins that run side by side are parallel venation. Plants with net-like veins usually have taproots. Plants with parallel veins usually have fibrous roots. Each part of a chickpea seed is a cotyledon. Plants with two cotyledons are dicotyledons. A maize (corn) seed has one thin cotyledon. Plants with seeds like maize are monocotyledons.
keyPoints: Leaves have net-like or side-by-side veins.
Leaf veins usually match taproots or fibrous roots.
Cotyledons help us name dicotyledons and monocotyledons.
activities.explanation: These patterns help you sort leaves, roots and seeds.

activities.prompt: Two potted plants have leaves with different vein patterns. What roots should they have?
steps: One leaf has a net-like pattern. This is reticulate venation.
A reticulate-veined plant usually has a taproot. So the first plant should have one main root.
The other leaf has veins side by side. This is parallel venation.
A parallel-veined plant usually has fibrous roots. So the second plant should have many thin roots of similar size.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Seeds and Plant Groups
activities.body: Plants can be grouped by their seed parts. Each part of a chickpea seed is called a cotyledon. Plants with two cotyledons are called dicotyledons. A maize seed has one thin cotyledon. Plants with maize-like seeds are called monocotyledons. Dicots usually have reticulate venation and taproot systems. Parallel-veined plants usually have fibrous roots.
keyPoints: A chickpea seed has parts called cotyledons.
Two cotyledons mean a dicotyledon.
Maize-like seeds belong to monocotyledons.
activities.explanation: Seed parts and leaf patterns give useful clues about plants.

activities.title: A Leaf with a Net
activities.prompt: Imagine a leaf. Its veins make a net. Which description shows its venation (the pattern of veins)?
options: Veins joined in a net
Veins running side by side
One main root
A bunch of thin roots of about the same size
activities.explanation: A pattern like a net is called reticulate venation.

activities.title: Side-by-Side Veins
activities.prompt: Veins that run side by side show parallel venation.
activities.explanation: Yes. Side-by-side veins form a parallel venation pattern.

activities.title: The Main Root
activities.prompt: A plant's main root is called its ______.
activities.hint: This root has a special name from the lesson.
activities.explanation: A plant's main root is called a taproot.

activities.title: Match the Plant Parts
activities.prompt: Match each description to its name.
pairs: Many thin roots of the same size
activities.explanation: Each name is for a leaf pattern, root type, or seed part.

activities.title: Two Cotyledons
activities.prompt: A plant has a seed with two cotyledons. What is this plant called?
options: A monocotyledon
A dicotyledon
A taproot
A fibrous root
activities.explanation: Plants with seeds that have two cotyledons are called dicotyledons.

activities.title: Match the Leaf Pattern and Roots
activities.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a leaf's venation with its usual roots?
options: Reticulate venation — fibrous roots
Parallel venation — taproot
Reticulate venation — taproot
Parallel venation — fibrous roots
activities.explanation: Parallel-veined plants generally have fibrous roots. These roots are similar-sized and thin.

activities.prompt: A gardener sees a leaf with reticulate venation (net-like veins). Which roots does the plant usually have?
options: The plant should have a taproot.
The plant should have fibrous roots.
The plant should have both root types.
The plant's roots cannot be predicted.

This mixes up net-like veins with veins that run side by side.
This thinks one plant has both root types.
This says no guess is possible. But there is a usual link.

activities.explanation: This is right. Reticulate venation usually goes with a taproot (one big main root).

activities.prompt: A seedling grows from a seed with two cotyledons. What leaves and roots do you usually expect?
options: Net-like veins and a taproot.
Net-like veins and fibrous roots.
Side-by-side veins and a taproot.
Side-by-side veins and fibrous roots.

This gets the leaf pattern right but has the wrong root type.
This has the wrong leaf pattern but the right root type.
This reverses both usual links between leaves and roots.

activities.explanation: This is right. Two cotyledons mean a dicotyledon. It usually has reticulate venation and a taproot.

activities.prompt: A plant is pulled up. It has many thin roots of about the same size. What are its leaf veins usually like?
options: The veins make a net-like pattern.
The veins run side by side.
The veins all meet at one point.
The veins form no clear pattern.

This is wrong. Fibrous roots usually go with parallel veins.
This makes up a leaf pattern. The roots do not show it.
This thinks fibrous roots give no useful clue.

activities.explanation: This mixes up fibrous roots with reticulate venation (net-like veins).

activities.prompt: A student sees a plant with reticulate venation. The student guesses its roots. Which guess fits the lesson best?
options: It will probably have a taproot. This is a usual rule.
It will surely have a taproot every time.
It will probably have fibrous roots. This is a usual rule.
It cannot have any roots at all.

why.It will surely have a taproot every time: This makes a usual link into a sure rule.
why.It will probably have fibrous roots. Thi: This flips the usual link between veins and roots.
This says a claim with no proof is impossible.

activities.explanation: This is right. The lesson gives a usual link, not a sure rule.

lessons.sceneCaption: Reticulate venation forms a clear net-like pattern across this backlit leaf.

funFacts: The banyan tree grows roots from its branches, and they become new trunks.
Potatoes are stems, not roots, so you can grow a new plant from one.
A coconut is a fruit, and the seed is inside it.

lessons.title: Grouping Animals and Changing Surroundings

activities.prompt: What can we learn by comparing animals and their surroundings?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Animals, Regions and Protection
activities.body:
Welcome to a wildlife tour. You will group animals by looking at their bodies, movement and surroundings. Animals differ greatly from one another. Some fly, run, crawl, walk, hop or jump. Each uses different body parts to move.

Now look at fish in water. Their streamlined bodies and fins help them move. Goats live in grassy areas and use their legs to move. You can compare these animals and notice how their bodies suit their lives.

Different animals live in different surroundings. Plants and animals found in one kind of region differ from those found elsewhere. Grouping animals helps you understand their diversity.

Next, you meet Janaki Ammal, an Indian botanist who worked for environmental protection. She helped document and preserve India's rich plant biodiversity.

You then visit Silent Valley, where people opposed a hydroelectric dam across the Kunthipuzha river. Their movement succeeded in saving Silent Valley. Your tour ends with a big lesson. Animals and plants differ from one region to another. You can group animals to understand their diversity.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Animals Move in Different Ways
activities.body: Animals are very different. They move in many ways. Some fly. Some run. Some crawl, walk, hop or jump. They use different body parts to move. Grouping animals helps us understand their variety. Biodiversity means this variety of life. Different animals live in different places. Fish have smooth bodies and fins to swim. Goats live in grassy places and walk on their legs. The Silent Valley movement saved Silent Valley.
keyPoints: Animals move in different ways.
Different body parts help animals move.
Animals live in different places.
activities.explanation: Learning how animals move helps us group them.

activities.prompt: A fish and a goat are moved to a place with deep water but very little grass. Which animal is better suited to move around there, and why?
steps: The fish is better suited because its streamlined body and fins help it move in water.
The goat is less suited there because it lives in grassy areas and uses its legs to move.
This shows that different animals have different body parts and live in different surroundings.
Grouping animals by movement and surroundings helps us understand their diversity because it shows what makes them different.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Match each animal or group with how it moves.
activities.explanation: Fish use streamlined bodies and fins in water. Goats live in grass and use their legs.

activities.prompt: Why does grouping animals help us?
options: It makes all animals look the same.
It helps us understand their diversity.
It changes where every animal lives.
It makes every animal move faster.
activities.explanation: Grouping animals helps us understand their diversity. It shows how much animals differ.

activities.prompt: Put the Silent Valley story in order.
items: A dam across the Kunthipuzha river
The Silent Valley movement stood against the dam
The movement saved Silent Valley
activities.explanation: The movement stood against the dam across the Kunthipuzha river. It saved Silent Valley.

activities.prompt: A guide sees fish in water. The guide sees goats in grassy places. Which sentence is true?
options: Fish use streamlined bodies and fins in water.
Goats use streamlined bodies and fins in water.
Both animals live in the same places.
Plants and animals are the same in every place.
activities.explanation: Fish use streamlined bodies and fins in water. Goats live in grassy places and use their legs.

activities.prompt: This Indian botanist helped document and preserve India's rich plant ______.
activities.hint: Use the lesson word for the variety of life.
activities.explanation: Janaki Ammal helped document and preserve India's rich plant biodiversity. This was part of her environmental protection work.

activities.prompt: What would probably happen to a fish on dry land?
options: The fish would probably struggle on dry land.
The fish would probably swim fast on dry land.
The fish would probably hop across dry land.
The fish would probably run faster than goats.

why.The fish would probably swim fast on dry: This wrongly thinks fins help it swim on land.
why.The fish would probably hop across dry l: This wrongly thinks a fish hops like a land animal.
why.The fish would probably run faster than: This wrongly thinks a fish can run like a goat.

activities.explanation: This is right because a fish's streamlined body and fins help it move in water.

activities.prompt: A child wants to show how a fish and a goat are different. Which rule is best?
options: By the body parts they use to move.
By how many legs they have.
By the usual size of each animal.
By the kind of food they usually eat.

This counts only legs. It misses the fish's fins.
This thinks size is the useful clue, not body parts.
This says food explains how they move, not body parts.

activities.explanation: This is right because different animals use different body parts to move.

activities.prompt: Which way is fairest to compare how fish and goats suit their surroundings?
options: Watch each animal in its usual surroundings.
Watch both animals in a dry, empty room.
Ask each animal to move without water or grass.
Compare them only by how fast they move.

This takes away the water and grass they need.
why.Ask each animal to move without water or: This changes both animals' surroundings. So the test is not fair.
This compares only speed. It ignores how body parts and surroundings help.

activities.explanation: This is right. It keeps each animal in surroundings that suit it.

activities.prompt: The Silent Valley movement opposed a dam that makes power from water. If the movement had failed, what most likely could have happened?
options: A dam could cross the Kunthipuzha river.
The Kunthipuzha river could have disappeared.
Silent Valley could have gained many more goats.
India's plant biodiversity could have disappeared.

why.The Kunthipuzha river could have disappe: This mistake thinks a dam would remove the whole river.
why.Silent Valley could have gained many mor: This mistake links a dam to goats. There is no link.
why.India's plant biodiversity could have di: This mistake thinks one dam would make all of India's plant biodiversity disappear.

activities.explanation: This is right. The movement opposed a dam across the Kunthipuzha river.

Kingfishers dive headfirst into water to catch fish.

lessons.title: Adaptations and Habitats

activities.prompt: How do plants and animals stay alive in different places?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Surviving in Different Habitats
activities.body:
Imagine that you are visiting different habitats. You soon notice that each place has its own needs. A habitat is where plants and animals live. It provides food, water, air, shelter, and other needs for survival.

Now, step into a hot desert. Very little water is available here. Desert plants store water in their fleshy stems. These helpful features let plants and animals survive in a region. Such features are called adaptations.

Next, meet a hot-desert camel. It has long legs and wide hooves. It has one hump, and it does not sweat. These adaptations help it live where very little water is available.

Travel onwards to a cold desert. A cold-desert camel has shorter legs and two humps. Its shorter legs help it walk easily in mountainous regions. Nearby, deodar trees have a conical shape and sloping branches.

Finally, compare the variety around you. Biodiversity varies from region to region because conditions are different. You begin to see why special features matter in each habitat.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Living in a Habitat
activities.body: Plants and animals live in a habitat. A habitat gives food, water, air and shelter. Special features that help them survive are called adaptations. Deserts have very little water. Desert plants can store water in thick stems. Deodar trees have a cone-like shape and sloping branches.
keyPoints: A habitat is where plants and animals live.
Habitats give living things what they need.
Adaptations are special features that help living things survive.
activities.explanation: Habitats give living things what they need to survive.

activities.prompt: Look at two camels. One camel has one hump, long legs and wide hooves. The other camel has two humps and shorter legs. Which camel lives in a hot desert? Which camel lives in a cold desert?
steps: The one-humped camel fits a hot desert. Hot-desert camels have one hump, long legs and wide hooves.
The two-humped camel fits a cold desert. Cold-desert camels have two humps and shorter legs.
Shorter legs suit the cold desert. They help the camel walk easily in the mountains.
So each camel has features for its habitat (where it lives). These features help it survive there.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What do we call the place where plants and animals live?
options: A habitat
An adaptation
A hump
A thick, juicy stem
activities.explanation: A habitat is the place where plants and animals live.

activities.prompt: Match each plant or animal with what makes it special.
pairs: Have a cone shape and branches that slope down
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a plant or animal with what makes it special.

activities.prompt: Camels in hot deserts have long legs and wide ______.
activities.hint: Think about the part of a camel's leg that touches the ground.
activities.explanation: Camels in hot deserts have wide hooves. This is an adaptation.

activities.prompt: Which camel can walk easily in mountains?
options: A hot-desert camel
A cold-desert camel
Both kinds of camel
Neither kind of camel
activities.explanation: Cold-desert camels have short legs. This helps them walk easily in mountains.

activities.prompt: Why does biodiversity change from place to place?
options: Every place has the same conditions.
All places have very little water.
Conditions are different.
Plants and animals have no habitats.
activities.explanation: Different conditions lead to different biodiversity in different places.

activities.prompt: Deodar trees have a ______ shape and branches that slope down.
activities.hint: Their shape is like a cone.
activities.explanation: Deodar trees have a conical shape and branches that slope down.

activities.prompt: A park gets two camels. One has one hump, long legs and wide hooves. The other has two humps and shorter legs. Which camel came from a hot desert?
options: The camel with one hump and long legs
The camel with two humps and shorter legs
The camel with one hump and shorter legs
The camel with two humps and long legs

why.The camel with two humps and shorter leg: Two humps and shorter legs mean a cold-desert camel.
why.The camel with one hump and shorter legs: This mixes one hump from a hot desert with legs from a cold desert.
why.The camel with two humps and long legs: This mixes two humps from a cold desert with legs from a hot desert.

activities.explanation: Hot-desert camels have one hump, long legs and wide hooves.

activities.prompt: A desert has very little water. A plant with a thick, juicy stem lives there. A child says its stem and its desert are both adaptations. What is the best fix?
options: The stem is an adaptation, and the desert is its habitat.
The stem is a habitat, and the desert is an adaptation.
The stem and the desert are both adaptations.
The stem and the desert are both habitats.

why.The stem is a habitat, and the desert is: This mixes up adaptation and habitat.
why.The stem and the desert are both adaptat: The stem helps the plant. The desert is where the plant lives.
why.The stem and the desert are both habitat: The stem stores water. The desert is where the plant lives.

activities.explanation: The juicy stem stores water. So it is an adaptation. The desert is where the plant lives. So it is its habitat.

activities.prompt: A place has very little water. A gardener sees a fleshy-stem plant and a conical plant with sloping branches. Which plant has the stated way to store water?
options: The plant with the fleshy stem
The plant with the conical shape
The plant with the sloping branches
Both of the plants can do this

why.The plant with the conical shape: A conical shape is a deodar feature, not the stated water store.
why.The plant with the sloping branches: Sloping branches are a deodar feature, not the stated water store.
why.Both of the plants can do this: Only the fleshy-stem plant is described as storing water in this way.

activities.explanation: Desert plants can store water in their fleshy stems.

activities.prompt: A place gives animals food, water, air and shelter. A camel lives in the same place. It has long legs and wide hooves. Which sentence is true?
options: The place is a habitat; its legs are adaptations.
The place is an adaptation; its legs are a habitat.
Both the place and its legs are adaptations.
Both the place and its legs are habitats.

why.The place is an adaptation; its legs are: This mixes up habitat and adaptation.
why.Both the place and its legs are adaptati: A place is not a body feature that helps an animal survive.
why.Both the place and its legs are habitats: Legs are special body features, not places where animals live.

activities.explanation: The place gives things animals need. Special body features are adaptations.

lessons.sceneAlt: A dromedary camel with one hump stands in the Thar Desert in India.
lessons.sceneCaption: A one-humped dromedary camel in the Thar Desert, India.
