sceneCredit.creator: Clément Bardot

funFacts: A camel's hump is made of fat, not water, which helps it survive in the desert.
Desert cactus has spines instead of leaves, which helps it hold water.
Polar bears have black skin under their white fur.

lessons.title: Protecting Habitats and Biodiversity

activities.prompt: How could we protect the many homes of life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Protecting Habitats
activities.body:
You begin your journey across land and water. Land habitats are called terrestrial habitats. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.

A frog shows you how different habitats can meet. Frogs can live in water as well as on land. Animals that can live both in water and on land are called amphibians.

Next, you see what happens when people damage these places. Damage takes away homes, food and other resources. Human activities cause the loss of natural habitats.

Good news surrounds you. Project Tiger was initiated in 1973. The Cheetah Reintroduction Project was initiated in 2022. It aims to restore the cheetah population. Great Indian Bustard habitats have been declared protected areas.

Sacred groves show you another way to care. They are undisturbed patches of forest. Nobody is allowed to harm animals or cut trees in sacred groves. Protecting biodiversity helps our planet remain full of life.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Habitats and Living Things
activities.body: A habitat is a place where plants and animals live. Land habitats are on land. Aquatic habitats are in water. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats. Frogs live in water and on land. Animals that live in both are called amphibians. Protecting habitats keeps homes and food safe. It also protects biodiversity, the many kinds of living things.
keyPoints: Plants and animals have terrestrial (land) habitats.
Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.
Animals that live in water and on land are amphibians.
activities.explanation: These ideas show why habitats need protection.

activities.prompt: A family wants to remove plants around a pond where frogs live. What could happen? What should they do?
steps: The pond is an aquatic habitat (a home in water). The land nearby is a terrestrial habitat (a home on land). Both are habitats.
Frogs are amphibians. So they use both water and land.
Removing plants can cause habitat loss. Habitat loss takes away homes, food, and other things animals need.
Protecting both places helps biodiversity, the many kinds of life on Earth. So the family should protect both places.
activities.explanation: Think about it with Hooty.

activities.title: Find an aquatic habitat
activities.prompt: Which one is an aquatic habitat?
options: A pond
Land
A terrestrial habitat
A plant
activities.explanation: Ponds, lakes, rivers, and oceans are aquatic habitats.

activities.title: Name the animal group
activities.prompt: Animals that live in water and on land are called ______.
activities.hint: Frogs belong to this animal group.
activities.explanation: Frogs can live in water and on land, so they are amphibians.

activities.title: Match each description
activities.prompt: Match each description with the correct term.
pairs: Plants and animals living on land
Animals living in water and on land
activities.explanation: Each description matches a habitat or animal group from the lesson.

activities.title: What does habitat damage cause?
activities.prompt: What happens when habitats are damaged?
options: Homes, food and other resources are taken away.
Only water habitats are affected.
Plants and animals get more food and shelter.
Sacred groves become normal forests.
activities.explanation: Damage takes away homes, food and other resources of plants and animals.

activities.title: Protect life
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order.
items: People cause the loss of natural habitats.
Damage takes away homes, food and other things we need.
We must protect biodiversity.
Our planet stays full of life.
activities.explanation: Losing habitats harms plants and animals. So protecting biodiversity helps life grow.

activities.title: Find the conservation project
activities.prompt: Which project started in 2022 to bring back cheetahs?
options: The Cheetah Reintroduction Project
Project Tiger
Sacred groves
Protected areas for Great Indian Bustards
activities.explanation: This project started in 2022 to bring back cheetahs.

activities.prompt: People cut down plants near a pond. Frogs live in the pond and on land nearby. What will most likely happen to the frogs?
options: The frogs may lose homes and resources.
The frogs may gain homes and resources.
The frogs will need no more food.
The pond and land will stay the same.

This answer thinks habitat damage gives animals extra resources.
This answer thinks animals need no food after they lose a habitat.
This answer thinks cutting plants does not harm habitats.

activities.explanation: This is right. Habitat damage takes away homes, food and other resources.

activities.prompt: A town wants to protect animals in a river and animals in a forest. Which action best protects their habitats?
options: Leave both habitats undamaged.
Clear plants from both habitats.
Move all animals away from them.
Cut trees from the forest.

This mistake assumes removing plants helps plants and animals.
This mistake assumes moving animals away removes their need for protection.
This mistake assumes cutting trees does not damage a forest habitat.

activities.explanation: This is right because undamaged habitats can keep homes, food, and other resources.

activities.prompt: A path is planned through a sacred grove (a small holy forest). What should happen to the plan?
options: Stop it. Harming animals and trees is not allowed.
Go on if only a few trees are cut.
Go on if visitors only watch the animals.
Move the animals away. Then cut the trees.

This wrongly thinks cutting a few trees is allowed in a sacred grove.
why.Go on if visitors only watch the animals: This wrongly thinks watching animals makes cutting trees okay.
why.Move the animals away. Then cut the tree: This wrongly thinks moving animals makes cutting trees okay.

activities.explanation: This is right. Nobody may harm animals or cut trees in a sacred grove.

activities.prompt: The Cheetah Reintroduction Project began in 2022. It wants to bring back the cheetah population. If the plan works, what should happen?
options: The cheetah population should get bigger.
The cheetah population should disappear.
Cheetahs should stop needing habitats.
All habitats should become protected areas.

This mistake is the opposite of the project's goal.
This mistake thinks cheetahs will not need habitats any more.
why.All habitats should become protected are: This mistake thinks one project makes every habitat protected.

activities.explanation: This is right. The project started to bring back the cheetah population.

activities.prompt: After rain, a pond forms on the ground. Frogs live in the water and on the land next to it. Which places need habitat protection (keeping animal homes safe)?
options: Both the pond and the land next to it.
Only the pond, not the land.
Only the land, not the pond.
Neither the pond nor the land.

This mistake says frogs can live only in water.
This mistake says frogs can live only on land.
This mistake says frogs can move, so the places need no protection.

activities.explanation: This is right. The pond is an aquatic habitat (a water home). The land is a terrestrial habitat (a land home). Frogs use both.

Tiny animals called corals build reefs, which are homes for many fish.
The Ganges river dolphin finds food by making clicking sounds in muddy river water.

activities.context: A class goes on a nature walk through an area with grasses, bushes and large trees. The students see colourful flowers, leaves of different shapes and birds making different chirps. A frog moves near both land and water. One student wants to pick up a bird, while another says all frogs must live only in water. The class wonders how the many kinds of living things are connected and how they should behave during the walk.
activities.prompt: One student wants to pick up the bird. What should the class do instead?
options: Leave the bird where it is and watch without touching it.
Hold it briefly so the class can hear its chirp more clearly.
Follow it closely so the class can observe its movement.
Call to it and move closer to see how it responds.

why.Hold it briefly so the class can hear it: Incorrect: holding the bird would disturb it.
why.Follow it closely so the class can obser: Incorrect: following closely would not let the bird live undisturbed.
why.Call to it and move closer to see how it: Incorrect: calling and moving closer would disturb the bird.

activities.explanation: Correct: observing without touching respects the bird.

activities.context: A class goes on a nature walk through an area with grasses, bushes and large trees. The students see colourful flowers, leaves of different shapes and birds making different chirps. A frog moves near both land and water. One student wants to pick up a bird, while another says all frogs must live only in water. The class wonders how the many kinds of living things are connected and how they should behave during the walk.
activities.prompt: The frog moves from the water's edge onto land. How should the class respond to the student's claim that all frogs live only in water?
options: Correct the claim, because frogs can live on land as well as in water.
Accept the claim, because every frog must stay in water.
Accept the claim, because an animal can use only one habitat.
Accept the claim, because frogs and birds are both animals.

why.Accept the claim, because every frog mus: Incorrect: the frog on land shows that the claim is incomplete.
why.Accept the claim, because an animal can: Incorrect: this wrongly assumes that each animal has only one habitat.
why.Accept the claim, because frogs and bird: Incorrect: belonging to the same animal group does not mean sharing the same habitat.

activities.explanation: Correct: frogs can live in both land and water.

activities.context: A class goes on a nature walk through an area with grasses, bushes and large trees. The students see colourful flowers, leaves of different shapes and birds making different chirps. A frog moves near both land and water. One student wants to pick up a bird, while another says all frogs must live only in water. The class wonders how the many kinds of living things are connected and how they should behave during the walk.
activities.prompt: If the class removes a bush to clear the path, what is a likely consequence for the area's living things?
options: Other plants and animals could be affected because they depend on one another.
Only the bush would change, because living things in the area are separate.
The other plants would change, but the animals would not, because habitats are separate.
Nothing would change, because biodiversity means every living thing is independent.

why.Only the bush would change, because livi: Incorrect: this wrongly treats living things as independent of one another.
why.The other plants would change, but the a: Incorrect: this wrongly separates plants from animals.
why.Nothing would change, because biodiversi: Incorrect: this wrongly treats biodiversity as independence.

activities.explanation: Correct: dependence means one change may affect other living things.

activities.prompt: How are leaves and flowers different, and how should students treat living creatures during the walk?
activities.answer: Leaves can differ in shape and in their arrangement on stems or branches. Flowers can differ in colour, shape and scent. Students should respect living creatures and watch them without disturbing them, so they can experience the beauty and variety of the nature walk.
points: Leaves can differ in shape.
Leaves can differ in their arrangement.
Flowers can differ in colour, shape and scent.
Students should observe living creatures without disturbing them.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A gardener wants to understand the plants and animals in a garden. Instead of studying every living thing separately, the gardener groups the plants by height and by the presence or absence of flowers. The animals are grouped by food, place, colour and movement. One plant has a weak stem and needs support to climb, while another grows along the ground. The gardener also notices that some plants have hard, thick, brown and woody stems.
activities.prompt: The plant with the weak stem is separated from its support. What should the gardener do?
options: Help it find something to lean on so it can keep growing upward.
Let it grow along the ground without any support.
Move it beside the plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems.
Wait for its weak stem to become hard and woody before helping it.

why.Let it grow along the ground without any: Growing along the ground describes a creeper, not this plant.
why.Move it beside the plants with hard, thi: A hard, thick, brown and woody stem would suggest a tree.
why.Wait for its weak stem to become hard an: A weak stem does not automatically change into a hard, woody one.

activities.explanation: The plant is a climber because its weak stem needs support.

activities.context: A gardener wants to understand the plants and animals in a garden. Instead of studying every living thing separately, the gardener groups the plants by height and by the presence or absence of flowers. The animals are grouped by food, place, colour and movement. One plant has a weak stem and needs support to climb, while another grows along the ground. The gardener also notices that some plants have hard, thick, brown and woody stems.
activities.prompt: Two animals in the garden move in different ways. Which feature should the gardener use to separate them into groups?
options: the way they move
the food they eat
the place they stay
the colour they have

why.the food they eat: Food can be used, but it does not match the difference described.
why.the place they stay: Place can be used, but it does not match the difference described.
why.the colour they have: Colour can be used, but it does not match the difference described.

activities.explanation: Movement is one of the features used to group animals.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between climbers and creepers.
activities.answer: Climbers have weak stems and need support to climb and grow. Creepers grow along the ground. Therefore, a plant that needs support is a climber, while a plant that spreads along the ground is a creeper.
points: Climbers have weak stems.
Climbers need support to climb and grow.
Creepers grow along the ground.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A gardener notices thin lines on the leaves of many plants. One plant has a net-like arrangement of veins and one main root. Another has veins running side by side and a bunch of similar-sized thin roots. The gardener calls the first pattern reticulate venation and the second parallel venation. She also examines a maize seed and notes that it has one thin cotyledon.
activities.prompt: If another plant has a net-like arrangement of veins, which root system would the gardener generally expect?
options: A taproot system
A fibrous-root system
A taproot system and a fibrous-root system together
No root system can be suggested from the vein pattern

why.A fibrous-root system: That general link applies to parallel venation and fibrous roots.
why.A taproot system and a fibrous-root syst: The facts do not say that a plant should have both root systems.
why.No root system can be suggested from the: The relationship is general, so a root system can still be suggested.

activities.explanation: Reticulate venation is generally linked with taproots.

activities.context: A gardener notices thin lines on the leaves of many plants. One plant has a net-like arrangement of veins and one main root. Another has veins running side by side and a bunch of similar-sized thin roots. The gardener calls the first pattern reticulate venation and the second parallel venation. She also examines a maize seed and notes that it has one thin cotyledon.
activities.prompt: If the maize seed in the case had two cotyledons instead of one, into which plant group would it fit?
options: Dicotyledons
Monocotyledons
Plants with taproot systems
Plants with fibrous-root systems

why.Monocotyledons: Monocotyledons have seeds like maize, with one thin cotyledon.
why.Plants with taproot systems: A taproot system does not determine the cotyledon group.
why.Plants with fibrous-root systems: A fibrous-root system does not determine the cotyledon group.

activities.explanation: Plants with two cotyledons are called dicotyledons.

activities.context: A gardener notices thin lines on the leaves of many plants. One plant has a net-like arrangement of veins and one main root. Another has veins running side by side and a bunch of similar-sized thin roots. The gardener calls the first pattern reticulate venation and the second parallel venation. She also examines a maize seed and notes that it has one thin cotyledon.
activities.prompt: The gardener finds that the plant with net-like veins has a bunch of similar-sized thin roots rather than one main root. What is the best conclusion?
options: It differs from the general link between net-like veins and taproots.
It fits the general link between side-by-side veins and fibrous roots.
It shows that net-like veins must always produce one main root.
It shows that venation gives no general clue about roots.

why.It fits the general link between side-by: Its veins are net-like, not arranged side by side.
why.It shows that net-like veins must always: The relationship says generally, not always.
why.It shows that venation gives no general: Venation does provide a general clue about root systems.

activities.explanation: The usual link is not an absolute rule for every plant.

activities.prompt: Explain how venation patterns and root systems differ, and state the general link between them.
activities.answer: Reticulate venation is a net-like arrangement of leaf veins, while parallel venation has veins running side by side. A taproot system has one main root, and a fibrous-root system is a bunch of similar-sized thin roots. Reticulate venation generally goes with taproots; parallel venation generally goes with fibrous roots.
points: Defines reticulate venation
Defines parallel venation
Explains taproot and fibrous roots
States both general links
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student visits the Silent Valley area and watches fish using their streamlined bodies and fins to move in water. In a grassy area nearby, goats use their legs to move. The student learns that the Silent Valley movement opposed a hydroelectric dam across the Kunthipuzha river and succeeded in saving the valley. Janaki Ammal's work helped document and preserve India's plant biodiversity, showing why protecting each region's plants and animals matters.
activities.prompt: If the student observes fish in another watery region, which features should the student look for as helping them move?
options: The streamlined shape and fins that support swimming
The legs used for moving across grass
The body parts that let them crawl over land
The movement style shared with goats

why.The legs used for moving across grass: Legs help goats move in grassy areas.
why.The body parts that let them crawl over: Crawling over land is not how fish move here.
why.The movement style shared with goats: Fish and goats do not share the same movement features.

activities.explanation: These are the fish's features for moving in water.

activities.context: A student visits the Silent Valley area and watches fish using their streamlined bodies and fins to move in water. In a grassy area nearby, goats use their legs to move. The student learns that the Silent Valley movement opposed a hydroelectric dam across the Kunthipuzha river and succeeded in saving the valley. Janaki Ammal's work helped document and preserve India's plant biodiversity, showing why protecting each region's plants and animals matters.
activities.prompt: A student wants to compare animals from different regions and explain their diversity. What is the best way to prepare the comparison?
options: Group animals by the body parts and movements they use, while noting their different surroundings.
Put all animals in one group because they can all move, and ignore their differences.
Group animals only by where they live and do not record how they move.
Choose one movement method and use it to describe every animal.

why.Put all animals in one group because the: One group would hide the animals' diversity.
why.Group animals only by where they live an: Habitat alone does not show how the animals move.
why.Choose one movement method and use it to: Different animals do not all move in the same way.

activities.explanation: This method shows both movement differences and habitat differences.

activities.prompt: Explain how fish and goats move, and how their movements relate to their surroundings.
activities.answer: Fish have streamlined bodies and fins that help them move in water. Goats live in grassy areas and use their legs to move. This difference shows that animals use different body parts to move and that different animals are suited to different surroundings.
points: Fish move in water using streamlined bodies and fins.
Goats live in grassy areas and move using their legs.
Animals use different body parts for movement.
Movement features are related to an animal's surroundings.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school nature exhibition, a student examines a desert plant with a fleshy stem, a deodar tree, and two camel displays. The exhibition explains that deserts have very little water. The camel from the hot desert has long legs, wide hooves, one hump, and no sweating. The cold-desert display has a camel with shorter legs and two humps. The deodar is shown with a conical shape and sloping branches.
activities.prompt: Why is the desert plant's fleshy stem useful in its habitat?
options: It can keep some water for use when the water supply is limited.
It helps the plant collect food from the dry surroundings.
It provides shelter for the plant in the desert.
It helps the plant obtain more air in the desert.

why.It helps the plant collect food from the: Food collection is not the stated purpose of the stem.
why.It provides shelter for the plant in the: Shelter is a habitat need, not the stem's use.
why.It helps the plant obtain more air in th: Air is a habitat need, but the stem stores water.

activities.explanation: Water storage helps when little water is available.

activities.context: At a school nature exhibition, a student examines a desert plant with a fleshy stem, a deodar tree, and two camel displays. The exhibition explains that deserts have very little water. The camel from the hot desert has long legs, wide hooves, one hump, and no sweating. The cold-desert display has a camel with shorter legs and two humps. The deodar is shown with a conical shape and sloping branches.
activities.prompt: Why should the student call the deodar's conical shape and sloping branches adaptations rather than its habitat?
options: They are special features that help it survive in its region.
They are needs supplied by the place where the tree lives.
They are features shared by every organism in the same habitat.
They are changes in biodiversity from one region to another.

why.They are needs supplied by the place whe: A habitat is a place and the needs it provides.
why.They are features shared by every organi: Different regions have different conditions and features.
why.They are changes in biodiversity from on: Biodiversity is variation among regions, not a tree feature.

activities.explanation: Special survival features are called adaptations.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between an adaptation and a habitat.
activities.answer: Adaptations are special features that help plants and animals survive in a region. A habitat is the place where they live and provides food, water, air, shelter and other needs. The deodar's conical shape and sloping branches are adaptations, while the place where the tree lives is its habitat.
points: Defines adaptations as special survival features.
Defines habitat as the place where organisms live.
Mentions needs provided by a habitat.
Uses the deodar's features as an example of adaptations.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A community planned a new path near a pond, land where frogs lived, and a sacred grove. The path could damage the pond’s surroundings and the forest. Nearby, people wanted to remove bushes where Great Indian Bustards lived. Children learned that human activities can cause the loss of natural habitats, and that habitats of Great Indian Bustards have been declared protected areas. They asked whether the different places should all be protected.
activities.prompt: After hearing the children, what should the community do about the planned path?
options: Change the plan so it does not damage the habitats near the pond or in the forest.
Continue with the plan because only aquatic habitats need protection.
Cut trees in the sacred grove to make room for the path.
Remove the protected status of the Great Indian Bustards’ habitat.

why.Continue with the plan because only aqua: Land and forests are also habitats, not just places containing water.
why.Cut trees in the sacred grove to make ro: Nobody is allowed to cut trees in a sacred grove.
why.Remove the protected status of the Great: The habitats of Great Indian Bustards have been declared protected areas.

activities.explanation: Protecting the habitats helps prevent plants and animals from losing their homes, food, and other resources.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Diversity in the Living World

activities.prompt: On a nature walk, how should you observe living creatures?
options: Observe them without disturbing them.
Disturb them to see their movements.
Pick them up for a closer look.
Remove leaves to find their homes.
activities.explanation: Living creatures deserve respect. Observe them without disturbing them.

activities.prompt: All the kinds of plants and animals in a region are part of its biodiversity.
activities.explanation: Yes. All the kinds of life in a region are part of its biodiversity.

activities.prompt: Match each plant group with its feature.
pairs: Hard, thick, brown and woody stems
Hard woody stems that branch close to the ground
Usually small plants with soft and green stems
Weak stems needing support to climb and grow
activities.explanation: Plant groups have different stem features. Grouping makes plants easier to study.

activities.prompt: Which phrase describes parallel venation (the pattern of veins in a leaf)?
options: A net-like pattern of veins
Veins that run side by side
A woody stem pattern
A main root that goes deep
activities.explanation: Parallel venation means veins run side by side.

activities.prompt: Plants and animals live in a place. We call that place their ______.
activities.hint: This place gives living things what they need to live.
activities.explanation: This is their habitat. It gives food, water, air, shelter and other needs.

activities.prompt: Match each plant or animal with what makes it special.
pairs: Have a cone shape and branches that slope down
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a plant or animal with what makes it special.

activities.prompt: Sacred groves allow people to cut trees whenever they wish.
activities.explanation: Sacred groves are undisturbed forest patches. Nobody may harm animals or cut trees there.

chapters.title: Mindful Eating: A Path to a Healthy Body
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what we eat and regional food; how cooking practices have changed; carbohydrates, fats and proteins; vitamins, minerals, roughage and water.

lessons.title: What We Eat and Regional Food

activities.prompt: What might you taste on a food tour across India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Regional Food
activities.body:
Imagine setting off on a food tour across India. Food is essential to daily life.

You soon notice that people in different places eat a variety of foods. You will see that each state's traditional food is usually based on crops grown there. India is an agricultural country with many kinds of soil and climate. Different crops grow according to each region's soil and climate. Local harvests help shape the traditional food of a state.

In Punjab, you might eat makki di roti, sarson da saag, or chhole bhature. In Karnataka, your plate may hold idli, dosa, sambhar, or coconut chutney. Some listed crops in Manipur include rice, bamboo, and soya bean.

Food items may arrive in many states, while others are eaten in just one state. Taste, culture, and traditions also guide regional choices.

During your tour, remember that healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities. Local traditions and available crops help explain what people eat.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Food Around Us
activities.body: Healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities. Food is essential in daily life. People in different places eat a variety of foods. Some food items are eaten in many different states, while others are eaten in only one particular state. A state's traditional food is usually based on crops grown there. Soil and climate affect crops. Taste, culture and traditions also affect regional food choices.
keyPoints: Healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities.
Regional food choices are linked with crops, soil and climate.
Taste, culture and traditions affect what people eat.
activities.explanation: These facts connect healthy eating with regional food and crops.

activities.prompt: A family moves to a region with different soil and weather. Why might its traditional food change?
steps: Compare the new soil and weather. Crops grow based on the conditions of the region.
Look at the crops grown there. A state's traditional food is usually based on those crops.
Think about taste, culture and traditions. They can also shape what people choose to eat.
So local farming often explains traditional food. Culture helps explain food choices.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Many Kinds of Food
activities.prompt: Which sentence about regional food is true?
options: People everywhere eat the very same food.
People in different places eat different kinds of food.
Every food is eaten in many different states.
Traditional food usually does not use crops grown there.
activities.explanation: People in different places eat different kinds of food. Traditional food usually uses crops grown there.

activities.title: Local Crops and Food
activities.prompt: A state's traditional food usually comes from crops grown there.
activities.explanation: Yes. Crops grown in an area usually shape its traditional food.

activities.title: Food in Different Places
activities.prompt: People in different places eat many kinds of ______.
activities.hint: Pick the plural word (more than one) from the sentence about places.
activities.explanation: The sentence says people in different places eat many kinds of foods.

activities.title: Foods and Places
activities.prompt: Match each food to its place.
activities.explanation: Makki di roti is a food from Punjab. Idli is from Karnataka. Rice is grown in Manipur.

activities.title: Find the Right Matches
activities.prompt: Which option matches each food or crop with the right place?
options: Punjab: idli and dosa; Karnataka: chhole bhature
Karnataka: rice and bamboo; Manipur: coconut chutney
Punjab: makki di roti; Karnataka: idli; Manipur: rice, bamboo and soya bean
Punjab: coconut chutney; Karnataka: rice and bamboo; Manipur: sarson da saag
activities.explanation: Makki di roti is a traditional food of Punjab. Idli comes from Karnataka. Rice, bamboo and soya bean are crops grown in Manipur.

activities.prompt: A farmer moves to a region with new soil and climate. What is the best first step?
options: Check crops suited to the new soil and climate.
Choose the crop that people eat most nearby.
Keep the crop used in the old region.
Pick a crop from a tradition they know.

why.Choose the crop that people eat most nea: What people eat does not decide which crop grows there.
The old region's soil and climate may be different.
Traditions can shape food. They are not the rule for growing crops.

activities.explanation: Crops grow well with the soil and climate of each region.

activities.prompt: Two regions grow different crops. Their soil and climate are different. What food difference should we expect?
options: Their traditional foods must be exactly the same.
Their foods can only come from one state.
Their traditional foods may be different.
Their food choices ignore culture.

why.Their traditional foods must be exactly: This ignores the link between local crops and traditional food.
why.Their foods can only come from one state: This mixes up states with regions and says too much.
Taste, culture and tradition can affect food choices.

activities.explanation: Traditional foods may differ. They come from different local crops.

activities.prompt: A project compares food lists from Punjab and Karnataka. It also has a crop list from Manipur. Which conclusion is careful?
options: Punjab's foods are also crops of Manipur.
The two lists give different kinds of information.
All of Manipur's crops are traditional foods.
All three lists show foods eaten in many states.

why.Punjab's foods are also crops of Manipur: The facts do not put Punjab's foods in Manipur's crop list.
why.All of Manipur's crops are traditional f: The project mixes up a crop list with a food list.
why.All three lists show foods eaten in many: No list says these foods are eaten in many states.

activities.explanation: Punjab and Karnataka list foods. Manipur's list names crops.

lessons.title: How Cooking Practices Have Changed

activities.prompt: How would your cooking feel like without today's tools?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Cooking Changed
activities.body:
Imagine joining a family for a cooking lesson. You begin by learning how cooking was usually done earlier. People's food choices and methods of preparing food can be different. This difference helps you see how cooking practices have changed.

Now, step towards the old cooking area. Earlier, most cooking was done on a chulha. You watch the traditional method. Next, look at preparing ingredients. Earlier, most grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta.

Now, step into a modern kitchen. Today, most people cook using a modern gas stove. An electrical grinder makes grinding easier. You compare these tools with earlier methods. This clear difference shows you traditional and modern cooking practices.

Before you leave, consider why cooking changed. Technological development is one reason cooking practices have changed. Better transport and communication have also helped change cooking practices. Your tour ends with a simple lesson. Food choices and cooking methods can differ. Which changes would you welcome in your own kitchen?
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Cooking Then and Now
activities.body: Traditional practices are old ways of cooking. Modern practices are ways of cooking used today. In the past, most people cooked on a chulha. Today, most people use a modern gas stove. In the past, most grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta. Today, an electric grinder makes grinding easier. Technology, transport and communication have helped cooking practices change.
keyPoints: Traditional and modern cooking practices are different.
Cooking and grinding methods have changed.
Technology, transport and communication helped these changes.
activities.explanation: Cooking practices have changed. The reasons and methods are clear.

activities.prompt: How has grinding food and cooking changed, from the past to today?
steps: In the past, most people ground food by hand with a sil-batta. This was the usual way.
Today, most people cook on a gas stove. This is the common way now.
Today, people can also use an electric grinder. It makes grinding easier.
So the way people cook has changed. New technology is one reason. Better transport and communication also helped.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In the past, where did most people cook?
options: On a chulha
On a new gas stove
With an electric grinder
With a sil-batta
activities.explanation: In the past, most people cooked on a chulha.

activities.prompt: An electric grinder makes grinding easier today.
activities.explanation: Yes. An electric grinder makes grinding easier today.

activities.prompt: Match each old or new way to its task.
pairs: Mostly done on a new gas stove
Mostly done by hand with a sil-batta
Made easier by an electric grinder
activities.explanation: Each task shows how cooking and grinding have changed.

activities.prompt: New technology is one reason cooking ______ have changed.
activities.hint: Use the word for the ways people prepare food.
activities.explanation: New technology is one reason cooking practices have changed.

activities.prompt: What helps make grinding easier today?
options: An electric grinder
A sil-batta used by hand
A modern gas stove
A chulha
activities.explanation: Today, an electric grinder makes grinding easier.

activities.prompt: Which sentence is about a modern way of cooking?
options: Today, most people cook on a modern gas stove.
Earlier, most cooking was done on a chulha.
Earlier, most grinding was done by hand.
Earlier, most grinding used a sil-batta.
activities.explanation: Most people use a modern gas stove today.

activities.prompt: A family makes two displays about grinding and cooking. One shows earlier times. One shows today. Which choice is right?
options: Earlier: sil-batta and chulha. Today: electric grinder and gas stove.
Earlier: electric grinder and gas stove. Today: sil-batta and chulha.
Earlier: sil-batta and gas stove. Today: electric grinder and chulha.
Earlier: chulha and gas stove. Today: sil-batta and electric grinder.

This mistake swaps the earlier and today tools.
why.Earlier: sil-batta and gas stove. Today:: This mistake puts the gas stove in the earlier time. Gas stoves are used today.
why.Earlier: chulha and gas stove. Today: si: This mistake mixes the earlier stove with today's electric grinder.

activities.explanation: This is right. It matches earlier tools with tools used today.

activities.prompt: A student wants proof that cooking has changed. Which way to check is most fair?
options: Compare the same tasks in the old days and today. Use the tools for each task.
Ask which foods people like. Do not check how the food is made.
Compare tools for different foods. Different foods make tool changes clear.
Compare only new cooking tools. Old tools do not show what people used.

why.Ask which foods people like. Do not chec: This mistake looks at food choices. It ignores how food is made.
why.Compare tools for different foods. Diffe: This mistake lets food choices differ. Then the tool change is less clear.
why.Compare only new cooking tools. Old tool: This mistake leaves out old practices. So it cannot show a change.

activities.explanation: This is right. It compares how people did the same tasks at different times.

activities.prompt: Someone says, “Technology is the only reason cooking has changed.” What is the best reply?
options: Technology is one reason; transport and communication also helped.
Technology played no part in changing cooking.
Transport and communication were the only reasons.
Old and new cooking are always exactly the same.

why.Technology played no part in changing co: This says technology did not change cooking at all.
why.Transport and communication were the onl: This forgets technology and names only transport and communication.
why.Old and new cooking are always exactly t: This says old and new cooking are the same, which is false.

activities.explanation: Technology is only one reason why cooking has changed.

activities.prompt: A cook hears about a new way to cook. Transport is better than before. What may happen next?
options: The cooking may change. Talking and travel can help change it.
The cooking must stay the same. Only new tools can change it.
The cooking will go back to old ways. New ideas always make cooking go back.
The cook will stop cooking. Better transport makes cooking unnecessary.

why.The cooking must stay the same. Only new: This mistake thinks only new tools can change cooking.
why.The cooking will go back to old ways. Ne: This mistake thinks new ideas always bring back old ways.
why.The cook will stop cooking. Better trans: This mistake thinks better transport means people need not cook.

activities.explanation: This is right. Travel and talking have helped change cooking.

activities.prompt: A display shows an old kitchen and a new kitchen. Which fact best shows that cooking has changed?
options: Old side: chulha and sil-batta. New side: gas stove and electric grinder.
Both sides use a chulha. Old and new cooking are the same.
One side lists foods. The other lists only foods people like.
Both sides use a gas stove. Only the taste of food is different.

why.Both sides use a chulha. Old and new coo: This mistake thinks both times used the same cooking tools.
why.One side lists foods. The other lists on: This mistake shows food choices but not how food is prepared.
why.Both sides use a gas stove. Only the tas: This mistake says only taste differs. It ignores the different cooking tools.

activities.explanation: This is right. It shows the old and new tools for cooking and grinding.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, Fats and Proteins

activities.prompt: What do carbohydrates, fats and proteins do in your body?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Food
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a tour of your food. At the first stop, you meet sugar. Common sugar is also a type of carbohydrate. You remember that sugar belongs to this group.

Your next stop brings you to oils. Many oils belong to the food component called fat. Soon, you also meet nuts. Groundnuts, walnuts, coconuts and almonds provide fat. Each one provides fat.

Keep walking, and you discover fat's special role. Fat is a source of stored energy. Your guide points to the word stored. Energy can wait inside fat, ready for later.

At the final stop, you find milk products and pulses. These are good sources of protein. You also learn that people obtain protein from both plants and animals. Protein-rich foods help the body grow and repair itself. Your tour ends as you understand the different jobs.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Food Components
activities.body: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are food components. Sugar is a carbohydrate. Many oils are fats. Nuts give fat. Fat stores energy for the body. Milk products and pulses (like dal) give protein. People get protein from plants and animals. Protein helps the body grow and repair itself.
keyPoints: Sugar is a carbohydrate.
Many oils and nuts give fat.
Milk products and pulses give protein.
Fat stores energy. Protein helps growth and repair.
activities.explanation: These parts give your body energy. They help it grow.

activities.prompt: A child wants a snack with stored energy. Should the child choose almonds or common sugar?
steps: Common sugar is a carbohydrate, not a fat.
Many oils are fats. Nuts like almonds give us fat.
Fat gives stored energy. So fat is what the child needs.
So the child should choose almonds, not common sugar.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Name the Carbohydrate
activities.prompt: Common ______ is a type of carbohydrate.
activities.hint: Think of the sweet food used in your kitchen.
activities.explanation: Common sugar is a type of carbohydrate.

activities.title: Protein Sources
activities.prompt: Where do people get protein?
options: Only from plants
Only from animals
From both plants and animals
Only from milk products
activities.explanation: People get protein from both plants and animals.

activities.title: Foods for Growth and Repair
activities.prompt: Protein helps the body grow and repair itself. Which pair has foods rich in protein?
options: Milk products and pulses
Common sugar and many oils
Many oils and groundnuts
Common sugar and pulses
activities.explanation: Milk products and pulses are good protein sources. Protein helps the body grow and repair itself.

activities.title: What Protein Does
activities.prompt: Protein-rich foods help the body grow and ______ itself.
activities.hint: Your body fixes and makes parts of itself again.
activities.explanation: Protein-rich foods help your body grow and repair itself.

activities.title: Stored Energy
activities.prompt: Which food component is a source of stored energy?
options: Carbohydrate
Fat
Protein
activities.explanation: Fat is a source of stored energy for your body.

activities.prompt: At a food lesson, a child says common sugar should give stored energy like almonds. How can the class correct the claim?
options: Common sugar is carbohydrate; almonds provide fat.
Common sugar provides fat; almonds are carbohydrate.
Both foods are carbohydrate; neither provides fat.
Both foods provide fat; neither is carbohydrate.

why.Common sugar provides fat; almonds are c: This swaps the food groups of common sugar and almonds.
why.Both foods are carbohydrate; neither pro: This wrongly treats almonds as a carbohydrate.
why.Both foods provide fat; neither is carbo: This wrongly treats common sugar as a source of fat.

activities.explanation: Common sugar is carbohydrate, while almonds provide fat, which is stored energy.

activities.prompt: A child sees cooking oil and says, “It cannot be fat because it is liquid.” What is the best reply?
options: Many oils are fats.
Only solid food is fat.
Every liquid food is fat.
No oil is fat.

This wrongly says fat must always be solid.
This wrongly says every liquid food is fat.
This wrongly says oils cannot be fat.

activities.explanation: Many oils are fats, even when they are liquid.

activities.prompt: A child eats almonds. Almonds have fat. What can fat do for the body?
options: It can give stored energy.
It can help the body grow.
It can help the body repair.
It can be a carbohydrate.

This mixes up fat with protein. Protein helps the body grow.
This mixes up fat with protein. Protein helps the body repair.
This mixes up fat with carbohydrate, which includes sugar.

activities.explanation: Fat gives stored energy.

activities.prompt: Two children pick snacks. The first child picks milk products and pulses. The second child picks common sugar and oil. Which child picked foods for growth and repair?
options: The first child, because both choices are protein sources.
The second child, because both choices are protein sources.
The first child, because both choices give stored energy.
The second child, because both choices give stored energy.

why.The second child, because both choices a: This wrongly says common sugar and oil are protein sources.
why.The first child, because both choices gi: This mixes up what protein does with what fat does.
why.The second child, because both choices g: This mixes up the food groups, and the jobs of fat and protein.

activities.explanation: Milk products and pulses are good sources of protein. Protein-rich foods help growth and repair.

activities.prompt: A child says: 'Protein comes only from animals.' Which reply is best?
options: Protein can come from both plants and animals.
Protein comes only from plant foods.
Protein comes only from animal foods.
Protein comes from neither plants nor animals.

This mistake thinks only plants give protein.
This mistake thinks only animals give protein.
why.Protein comes from neither plants nor an: This wrongly says people get no protein from plants or animals.

activities.explanation: People get protein from both plants and animals.

activities.prompt: A class wants a fair test. The test checks if a protein-rich snack helps growth and repair. What should they do?
options: Keep other food the same; compare milk with no snack.
Keep other food the same; give both groups no snack.
Change all food for one group; compare milk with dal.
Change food and amounts; compare milk with sugar.

why.Keep other food the same; give both grou: Neither group gets the snack. So the snack is not tested.
why.Change all food for one group; compare m: Changing all food hides the snack's effect.
why.Change food and amounts; compare milk wi: Changing food and amounts makes the test unfair.

activities.explanation: Keep other food the same. Then the snack is the only thing that changes.

lessons.title: Vitamins, Minerals, Roughage and Water

activities.prompt: What might your food be secretly helping you do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Your Food
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a tour through the food on your plate. You meet vitamins and minerals, which are protective nutrients. They help your body function and stay healthy.

Your guide points to vitamins A, B1, C and D. It also shows you calcium, iodine and iron. Lemons and oranges contain vitamin C. Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.

At the salt shop, you see iodised salt. It is common salt mixed with the required amount of iodine salts. Nearby, a guide explains that goitre causes swelling at the front of the neck.

Then you visit the cooking pot. Some nutrients can be lost when food is cooked at high heat. Food components are called nutrients when they help your body function and stay healthy.

Finally, you follow roughage through your digestive journey. Dietary fibre is an essential part of food, even though it provides no nutrients. It helps food move smoothly through your body. Your tour ends with a full plate of new knowledge.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Nutrients that protect you
activities.body: Vitamins and minerals are nutrients. They help your body work and stay healthy. The chapter lists vitamins A, B1, C and D. It also lists the minerals calcium, iodine and iron. Lemons and oranges give vitamin C. Not having enough vitamin C causes scurvy. Iodised salt is common salt with iodine added. Dietary fibre gives no nutrients. But it helps food move smoothly through your body.
keyPoints: The vitamins listed are A, B1, C and D.
The minerals listed are calcium, iodine and iron.
Dietary fibre helps food move smoothly. It gives no nutrients.
activities.explanation: Vitamins, minerals and dietary fibre are all important for food and health.

activities.prompt: A cook says oranges and iodised salt protect health. But dietary fibre has no nutrients. Why should dietary fibre still be part of our food?
steps: Oranges contain vitamin C, and a lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, so this vitamin helps protect health.
Iodised salt contains iodine salts, and iodine is listed as a mineral, so minerals also help protect health.
Dietary fibre provides no nutrients, yet it is essential and helps food move smoothly through the body.
Therefore, vitamins and minerals protect health, while dietary fibre has a different but essential job.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Protect nutrients and understand fibre
activities.body: Vitamins and minerals are protective nutrients. They help your body work and stay healthy. The chapter lists vitamins A, B1, C and D. It also lists the minerals calcium, iodine and iron. Some nutrients can be lost when food is cooked at high heat. Dietary fibre gives no nutrients. But it helps food move smoothly through the body.
keyPoints: Vitamins and minerals are called protective nutrients.
Some nutrients can be lost when food is cooked at high heat.
Dietary fibre gives no nutrients. But it helps food move smoothly.
activities.explanation: Protective nutrients support health. Dietary fibre helps food move through the body.

activities.prompt: Which pair does the lesson say has vitamin C?
options: Lemons and oranges
Calcium and iron
Vitamins A and D
Common salt
activities.explanation: The lesson says lemons and oranges have vitamin C.

activities.prompt: Dietary fibre gives nutrients to the body.
activities.explanation: Dietary fibre gives no nutrients. But it helps food move smoothly through the body.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its fact.
pairs: Causes swelling in the front of the neck
Helps food move smoothly through the body
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an item with the matching fact from the sheet.

activities.prompt: The chapter lists vitamins A, ______, C and D.
activities.hint: This vitamin comes between A and C.
activities.explanation: The vitamins are in this order: A, B1, C and D.

activities.prompt: Which action can make some nutrients go away when food is cooked?
options: Mixing common salt with iodine salts
Adding vitamin C to common salt
Cooking food at high heat
Keeping dietary fibre in food
activities.explanation: Some nutrients can be lost when food is cooked at high heat.

activities.prompt: Some nutrients can be lost when food cooks at high heat.
activities.explanation: The lesson says some nutrients can be lost when cooked at high heat.

activities.prompt: A person eats no food with vitamin C for a long time. What is likely to happen?
options: The person may get scurvy.
The person's neck may swell.
The person's food may move faster.
The person may have less roughage.

A swollen neck can be a sign of goitre, not of missing vitamin C.
This mixes up vitamin C with roughage. Roughage helps food move.
Nothing shows that missing vitamin C causes less roughage.

activities.explanation: Not enough vitamin C causes scurvy.

activities.prompt: A cook wants to test if high heat changes nutrients. The cook compares it with low heat. Which plan is fair?
options: Cook equal portions at high heat and low heat.
Cook equal portions at high heat and high heat.
Cook equal portions at high heat and no heat.
Cook equal portions of two foods at high heat.

why.Cook equal portions at high heat and hig: It compares two of the same thing, so no change can be found.
why.Cook equal portions at high heat and no: It compares high heat with no heat, not with low heat.
why.Cook equal portions of two foods at high: It changes the food too, so the cause is not clear.

activities.explanation: It changes only the heat. The food and amount stay the same.

activities.prompt: A child thinks dietary fibre is useless. It gives no nutrients. Which fact shows it should not be removed?
options: It helps food move easily through the body.
It supplies vitamin C to the body.
It mixes iodine salts into common salt.
It causes swelling at the front of neck.

Lemons and oranges give vitamin C. Dietary fibre gives no nutrients.
Iodised salt has iodine. Dietary fibre does not add iodine to salt.
Neck swelling is a sign of goitre, not of dietary fibre.

activities.explanation: Dietary fibre helps food move easily through the body.

activities.prompt: A child says vitamins and minerals are useless. Which answer shows that this idea is wrong?
options: They help the body work and stay healthy.
They move food smoothly through the body.
They give dietary fibre to food.
They add iodine to common salt.

why.They move food smoothly through the body: Dietary fibre does this job, not vitamins and minerals.
Dietary fibre gives no nutrients. Vitamins and minerals do.
This is about making iodised salt, not about vitamins and minerals.

activities.explanation: Vitamins and minerals are protective nutrients. So they help the body.

activities.prompt: Riya says oranges and iodised salt are both good for us. She says one gives a vitamin and the other a mineral. Is her reason correct?
options: Yes; orange has vitamin C and salt has iodine.
No; orange has iodine and salt has vitamin C.
No; both foods have only dietary fibre.
No; both foods have only calcium and iron.

why.No; orange has iodine and salt has vitam: This swaps the vitamin and mineral in the two foods.
Dietary fibre gives no nutrients. It is not said to be in these foods.
why.No; both foods have only calcium and iro: This wrongly thinks both foods give all the listed minerals.

activities.explanation: Oranges have vitamin C. Iodised salt has iodine. Both are protective nutrients, which keep us healthy.

lessons.title: Testing Food for Nutrients

activities.prompt: What secrets are hiding inside the food we eat?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Food Testing Tour
activities.body:
You begin your food testing tour with starch, fat and protein. Each has a fairly simple testing method. You take turns using these methods on food items.

For starch, you place diluted iodine solution on each food item. You use two or three drops each time. A blue-black colour then shows that the food contains starch.

Next, you look for fat. Oil or butter leaves an oily patch on paper. An oily patch shows that the food item contains fat. Light can faintly shine through the oily patch.

For protein, you add water to each test tube and shake the mixture well. You then add two drops of copper sulfate solution to each tube. A violet colour shows that the food item contains proteins.

You must handle the chemicals used in the protein test carefully. Some other nutrients can only be detected in a well-equipped laboratory.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Food Shows Nutrients
activities.body: Food can be tested for starch, fat and protein. For starch, diluted iodine solution is placed on the food. A blue-black colour shows starch. For fat, oil or butter leaves an oily patch on paper. For protein, water is added and the mixture is shaken well. Copper sulfate solution is added. A violet colour shows proteins. Other nutrients need a well-equipped laboratory. Protein-test chemicals need careful handling.
keyPoints: Blue-black colour shows starch.
An oily patch shows fat.
Violet colour shows proteins.
activities.explanation: Different test results help us find nutrients in food.

activities.prompt: A child tests food with iodine. The child wants to know what a colour change means.
steps: Two or three drops of diluted iodine are put on the food. This is a simple test for starch.
If the food turns blue-black, it contains starch. Blue-black shows that starch is there.
If the food is not blue-black, the child cannot say it has starch. Blue-black is needed to show starch.
So the blue-black food has starch. The child cannot say the same for the other food.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which colour shows that food has starch?
options: Violet
Blue-black
Oily patch
Faint shine
activities.explanation: A blue-black colour shows that food has starch. Well done!

activities.prompt: An oily patch on paper shows the food has fat.
activities.explanation: An oily patch shows fat. Light can shine faintly through this patch.

activities.prompt: A ______ colour shows that food has proteins.
activities.hint: Look at the protein test result.
activities.explanation: The protein test gives a violet colour. This shows proteins are in the food.

activities.prompt: Match each result with what it shows.
pairs: Leaves an oily patch on paper
activities.explanation: Each colour or patch gives a clue about a nutrient. Well done!

activities.prompt: Put the starch test steps in order.
items: Put diluted iodine solution on the food
Use two or three drops for each food
A blue-black colour appears
activities.explanation: Drops go on before the colour appears. A blue-black colour shows starch.

activities.prompt: Where must you go to test some other nutrients?
options: In a well-equipped laboratory
On food paper
In a violet colour
Beside an oily patch
activities.explanation: Some nutrients need a well-equipped laboratory. Simple tests check starch, fat and protein.

activities.prompt: Some nutrients can only be detected using the simple methods described.
activities.explanation: Some nutrients can only be detected in a well-equipped laboratory. Simple methods do not detect all nutrients.

activities.prompt: A child puts two or three drops of weak iodine liquid on food. What would show that the food has starch?
options: A blue-black colour appears in the food.
A violet colour appears in the food.
An oily patch appears on the food.
A blue colour appears in the food.

This mistake mixes up the violet colour of the protein test.
This mistake thinks an oily patch is a colour change.
This mistake gets confused by the blue colour.

activities.explanation: A blue-black colour means the food has starch.

activities.prompt: A child rubs a food on paper. An oily patch forms. Light shines through the patch. Which conclusion fits both facts?
options: Light shines faintly, and the food has fat.
Light shines brightly, and the food has starch.
Light cannot shine through, and the food has protein.
A blue-black colour appears, and the food has starch.

why.Light shines brightly, and the food has: The child expects bright light. The text says the light is faint.
why.Light cannot shine through, and the food: This mixes up the paper test with the protein test.
why.A blue-black colour appears, and the foo: This mixes up the paper test with the iodine test for starch.

activities.explanation: Light shines faintly through the oily patch. The patch shows that fat is there.

lessons.title: Balanced Diet, Millets and Food Miles

activities.prompt: What can a simple lunch reveal about food, farms and your body?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lunch, Millets and Food Miles
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a school lesson with a simple packed lunch. You look at its foods and wonder what your body needs. Your nutrient needs may change with age, gender, physical activity and health.

You discover that a balanced diet contains essential nutrients, roughage and water. It provides these in the right amounts. Foods high in sugar and fat but low in useful nutrients are called junk foods.

Junk foods are not healthy for the body. Eating junk foods often can make a person obese.

You then visit a millet field and see why millets matter. Millets contribute significantly to a balanced diet for normal body functioning. You also spot iodised salt and some baby foods on a shop shelf. These are examples of fortified foods. Adding nutrients during food processing improves the food's nutritional quality.

Next, you follow your lunch from producer to consumer. Food miles measure the distance food travels from producer to consumer. Reducing food miles can support local farmers and keep food fresh and healthy. The FSSAI also helps regulate food quality in India.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Makes Food Healthy?
activities.body: A balanced diet has nutrients, roughage and water. It has them in the right amounts. Your needs can change with age, gender, activity and health. Millets are very helpful for a balanced diet. Junk food has a lot of sugar and fat. It has few useful nutrients. Eating junk food often can make a person obese.
keyPoints: A balanced diet has nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts.
Millets are very helpful for a balanced diet.
Eating junk food often can make a person obese.
activities.explanation: Good food choices help your body get what it needs.

activities.prompt: A child often eats a sugary, fatty snack. Another meal has nutrients, roughage and water in good amounts. Which choice is better for the body, and why?
steps: The sugary, fatty snack is junk food. It has few useful nutrients.
Junk food is not healthy. So it is not the better choice.
Eating it often can make a person obese (very fat). So it is an even worse choice.
The other meal is balanced. It has nutrients, roughage and water in good amounts. So it is the better choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Closer Food and Better Quality
activities.body: Food miles show how far food travels. It goes from the producer to the consumer. The producer grows or makes the food. The consumer buys and eats it. Cutting food miles can help local farmers. It can also keep food fresh and healthy. Fortified foods have nutrients added when they are made. This makes their nutrition better. Iodised salt and some baby foods are examples of fortified foods. The FSSAI makes rules for food quality in India.
keyPoints: Food miles measure how far food travels.
Fortified foods have added nutrients. They are better for health.
The FSSAI makes rules for food quality in India.
activities.explanation: Food from nearby, and better food, can help everyone.

activities.prompt: Which answer tells what a balanced diet is?
options: Essential nutrients, roughage and water in any amounts.
Only essential nutrients, with no roughage or water.
Essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts.
Mostly sugar and fat, with few good nutrients.
activities.explanation: A balanced diet has all these in the right amounts.

activities.prompt: Food miles measure the ______ food travels from producer to consumer.
activities.hint: Food miles tell you how far food has travelled.
activities.explanation: Food miles measure the distance food travels from producer to you.

activities.prompt: Match each food word with its meaning.
pairs: Right amounts of nutrients, roughage and water
Nutrients added when food is made
Lots of sugar and fat, few useful nutrients
Sets rules for food quality in India
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a food word with the right fact.

activities.prompt: A market wants fresh food. It also wants to help local farmers. What should it do?
options: Reduce food miles.
Increase food miles.
Measure the distance people travel.
Add nutrients after shoppers pick food.
activities.explanation: Reducing food miles can help local farmers. It keeps food fresh and healthy.

activities.prompt: One pair names fortified food and the food-checking group in India. Which pair is right?
options: The food is fortified; the FSSAI measures food miles.
The food is junk food; the FSSAI checks food quality in India.
The food has no added nutrients; the FSSAI supports local farmers.
The food is fortified; the FSSAI checks food quality in India.
activities.explanation: Adding nutrients to food makes it healthier. Iodised salt is fortified. FSSAI checks food quality in India.

activities.prompt: Put these food miles ideas in the right order.
items: A producer gives food.
Food travels from the producer to the consumer.
The distance food travels is measured in food miles.
Fewer food miles can help local farmers. Food stays fresh and healthy.
activities.explanation: Food starts with the producer. It travels to the consumer. Its distance is measured in food miles.

activities.prompt: A first plate has nutrients, roughage and water. Its amounts are wrong. A second plate has the same three, in the right amounts. Which plate is balanced, and why?
options: The second plate, because its amounts are right
The first plate, because it has all three things
The second plate, because it has the most food
The first plate, because water makes any meal balanced

why.The first plate, because it has all thre: This wrongly thinks having all three things is enough.
why.The second plate, because it has the mos: This wrongly thinks more food means a balanced diet.
why.The first plate, because water makes any: This wrongly thinks water alone makes a meal balanced.

activities.explanation: This is right. Right amounts of nutrients, roughage and water make a balanced diet.

activities.prompt: Two children differ in age, gender, activity and health. Why might their balanced diet plans need different amounts?
options: Their nutrient needs can change with these differences
Their nutrient needs never change after childhood
They should both have the same amounts, always
They need more junk food when their needs differ

why.Their nutrient needs never change after: This is wrong, because needs can change after childhood.
why.They should both have the same amounts,: This is wrong, because people do not all need the same amounts.
why.They need more junk food when their need: This is wrong. Junk food is not a way to meet changing needs.

activities.explanation: This is right. Nutrient needs can change with age, gender, activity and health.

activities.prompt: A child often eats food with much sugar and fat. It has few useful nutrients. What can happen over time, and why?
options: The child can become obese from eating often.
The child can stay thin even if eating often.
The child can need less balanced food over time.
The child can become healthier from eating often.

why.The child can stay thin even if eating o: This wrongly assumes junk food often cannot make a child obese.
why.The child can need less balanced food ov: This wrongly says a child needs less balanced food after junk food.
why.The child can become healthier from eati: This wrongly says eating junk food often makes the body healthier.

activities.explanation: This is right. Eating junk food often can make a person obese.

activities.prompt: A shop buys vegetables from a nearby producer, not a faraway one. This cuts the distance the food travels. What can this change do?
options: Help local farmers and keep food fresh and healthy
Add more food miles and keep food fresh and healthy
Help local farmers and lower food quality
Add more food miles and help local farmers

why.Add more food miles and keep food fresh: This wrongly thinks less travel means more distance.
why.Help local farmers and lower food qualit: This wrongly thinks local food is poorer quality.
why.Add more food miles and help local farme: This wrongly thinks cutting food miles adds more distance.

activities.explanation: This is right. Fewer food miles can help local farmers and keep food fresh and healthy.

activities.prompt: A child wants food that helps the body work well. A sugary, fatty snack has few useful nutrients. Should the child choose millet or the snack?
options: Choose millet, because it helps with a balanced diet.
Choose the snack, because it has few useful nutrients.
Choose the snack, because it helps the body work well.
Choose millet, because sugar and fat are good for us.

why.Choose the snack, because it has few use: This wrongly says few useful nutrients is a good reason to choose the snack.
why.Choose the snack, because it helps the b: This wrongly thinks junk food helps the body work well.
why.Choose millet, because sugar and fat are: This wrongly thinks sugar and fat show a balanced diet.

activities.explanation: This is right. Millets help make a balanced diet and keep the body working well.

Food miles tell us how far food travels before it reaches your plate.
Your body needs different food as you grow, and even the amount you need can change with age.
