activities.context: At a school food fair, students are preparing tables about regional food. One table lists rice, bamboo and soya bean as crops grown in Manipur. Another presents traditional foods of Punjab and Karnataka. The students also explain that taste, culture and traditions shape food choices, and they plan to show how healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities.
activities.prompt: If the soil and climate of a region changed, what would most likely happen to its crops and traditional foods?
options: Farmers might grow different crops that suit the changed conditions, and the region's traditional foods could change with them.
The crops and traditional foods would remain exactly the same because soil and climate never affect food.
All crops would become the same across India because different regions would no longer have different conditions.
Traditional foods would depend more on taste than crops, so the crops could change without affecting them.

why.The crops and traditional foods would re: This wrongly treats regional crops and foods as unaffected by soil and climate.
why.All crops would become the same across I: This ignores that different regions grow different crops according to their own conditions.
why.Traditional foods would depend more on t: This wrongly removes the usual connection between local crops and traditional food.

activities.explanation: Crops are grown according to each region's soil and climate, and traditional food is usually based on those crops.

activities.context: At a school food fair, students are preparing tables about regional food. One table lists rice, bamboo and soya bean as crops grown in Manipur. Another presents traditional foods of Punjab and Karnataka. The students also explain that taste, culture and traditions shape food choices, and they plan to show how healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities.
activities.prompt: What should the students do so that the food fair also encourages healthy eating?
options: Offer wholesome choices and tell guests to keep the amount they eat moderate.
Offer every food in large amounts because choosing enough is the only part of healthy eating.
Offer only one food because a wider choice of foods cannot support healthy eating.
Offer many foods without mentioning amount because variety alone makes eating healthy.

why.Offer every food in large amounts becaus: This wrongly assumes more food is healthier and ignores moderate quantities.
why.Offer only one food because a wider choi: This confuses regional variety with healthy eating; variety itself does not remove the need for moderation.
why.Offer many foods without mentioning amou: This wrongly assumes a varied display settles the question of how much to eat.

activities.explanation: Healthy eating includes wholesome food and moderate quantities, so both food choice and amount matter.

activities.prompt: Explain why people in different regions may eat different traditional foods.
activities.answer: People in different regions grow different crops according to the soil and climate of their area. Since a state's traditional food is usually based on crops grown there, regional foods can differ. Taste, culture and traditions also affect what people choose to eat, adding variety to regional diets.
points: Crops depend on the soil and climate of each region.
Traditional foods are usually based on locally grown crops.
Taste, culture and traditions influence food choices.
People in different places eat a variety of foods.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family remembers that earlier most cooking in their home was done on a chulha and most grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta. Today, they cook using a modern gas stove and use an electrical grinder. The family also notices that food choices and preparation methods differ from place to place. They know that cooking practices have changed over time and that technological development, along with better transport and communication, has helped bring about the changes.
activities.prompt: The family's electrical grinder is not working, but they still need to grind food. What should they do?
options: Grind it by hand with a sil-batta.
Cook it on a modern gas stove.
Cook it on a chulha.
Use better transport to grind it.

A gas stove is used for cooking, not grinding.
A chulha is also used for cooking rather than grinding.
Transport can help bring about changes, but it cannot grind food.

activities.explanation: This was the earlier method of grinding.

activities.context: A family remembers that earlier most cooking in their home was done on a chulha and most grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta. Today, they cook using a modern gas stove and use an electrical grinder. The family also notices that food choices and preparation methods differ from place to place. They know that cooking practices have changed over time and that technological development, along with better transport and communication, has helped bring about the changes.
activities.prompt: If the family moves to a place where most people cook using a modern gas stove, what can they reasonably expect?
options: Their cooking method would likely move toward a modern gas stove.
They would certainly return to cooking on a chulha.
An electrical grinder would replace their cooking method.
Food choices and preparation methods would become identical everywhere.

why.They would certainly return to cooking o: There is no reason to expect a certain return to traditional cooking.
why.An electrical grinder would replace thei: An electrical grinder helps with grinding, not cooking.
why.Food choices and preparation methods wou: Food choices and preparation methods can remain different across places.

activities.explanation: A modern gas stove is the common method in the place described.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between traditional and modern cooking practices?
activities.answer: There is a clear difference between traditional and modern cooking practices. Earlier, most cooking was done on a chulha, and most grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta. Today, people mostly cook with a modern gas stove, while an electrical grinder makes grinding easier.
points: A chulha was the earlier main cooking method.
A modern gas stove is common today.
Earlier grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta.
An electrical grinder now makes grinding easier.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi is getting ready for a school sports activity. He packs groundnuts, common sugar, milk and pulses for the day. Ravi wants food that gives him stored energy, and he also wants food that helps his body grow and repair itself. His teacher asks him to explain which foods he packed for each purpose and to suggest one change to his meal.
activities.prompt: Ravi wants a food that gives him stored energy. Which kind of food should he choose from his meal?
options: A food that provides fat
A food that provides protein
A food that is a carbohydrate
A food that helps the body grow and repair itself

why.A food that provides protein: Protein-rich foods help with growth and repair.
why.A food that helps the body grow and repa: This describes protein-rich foods rather than stored-energy fat.

activities.explanation: Fat is a source of stored energy.

activities.context: Ravi is getting ready for a school sports activity. He packs groundnuts, common sugar, milk and pulses for the day. Ravi wants food that gives him stored energy, and he also wants food that helps his body grow and repair itself. His teacher asks him to explain which foods he packed for each purpose and to suggest one change to his meal.
activities.prompt: Ravi wants to support his growth and repair after the activity. Which foods should he keep in his meal?
options: Milk products and pulses
Common sugar and oils
Only common sugar
Only oils

why.Common sugar and oils: These choices match the carbohydrate and fat roles instead.
why.Only common sugar: Common sugar is a carbohydrate, while protein supports growth and repair.
why.Only oils: Oils relate to fat and stored energy, while protein supports growth and repair.

activities.explanation: Milk products and pulses are good sources of protein.

activities.prompt: Explain why the groundnuts in Ravi's meal can help provide him with stored energy.
activities.answer: Groundnuts provide fat, and fat is a source of stored energy. That makes them suitable for Ravi when he wants food for stored energy. Common sugar is a carbohydrate, while milk products and pulses are protein sources that help the body grow and repair itself.
points: Groundnuts provide fat.
Fat is a source of stored energy.
Common sugar is a carbohydrate.
Protein sources support growth and repair.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner regularly eats oranges and lemons. The family uses iodised salt for cooking. Some nutrients may be lost when the learner's meals are cooked at high heat. The family has started adding dietary fibre to meals because it helps food move smoothly through the body. During a health check, the front of the learner's neck is swollen.
activities.prompt: If the learner stops eating oranges and lemons and gets vitamin C from no other food, which change is most likely?
options: A lack of vitamin C, which can cause scurvy.
A lack of iodine, which can cause goitre.
A lack of calcium, which can cause scurvy.
A lack of iron, which can cause goitre.

why.A lack of iodine, which can cause goitre: Wrong: this describes an iodine-related problem, not a vitamin C problem.
why.A lack of calcium, which can cause scurv: Wrong: the stated change concerns vitamin C, not calcium.
Wrong: the stated change concerns vitamin C, not iron.

activities.explanation: Correct: oranges and lemons provide vitamin C, and its lack causes scurvy.

activities.context: A learner regularly eats oranges and lemons. The family uses iodised salt for cooking. Some nutrients may be lost when the learner's meals are cooked at high heat. The family has started adding dietary fibre to meals because it helps food move smoothly through the body. During a health check, the front of the learner's neck is swollen.
activities.prompt: Why has the family started adding dietary fibre to the learner's meals?
options: It assists the movement of food through the body.
It supplies vitamin C to the body.
It supplies calcium and iron to the body.
It prevents every nutrient from being lost during cooking.

Wrong: dietary fibre provides no nutrients, including vitamin C.
why.It supplies calcium and iron to the body: Wrong: dietary fibre does not provide calcium or iron.
why.It prevents every nutrient from being lo: Wrong: dietary fibre does not prevent all losses caused by high-heat cooking.

activities.explanation: Correct: dietary fibre helps food move smoothly through the body.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between vitamins and minerals and dietary fibre.
activities.answer: Vitamins and minerals are protective nutrients, so they help the body function and stay healthy. Dietary fibre is also essential, but it provides no nutrients. Its main job is to help food move smoothly through the body.
points: Vitamins and minerals are protective nutrients.
They help the body function and stay healthy.
Dietary fibre provides no nutrients but helps food move smoothly through the body.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school activity, a learner wants to find out whether a food item contains starch, fat or protein. The learner puts two or three drops of diluted iodine solution on the food item, then checks the colour. The learner also rubs some of the food on paper, adds water to a test tube and shakes the mixture well before adding copper sulfate solution. The teacher reminds the learner to handle the chemicals carefully.
activities.prompt: After the diluted iodine solution is dropped on the food, a blue-black colour appears. What does this result mean?
options: The food has starch in it.
The food has protein in it.
The food has fat in it.
The food has no starch in it.

Protein is shown by a violet colour in the protein test.
An oily patch, not a blue-black colour, shows fat.
The blue-black colour does not show the absence of starch.

activities.explanation: A blue-black colour is the result of the starch test.

activities.context: At a school activity, a learner wants to find out whether a food item contains starch, fat or protein. The learner puts two or three drops of diluted iodine solution on the food item, then checks the colour. The learner also rubs some of the food on paper, adds water to a test tube and shakes the mixture well before adding copper sulfate solution. The teacher reminds the learner to handle the chemicals carefully.
activities.prompt: The learner adds copper sulfate solution without first adding water and shaking the mixture well. Which part of the protein test has been changed?
options: The water-and-shaking step was left out.
The iodine test was used instead.
Copper sulfate solution was replaced with iodine.
The food was first placed on paper.

Iodine solution belongs to the separate starch test.
why.Copper sulfate solution was replaced wit: Copper sulfate solution is used in the protein test.
Placing food on paper belongs to the separate fat test.

activities.explanation: Water must be added and the mixture shaken well before copper sulfate solution.

activities.prompt: How can starch and fat be tested in food?
activities.answer: To test for starch, place two or three drops of diluted iodine solution on the food. A blue-black colour shows that starch is present. To test for fat, rub the food on paper. An oily patch appears, and light can faintly shine through it, showing that fat is present.
points: Use two or three drops of diluted iodine solution.
A blue-black colour shows starch.
Rub the food on paper to look for an oily patch.
An oily patch shows fat.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Why should a student's balanced diet be matched to age, gender, physical activity and health?
activities.answer: A balanced diet contains essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts. Nutrient needs can change with age, gender, physical activity and health, so one person's diet may not suit another. Choosing suitable amounts for the person's circumstances supports normal body functioning and helps make the overall diet balanced.
points: A balanced diet includes nutrients, roughage and water.
Nutrient needs can change with age, gender, activity and health.
The correct amounts should match the person's needs.
A suitable balanced diet supports normal body functioning.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

Idli, dosa, sambhar and coconut chutney

Add vitamins while making food

chapters.title: Exploring Magnets
chapters.summary: In this chapter: magnets and magnetic materials; the poles of a magnet; using a suspended magnet to find directions; making and using a magnetic compass.

lessons.title: Magnets and Magnetic Materials

activities.prompt: What will you discover when you explore the world of magnets?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Magnet Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you are travelling when the stars cannot be seen. You hold a magnetic compass. It helps you find directions. Your journey continues with a useful guide.

Long ago, people discovered lodestones. These are naturally occurring magnets. Later, people learned that magnets could also be made from iron. Magnets like this are artificial magnets.

Now you visit a shelf of colourful objects. Magnets appear in pencil boxes, stickers and toys. They are artificial magnets. You also see that magnets can be made in many different shapes.

As you explore, you test each object. Some objects are attracted to a magnet and stick to it. Materials attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic materials. You learn that iron is a magnetic material. At your next stop, you watch an iron object move towards a nearby magnet.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet the Magnets
activities.body: Travellers used a magnetic compass to find directions. They did this when they could not see the stars. Lodestones are natural magnets. People found them long ago. Later, people learned to make magnets from iron. Magnets in pencil boxes, stickers and toys are artificial magnets. Artificial means made by people. Magnets can have many shapes. A magnet attracts (pulls) some objects. They stick to it. Materials that stick to magnets are called magnetic materials. Iron is a magnetic material.
keyPoints: A magnetic compass helps travellers find directions.
Lodestones are natural magnets.
Iron is a magnetic material.
activities.explanation: Magnets can be natural, artificial or made from iron.

activities.prompt: A traveller cannot see the stars. The traveller needs to find a direction. What should the traveller use, and why?
steps: The stars are hidden. They cannot help the traveller choose a direction.
Travellers used a magnetic compass when they could not see the stars.
A compass is useful here. It can guide the traveller, even without stars.
So the traveller should use a magnetic compass.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Makes a Material Magnetic?
activities.body: Some objects are attracted to a magnet and stick to it. Materials attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic materials. This means the material moves towards the magnet. Iron is a magnetic material, so iron is attracted towards a magnet. Magnets can be made in many different shapes. People can make magnets from iron. Artificial magnets are used in pencil boxes, stickers and toys.
keyPoints: Attracted objects stick to a magnet.
Attracted materials are called magnetic materials.
Iron is attracted towards a magnet.
activities.explanation: Magnetic materials are attracted towards magnets, and iron is one of them.

activities.prompt: Which group describes lodestones?
options: Artificial magnets
Magnets of different shapes
Naturally occurring magnets
Materials attracted to magnets
activities.explanation: Lodestones are naturally occurring magnets. People found them long ago.

activities.prompt: Later, people learned that magnets can be made from ______.
activities.hint: This material is also a magnetic material.
activities.explanation: Iron can be used to make magnets. Iron is a magnetic material.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its right description.
activities.explanation: Lodestones are natural magnets. Pencil box magnets are artificial. Iron is magnetic.

activities.prompt: Why is iron attracted toward a magnet?
options: Because it is a magnetic material.
Because it is an artificial magnet.
Because it is a naturally occurring magnet.
Because it is a different magnet shape.
activities.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material. Materials like iron are attracted to a magnet.

activities.prompt: Put the traveller's steps in order.
items: Stars cannot be seen.
Use a magnetic compass.
Find directions.
activities.explanation: Travellers used a magnetic compass to find directions. They did this when stars could not be seen.

activities.prompt: You find a magnet in your pencil box. What type is it?
options: A naturally occurring magnet
An artificial magnet
A magnetic material
A different magnet shape
activities.explanation: Magnets in pencil boxes are artificial magnets.

activities.prompt: A magnet is under an iron nail. What will most likely happen to the nail?
options: The nail will move toward the magnet.
The nail will move away from the magnet.
The nail will stay still and unchanged.
The nail will become a magnet itself.

This mistake thinks magnets push magnetic materials away instead of pulling them.
This mistake thinks iron is not pulled, even though iron is a magnetic material.
This mistake confuses being pulled by a magnet with becoming a magnet.

activities.explanation: Iron is a magnetic material. So the magnet pulls the nail closer.

activities.prompt: A child wants to test if magnet shape changes an iron clip. Which test is a fair test?
options: Use two magnet shapes with one iron clip.
Use two magnet shapes with two iron clips.
Use one magnet shape with two iron clips.
Use natural and artificial magnets with one clip.

why.Use two magnet shapes with two iron clip: Two clips and two shapes change two things. You cannot tell which one matters.

Test only the toy magnet with an iron nail.
Test only the lodestone with a wooden peg.
Test each magnet with a different metal thing.

why.Test only the toy magnet with an iron na: Testing one magnet cannot show if both attract iron.
why.Test only the lodestone with a wooden pe: A wooden peg is not iron. Only one magnet is tested.
why.Test each magnet with a different metal: Different metals change the test. The results cannot be compared fairly.

activities.explanation: Using the same iron nail is a fair test. Both magnets try to attract the same metal.

activities.prompt: Two artificial magnets have different shapes. Put the same iron clip near each one. What can you say from this?
options: Both magnets should attract the clip.
Only the round magnet should attract it.
Only the flat magnet should attract it.
Neither magnet should attract it.

This wrongly thinks only a round magnet can attract magnetic material.
This wrongly thinks only a flat magnet can attract magnetic material.
This wrongly thinks different shapes stop magnets from attracting iron.

lessons.title: The Poles of a Magnet

activities.prompt: What happens if you break a magnet into tiny pieces?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of the Magnet’s Poles
activities.body:
Imagine entering a science room with a bar magnet and a tray of iron filings. You gently sprinkle them over the magnet. Many cling near its ends, while only a few stick along the rest. The ends are the North pole and the South pole.

Now you move the magnet towards scattered filings. The greatest number gather near the two ends. Few filings stick to the remaining part. You have found where the filings gather most.

Then you wonder whether you can keep just one end. You try breaking the bar magnet into smaller pieces. Every smaller piece becomes a magnet. Each has its own North pole and South pole.

You look closely and notice something surprising. North and South poles always exist in pairs. A single North pole or a single South pole cannot exist. It is not possible to obtain a magnet with only one pole.

Each broken piece remains a magnet with both poles. Your experiment ends with this surprising discovery.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet the Magnet's Poles
activities.body: A bar magnet has two poles. One is the North pole. The other is the South pole. Iron filings are tiny pieces of iron. Most iron filings stick near the ends of the magnet. Only a few stick to the middle part. If you break a magnet, each piece still has two poles. So, one pole alone cannot exist.
keyPoints: The poles are the North pole and the South pole.
Most iron filings stick near the magnet's ends.
Every smaller magnet still has both poles.
activities.explanation: The ends hold the most iron filings, and every magnet keeps both poles.

activities.title: Bring two magnets together

tasks.then: Like poles face each other and push apart.

tasks.say: Flip it back and bring them close.
tasks.then: Unlike poles pull together, more strongly when close.

activities.takeaway: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
activities.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

activities.prompt: A bar magnet breaks into smaller pieces. What happens to the poles?
steps: Break a bar magnet into smaller pieces.
Each piece is still a magnet. Each piece has a North pole and a South pole.

Most filings stick near the ends of each piece. This shows each piece still has two pole areas.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.explanation: Most iron filings gather near the ends of a bar magnet.

At the North end only
At the South end only
In the middle part

pairs: at the ends of a bar magnet
only a few iron filings stick
smaller magnets with North and South poles
activities.explanation: Each small magnet still has two poles, like the whole magnet.

activities.prompt: Every magnet has a North pole and a ______ pole.
activities.hint: This pole is the opposite of the North pole.
activities.explanation: North and South poles always come together.

options: Each piece has just one pole
Each piece has a North and a South pole

activities.explanation: Breaking makes smaller magnets. Each one still has a North and a South pole.

activities.prompt: Which sentence about magnet poles is correct?
options: A single North pole can exist.
A single South pole can exist.
North and South poles always exist in pairs.
One pole can stay after breaking.
activities.explanation: North and South poles always come in pairs.

activities.prompt: A bar magnet is broken into small pieces. Iron filings are sprinkled on the pieces. What pattern should you see?
options: Filings gather at both ends of each piece.
Filings gather only at one end of each piece.
Filings gather at the middle of each piece.
Filings gather on just one piece.

why.Filings gather only at one end of each p: This mistake thinks each small piece has only one pole.
why.Filings gather at the middle of each pie: This mistake says most filings gather in the middle.
This mistake thinks broken pieces cannot attract filings.

activities.explanation: This is right. Each small piece is a magnet. Most filings gather near its ends.

options: Spread iron filings and compare the ends with the middle.
Count the magnet pieces before the break.

why.Count the magnet pieces before the break: This mistake counts pieces but does not test where filings stick.
This mistake looks for a colour change that does not test the poles.
why.Measure the piece and choose its longer: This mistake uses size instead of checking where filings gather.

activities.explanation: This is right because filings show that most stick near the ends and few stick elsewhere.

lessons.title: Using a Suspended Magnet to Find Directions

activities.prompt: Could a hanging magnet help you find your way?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Magnet Finds the Way
activities.body:
You tie a thread around the middle of a bar magnet. Then you let it hang freely. First, turn it gently in the horizontal direction. After this, leave it to rest.

As the magnet settles, look along the line through its resting ends. This line shows its north-south direction. Turn the magnet again, then let it rest once more. It rests along the same line.

The end pointing north is called the North-seeking pole, or North pole. The end pointing south is called the South-seeking pole, or South pole. The Earth behaves like a giant magnet, guiding the suspended magnet.

Now try a small iron bar in the same way. It can rest in any direction because it is not a magnet. Only magnets rest along the north-south direction. A freely suspended magnet therefore shows you the north-south line.

This north-south resting property helps you find directions. You can use your suspended magnet to identify the north-south direction.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Magnet That Finds North and South
activities.body: Tie a thread around the middle of a bar magnet to suspend it. Turn it gently in the horizontal direction, then leave it to rest. The line through its resting ends shows the north-south direction. After another turn, it rests along the same line. A freely suspended magnet comes to rest along this direction. The end pointing north is the North pole. The end pointing south is the South pole.
keyPoints: The Earth behaves like a giant magnet.
Only magnets rest along the north-south direction.
The north-south resting property helps us find directions.
activities.explanation: The magnet's resting line reveals north and south.

activities.prompt: A child wants to find the north-south direction in a new place. How can a child use a bar magnet and a thread?
steps: Tie a thread around the middle of the bar magnet. Let it hang freely.
Turn the suspended magnet gently sideways. Leave it to rest. A freely suspended magnet settles along north-south.
Draw a line through the two resting ends. This line shows the north-south direction.
Call the end that points north the North-seeking pole. Call the end that points south the South-seeking pole. These names show which way each end points.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

Tie a thread around one end
Hold its middle with your hand
Place it on the ground

activities.prompt: You should leave the turned magnet to rest.

activities.title: Match Each Description
activities.prompt: Match each name to the right description.
activities.explanation: Each pole points to its direction. The Earth acts like a giant magnet.

activities.title: An Iron Bar That Is Not a Magnet

options: It can rest in any direction
It must point north
It must point south
It must rest north-south
activities.explanation: The iron bar is not a magnet. So it can rest in any direction.

activities.prompt: A small iron bar always lines up north and south.
activities.explanation: The iron bar is not a magnet. So it can rest in any direction.

activities.title: Finding Direction with a Suspended Magnet
activities.prompt: Put the steps for finding direction in order.
items: Tie a thread around the magnet's middle
Turn it gently in the horizontal (flat) direction
Leave it to rest
Look at the line through its two ends
activities.explanation: The magnet stops along north and south. Its ends show the direction.

activities.title: Why Suspended Magnets Help
activities.prompt: Why can a freely suspended magnet help you find directions?
options: Because its resting line shows north-south
Because it rests in any direction
Because its thread points north
Because it stays warmer in the north
activities.explanation: A freely suspended magnet rests along north-south, helping us find directions.

activities.prompt: Which setup shows the north-south direction best?
options: Suspend a bar magnet and let it rest.
Suspend an iron bar and let it rest.
Place a bar magnet on a flat table.
Hold a bar magnet by one end.

This mistake expects a non-magnet to show north-south.
This mistake thinks a magnet works without being suspended.
This mistake thinks holding one end lets it rest freely.

activities.explanation: This is right. A suspended magnet rests along north-south.

activities.prompt: A child says every object that hangs freely points north-south. Which test is the fairest?
options: Use a magnet and an iron bar, then compare where each rests.
Watch one magnet rest, then accept the result.
Hold an iron bar and note its angle.
Put a magnet on a table and watch it slide.

why.Watch one magnet rest, then accept the r: This checks only one magnet. It does not test every object.
This holds the iron bar, so it does not hang freely.
why.Put a magnet on a table and watch it sli: The magnet is not suspended, so it cannot show its resting direction.

activities.explanation: This is right. It compares a magnet with a non-magnet. It tests where each one rests.

lessons.title: Making and Using a Magnetic Compass

activities.prompt: How could you make a tiny compass with simple materials?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your First Magnetic Compass
activities.body:
You place an iron sewing needle on a wooden table. It looks simple, but it can become a compass. A magnetic compass holds a needle-shaped magnet. This magnet can rotate freely.

Take one pole of a magnet. Stroke the needle with it at least 30 to 40 times. Then test the needle with some pins. If pins or iron filings stick, the needle has become a magnet.

The attracted pins show that your needle is now magnetised. Next, pass it through a cork horizontally. The needle should rest across the cork. This makes a simple floating compass.

Float the cork and needle in a glass bowl filled with water. The magnetised needle can rotate freely on the water. Your simple magnetic compass is ready.

Long ago, Indians used a similar magnetic device for navigation at sea. The old device held a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece in oil. Your cork compass uses the same simple magnetic idea.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How to Make a Magnetic Compass
activities.body: A magnetic compass has a needle. The needle is a small magnet. It can turn freely. To make one, put an iron sewing needle on a wooden table. Rub it with one pole (end) of a magnet. Do this 30 to 40 times. If pins or iron filings stick, the needle is a magnet. Next, push the needle sideways through a cork. Float the cork and needle in water.
keyPoints: A compass needle can turn freely.
Rubbing it with one pole makes the needle magnetic.
The magnetised needle sits in a cork and floats on water.
activities.explanation: Start with the needle. Magnetise it. Then float it on the cork.

activities.prompt: How can an iron sewing needle become a magnetic compass?
steps: Place the iron sewing needle on a wooden table. This is where you start making the compass.
Stroke it with one pole of a magnet at least 30 to 40 times. This is how to magnetise the needle.
Test it with pins or iron filings. If they stick, the needle is a magnet.
Pass the magnetised needle through a cork sideways. Float it in water. This finishes the needle-and-cork compass.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What should you place on a wooden table first?
options: A cork
An iron sewing needle
A glass bowl
Some water

activities.prompt: Put a cork and a magnetised needle in a glass bowl full of ______.
activities.hint: This liquid lets the cork and needle float.
activities.explanation: The glass bowl holds the water. The cork and needle float in it.

activities.title: Magnetise the Needle
activities.prompt: What should you do to magnetise the needle?
options: Float it in a glass bowl
Stroke it with one pole of a magnet 30 to 40 times
Pass it straight up through a cork
Put it under an iron pin
activities.explanation: This step magnetises the needle.

activities.title: Match Each Thing to Its Use
activities.prompt: Match each thing to what it is used for.

activities.title: Put the Steps in Order
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Break a magnet into smaller pieces.
Each piece becomes a smaller magnet.
Each smaller magnet has a North pole and a South pole.
activities.explanation: Breaking makes smaller magnets. Each has a North pole and a South pole.

options: A cork filled with water

activities.explanation: Navigation means finding the way at sea. The old tool used fish-shaped iron kept in oil.

activities.prompt: An iron sewing needle lies on a wooden table. Nobody rubs it with a magnet. What is the best prediction?
options: No pins will stick to it.
Every pin will stick to it.
Some pins may stick to it.
It will spin freely in water.

This wrongly says every iron needle is a magnet.
This wrongly says iron alone can pull pins.
This wrongly mixes up an iron needle and a compass needle.

activities.explanation: This is right because putting iron on wood does not magnetise the needle.

activities.prompt: Which test best shows if the stroked needle is a magnet?
options: Hold pins near the stroked needle.
Check if it floats in water.
Check if it rests on wood.
Pass it through a cork.

Floating tests the compass, not magnetisation.
Resting on wood only shows where it sits.
Passing it through cork is a later step, not the magnet test.

activities.explanation: This is right. Pins or iron filings stick to it. That shows it is a magnet.

options: Pass it through cork horizontally, then float it in water.
Pass it through cork vertically, then float it in water.
Pass it through cork horizontally, then place it on wood.
Float the needle in water with no cork.

why.Pass it through cork vertically, then fl: This mistake pushes the needle through the cork the wrong way.
why.Pass it through cork horizontally, then: This mistake puts it on wood, not in water.
This mistake leaves out the cork, so it is not the right setup.

activities.explanation: This is right. The needle goes through the cork horizontally. Both then float in water.

activities.prompt: A child claims, "The needle became a magnet just because it is made of iron." What evidence would correct this claim?
options: Pins or iron filings stick to the needle.

The needle rests on a wooden table.
The needle passes through a cork horizontally.

This mistake offers no positive evidence that the needle is a magnet.
This mistake treats a simple placement on wood as evidence of magnetisation.

activities.explanation: This is right because attracted pins or iron filings show that the needle has become a magnet.

lessons.title: Attraction and Repulsion between Magnets

activities.prompt: What will you discover when two magnets meet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Magnetic Behaviour
activities.body:
You enter a tiny magnet workshop and hold two magnets. You bring their ends close together. A North pole attracts a South pole. The magnets move towards each other. But North poles repel each other. South poles repel each other too.

Next, you meet an iron bar. Both ends of the bar are attracted by a magnet. The magnet’s North and South poles attract both ends. You watch the bar respond to either pole.

Then you visit a magnetic compass. Its needle is also a magnet. Bring a North pole near the needle’s North pole. The needle moves away. Bring a South pole near that North pole. The needle moves closer.

You wonder how to check whether an object is a magnet. Repulsion can identify it. You hold the object near another magnet. A push-away response shows that it repels the magnet.

Finally, you place wood, cardboard, plastic or glass between the compass and a magnet. There is no appreciable change in the needle’s deflection. The magnetic effect can pass through non-magnetic materials. You watch the response through each material.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Like and Unlike Poles
activities.body: Like poles repel each other. Repel means push away. Two North poles push apart. Two South poles push apart too. Unlike poles attract each other. Attract means pull together. A North pole pulls towards a South pole. A magnet attracts both ends of an iron bar. A compass needle is also a magnet. So it can show these pushes and pulls.
keyPoints: A North pole and a South pole attract each other.
Two North poles repel each other.
Two South poles repel each other.
activities.explanation: Magnets attract unlike poles. They repel like poles.

activities.title: Explore attraction and repulsion!

tasks.say: Set the gap to 10 and leave flip at 0. Watch the facing poles.
tasks.then: The two magnets show either attraction or repulsion when their poles are close.

tasks.say: Keep the gap at 10 and change flip to 1. Compare the movement.
tasks.then: Flipping one magnet reverses whether the facing poles attract or repel.

tasks.say: Start at a gap of 80, then make the gap larger than 80 and compare.
tasks.then: The magnetic effect becomes stronger when the magnets are closer together.

activities.takeaway: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel, and magnets have a stronger effect when they are close.
activities.explanation: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel, and magnets have a stronger effect when they are close.

activities.prompt: A child puts a piece of cardboard between a magnet and a compass. The needle still moves. Why?
steps: The compass needle is a magnet. So another magnet can move it.
Cardboard does not change how far the needle turns. So it does not block the effect much.
The magnet's pull can pass through non-magnetic things, like cardboard. That is why the needle still moves.
So cardboard does not stop the magnet from moving the needle.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Using a Compass Needle
activities.body: You can tell a magnet by repulsion. Repulsion means pushing away. A compass needle is also a magnet. Its North pole moves away from a North pole. It moves closer to a South pole. Wood, cardboard, plastic and glass do not move the needle much. The magnetic effect can pass through non-magnetic materials.
keyPoints: A compass needle is a magnet.
Repulsion can tell you if something is a magnet.
Magnetic effects pass through non-magnetic materials.
activities.explanation: A compass needle helps you see attraction and repulsion.

activities.prompt: Two magnets have their North poles close together. What happens?
options: They attract each other.
They repel each other.
Nothing happens.
Only one pole moves.
activities.explanation: North poles repel each other. So they push away from each other.

activities.prompt: A North pole attracts a South pole.
activities.explanation: The North pole of one magnet attracts the South pole of another.

activities.prompt: Match each magnet fact to its result.
pairs: Both ends of an iron bar
activities.explanation: Like poles (same poles) repel. Unlike poles (different poles) attract. Iron bar ends attract too.

activities.prompt: A North pole comes near the North pole of a compass needle. What happens?
options: The needle moves closer.
The needle moves away.
The needle stays still.
The needle becomes iron.
activities.explanation: The needle's North pole moves away. Like poles repel (push away).

activities.prompt: Wood, cardboard, plastic and glass are ______ materials. A magnet's pull goes through them.
activities.hint: These materials do not change the needle much.
activities.explanation: A magnet's pull passes through these non-magnetic materials.

activities.prompt: A compass needle stays still when another North pole comes near its North pole.
activities.explanation: The needle moves away when its North pole meets another North pole.

activities.prompt: A magnet is outside a closed glass box. A compass needle is inside the box. What happens to the needle's deflection?
options: The needle turns farther away.
The needle's deflection changes a little.
The needle's deflection does not change much.
The needle stops moving.
activities.explanation: Glass does not change much. The magnet's pull can pass through glass.

activities.prompt: A South pole is brought near the North pole of a compass needle. What will happen to the needle?
options: The needle will move closer.
The needle will move away.
The needle will stay still.
The needle will spin faster.

This mistake treats like poles as attracting.
This mistake assumes cardboard blocks the magnetic action.
This mistake confuses movement with a faster spin.

activities.explanation: A South pole attracts the North pole of the compass needle.

activities.prompt: You put two North poles close together. What will the magnets do?
options: They will move farther apart.
They will move closer together.
They will stay in the same place.
They will move side by side.

This mistake treats two North poles like a North and a South pole.
This mistake thinks the poles do not push each other.
This mistake thinks the poles push them sideways.

activities.explanation: North poles repel each other, so they move farther apart.

lessons.title: Fun with Magnets and Keeping Them Safe

activities.prompt: What can magnets do, and how can you keep them safe?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Magnets
activities.body:
Imagine you meet a magnet during today’s science tour.
It can move some objects without even touching them.
Place one below a cardboard tray, and it can move steel balls through a maze.
Watch the steel balls move around the maze.
A magnet can pick up a steel paper clip that has fallen in water.

Now meet two magnet cars.
They may move towards each other or run away from each other.
Some magnets show their North and South poles with the letters N and S.
One North pole may be shown by a white dot.
Another may be painted red, while the South pole may be blue.

After the tour, you can arrange the magnets for storage.
Store them in pairs, with unlike poles on the same side.
Put a piece of wood between each pair.
Place two pieces of soft iron across the ends of the stored magnets.

Before you finish, check your storage steps.
Do not heat, drop or hammer magnets.
Those are the final rules for your magnet tour.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet Some Magnets
activities.body: Magnets can move some objects without touching them. A magnet below cardboard can move steel balls through a maze. It can pick up a steel paper clip from water. Two magnet cars may come together or run apart. Some magnets show North and South poles using N and S. White dots or red paint can mark North. Blue paint may mark South. Unlike means opposite.
keyPoints: Magnets can move some objects without touching them.
Magnet cars may come together or run apart.
Pole markings may include letters, white dots and colours.
activities.explanation: This card shows what magnets can do and how their poles may be marked.

activities.title: Explore Magnet Push and Pull

tasks.say: Flip the right magnet at a gap of 80 and compare it with the starting arrangement.
tasks.then: Different pole arrangements can make magnets move together or apart.

tasks.say: Keep this arrangement and reduce the gap to 20.
tasks.then: The magnetic push or pull becomes stronger when magnets are closer.

tasks.say: Keep the small gap and restore the starting orientation.
tasks.then: Turning a magnet around changes attraction into repulsion, or repulsion into attraction.

activities.takeaway: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract, and magnetic force is stronger when magnets are closer.
activities.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract, and magnetic force is stronger when magnets are closer.

activities.prompt: A steel ball is in a cardboard maze. Nobody touches it. How can the ball move?
steps: The ball moves when a magnet is under the cardboard tray.
This happens because magnets can move some things without touching them.
When you move the magnet under the tray, the ball moves through the maze.
So you can move the ball by moving the magnet under the tray.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Through the Maze
activities.prompt: A magnet moves steel balls through a cardboard maze. It does not touch them.
activities.explanation: Yes. A magnet under a cardboard tray can move steel balls.

activities.title: Match the Pole Marks
activities.prompt: Match each pole with a mark that can show it.
activities.explanation: These marks can show the poles. White dots and red paint can mark North. Blue paint can mark South.

activities.title: A Paper Clip That Fell
activities.prompt: A magnet can pick up a steel paper clip that fell in ______.
activities.hint: The paper clip fell into this.
activities.explanation: A magnet can pick up a steel paper clip in water.

activities.title: The Missing Wood
activities.prompt: When you store magnets, you should leave out the wood between each pair.
activities.explanation: Keep a piece of wood between each pair. This is one safe way to store them.

activities.title: Keep Magnets Safe
activities.prompt: Which is a safe way to keep these magnets?
options: Put all the magnets in one loose pile.
Heat the magnets before you keep them.
Pair them, put wood between them, and put soft iron across the ends.
Drop them on a hard floor before you keep them.
activities.explanation: Pairing, wood and soft iron keep magnets safe. Heating, dropping and hammering do not.

activities.title: Put the Storage Steps in Order
activities.prompt: Put these steps for storing magnets in order.
items: Store magnets in pairs.
Put unlike poles on the same side.
Keep wood between each pair.
Put two pieces of soft iron across the ends.
activities.explanation: These steps are in the right order. Each step helps keep the magnets safe.

activities.title: Use Magnets Carefully
activities.prompt: Which action helps keep a magnet safe?
options: Do not heat, drop or hammer it.
Heat it, then drop it, then hammer it.
Drop it onto a hard floor.
Hammer it before putting it away.
activities.explanation: Good choice. The lesson says not to heat, drop or hammer magnets.

activities.prompt: A child says a blue end on a magnet must be the North pole. What is the best answer?
options: It may be wrong, because blue may mark South.
It is right, because blue always marks North.
It may be wrong, because red may mark North.
It is right, because white dots mark South.

why.It is right, because blue always marks N: This mistake thinks blue is always the North pole.
why.It may be wrong, because red may mark No: This mistake swaps the red and blue markings.
why.It is right, because white dots mark Sou: This mistake swaps the meaning of the white dot.

activities.explanation: This is right. The South pole may be painted blue. So blue does not always mean North.

activities.prompt: Which plan is safest for storing many magnets?
options: Put unlike poles together, put wood between pairs, and use soft iron.
Put like poles together, put wood between pairs, and use soft iron.
Put unlike poles together, put wood between pairs, and heat them.
Put unlike poles together, drop them often, and use soft iron.

why.Put like poles together, put wood betwee: This mistake puts like poles together instead of unlike poles.
why.Put unlike poles together, put wood betw: This mistake heats the magnets. Magnets should not be heated.
why.Put unlike poles together, drop them oft: This mistake drops the magnets. Magnets should not be dropped.

activities.explanation: This plan is right. It follows the rules for unlike poles, wood between pairs, and soft iron on the ends.

activities.context: A traveller was in an unfamiliar place and could not see the stars, so a magnetic compass was used to find directions. In a classroom, a learner saw artificial magnets in a pencil box and on a sticker. These magnets had been made from iron, and a small iron object stuck to one of them. The learner also read that lodestones are naturally occurring magnets discovered long ago.
activities.prompt: What could the traveller do if the stars became visible during the journey?
options: It would remain a useful tool for finding directions.
It would be useless because it works only when stars cannot be seen.
It would change into a naturally occurring magnet.
It could then be used only to make magnets from iron.

why.It would be useless because it works onl: The compass is not limited to cloudy skies.
why.It would change into a naturally occurri: Visibility does not change what a compass is.
why.It could then be used only to make magne: Finding directions is not its magnetic-making role.

activities.explanation: A compass can help with directions.

activities.context: A traveller was in an unfamiliar place and could not see the stars, so a magnetic compass was used to find directions. In a classroom, a learner saw artificial magnets in a pencil box and on a sticker. These magnets had been made from iron, and a small iron object stuck to one of them. The learner also read that lodestones are naturally occurring magnets discovered long ago.
activities.prompt: The learner finds a magnet made from iron and wonders whether it is a lodestone or an artificial magnet. How should the learner classify it?
options: People made it, unlike a naturally occurring lodestone.
It is a lodestone because iron occurs in nature.
It is both a natural magnet and an artificial magnet.
It cannot be either because iron cannot be used to make magnets.

why.It is a lodestone because iron occurs in: Iron occurring naturally does not make it a lodestone.
why.It is both a natural magnet and an artif: A magnet cannot be both kinds here.
why.It cannot be either because iron cannot: Magnets can be made from iron.

activities.explanation: A magnet made from iron was made by people.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between a lodestone and an artificial magnet.
activities.answer: A lodestone is a naturally occurring magnet that was discovered long ago. An artificial magnet is made by people. Magnets used in pencil boxes, stickers and toys are artificial magnets. People can also make magnets from iron, and magnets can be made in many different shapes.
points: Lodestones occur naturally.
Artificial magnets are made by people.
Examples of artificial magnets are given.
Magnets can be made from iron and in different shapes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student scattered iron filings around a bar magnet. Many filings gathered at the two ends, but only a few attached along the rest of the bar. The student broke the magnet into two smaller pieces and checked them. Each piece had a North pole and a South pole, so the student wondered whether breaking it again could ever leave a piece with just one pole.
activities.prompt: If the student scattered iron filings around one of the smaller magnets, where would the greatest number of filings be expected to attach?
options: Near both ends of the smaller magnet
Only around the middle of the smaller magnet
Only at one end of the smaller magnet
Evenly along the whole smaller magnet

why.Only around the middle of the smaller ma: Only a few filings stick to the remaining part.
why.Only at one end of the smaller magnet: Both ends should show the greatest gathering.
why.Evenly along the whole smaller magnet: An even covering does not match the pattern.

activities.explanation: The greatest number of filings stick near the ends.

activities.context: A student scattered iron filings around a bar magnet. Many filings gathered at the two ends, but only a few attached along the rest of the bar. The student broke the magnet into two smaller pieces and checked them. Each piece had a North pole and a South pole, so the student wondered whether breaking it again could ever leave a piece with just one pole.
activities.prompt: What should the student tell someone who claims that breaking a magnet repeatedly could produce a magnet with only one pole?
options: The claim is impossible because a single kind of pole cannot exist by itself
Repeated breaking could eventually produce a piece with one pole
Keeping just one half would remove its other pole
Breaking in a different way could separate the two poles

why.Repeated breaking could eventually produ: Further breaking still leaves both poles in every piece.
why.Keeping just one half would remove its o: Choosing one half does not remove either pole.
why.Breaking in a different way could separa: No separate single pole can be obtained.

activities.explanation: North and South poles always exist in pairs.

activities.prompt: Explain why most iron filings gather near the ends of a bar magnet while only a few attach to its remaining part.
activities.answer: The greatest number of iron filings stick near the two ends of a bar magnet. This is why a large gathering appears at each end in the case. Only a few filings stick to the remaining part, so the middle does not have as many filings attached.
points: Iron filings are small pieces of iron.
The greatest number stick near the ends.
Only a few stick to the remaining part.
The case shows larger gatherings at the ends.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student is in a place where directions are unknown and has a bar magnet, a thread, and a small iron bar. The student suspends the magnet by tying the thread around its middle, turns it gently in the horizontal direction, and leaves it to rest. The magnet's resting ends form a north-south line. After another turn and release, it settles along the same line. The student then tests the small iron bar.
activities.prompt: After the magnet comes to rest, what should the student do to identify its north pole?
options: Call the end facing north the North-seeking pole.
Call the end facing south the North-seeking pole.
Record both ends as North-seeking poles.
Choose either end as the North-seeking pole.

why.Call the end facing south the North-seek: The south-pointing end should be called the South pole.
One end points north while the other points south.
why.Choose either end as the North-seeking p: The north pole must be the end actually pointing north.

activities.explanation: This option names the north-pointing end correctly.

activities.context: A student is in a place where directions are unknown and has a bar magnet, a thread, and a small iron bar. The student suspends the magnet by tying the thread around its middle, turns it gently in the horizontal direction, and leaves it to rest. The magnet's resting ends form a north-south line. After another turn and release, it settles along the same line. The student then tests the small iron bar.
activities.prompt: If the student suspends the small iron bar in place of the bar magnet, what should the student expect?
options: It will rest along the north-south line like the magnet did.
It will remain pointing in whichever direction it is turned.
It can stop in any direction because it is not a magnet.
Its north end will be the end facing north, just as with the magnet.

why.It will rest along the north-south line: The small iron bar does not have the north-south resting property of a magnet.
why.It will remain pointing in whichever dir: The iron bar is not a magnet, so it need not remain in the turned direction.
why.Its north end will be the end facing nor: The North and South pole terms apply to the magnet, not the iron bar.

activities.explanation: This correctly explains that the iron bar can rest in any direction.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between how a freely suspended bar magnet and a small iron bar come to rest.
activities.answer: A freely suspended bar magnet comes to rest along the north-south direction. A small iron bar is not a magnet, so it can rest in any direction. This difference happens because only magnets have the north-south resting property used to find directions.
points: A freely suspended magnet rests north-south.
A small iron bar can rest in any direction.
The iron bar is not a magnet.
The property helps us find directions.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the pins sticking to the needle show that the needle has become a magnet.
activities.answer: After the iron needle is stroked with one pole of a magnet, it acts like a magnet. The pins provide evidence of this change because they cling to the needle. This check helps the maker confirm that the needle is ready for the compass.
points: The needle was stroked with one pole of a magnet.
Attracted pins cling to the needle.
The attracted pins show that it has become a magnet.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child has two bar magnets, an iron bar, and a magnetic compass on a wooden table. One magnet is held with its North pole facing the compass needle’s North pole. The needle moves away. The child then places a cardboard sheet between the compass and the magnet. The needle still changes position. Finally, the child brings the magnet’s North pole near one end of the iron bar.
activities.prompt: What will happen when the magnet’s North pole is brought near the iron bar?
options: The near end of the iron bar will be pulled toward the magnet.
The near end of the iron bar will be pushed away from the magnet.
Neither end of the iron bar will move toward the magnet.
Only the far end of the iron bar will be pulled toward the magnet.

why.The near end of the iron bar will be pus: This wrongly treats attraction as repulsion.
why.Neither end of the iron bar will move to: This wrongly assumes that the iron bar will not respond.
why.Only the far end of the iron bar will be: This wrongly assumes that only the far end is attracted.

activities.explanation: Correct: a magnet attracts both ends of an iron bar.

activities.context: A child has two bar magnets, an iron bar, and a magnetic compass on a wooden table. One magnet is held with its North pole facing the compass needle’s North pole. The needle moves away. The child then places a cardboard sheet between the compass and the magnet. The needle still changes position. Finally, the child brings the magnet’s North pole near one end of the iron bar.
activities.prompt: What will happen to the compass needle after the cardboard sheet is placed between it and the magnet?
options: The needle will continue to move away from the magnet.
The needle will move closer to the magnet.
The needle will stay still and show no deflection.
The needle will turn toward the iron bar instead.

why.The needle will move closer to the magne: This wrongly treats North poles as attracting each other.
why.The needle will stay still and show no d: This wrongly assumes that cardboard blocks the magnetic effect.
why.The needle will turn toward the iron bar: Nothing in the case shows that the iron bar turns the compass needle.

activities.explanation: Correct: cardboard causes no appreciable change in the deflection.

activities.prompt: Explain why the compass needle moved away when the magnet’s North pole was brought near it.
activities.answer: Moving a North pole near the compass needle’s North pole makes the needle move away because North poles repel each other. The compass needle behaves as a magnet, so its North pole interacts with the North pole of the other magnet.
points: The compass needle is a magnet.
Two North poles repel each other.
The needle therefore moves away.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student places steel balls in a maze on a cardboard tray. When a magnet is moved below the tray, the balls move through the maze. The student then drops a steel paper clip into water and reaches for a magnet. Another magnet has a white dot and blue paint on its ends. Before storing the magnets, the student checks their poles and arranges them safely.
activities.prompt: What will most likely happen as the student moves the magnet below the cardboard tray?
options: The balls will travel through the maze while the magnet remains below the tray.
The balls will stay still until someone pushes them through the maze.
The balls will move only after the magnet touches them above the tray.
The balls will move straight through the cardboard instead of following the maze.

why.The balls will stay still until someone: The case does not say that the balls need a push.
why.The balls will move only after the magne: The magnet can move the balls without touching them.
why.The balls will move straight through the: The stated movement is through the maze, not through the cardboard.

activities.explanation: A magnet below cardboard can move steel balls through a maze.

activities.context: A student places steel balls in a maze on a cardboard tray. When a magnet is moved below the tray, the balls move through the maze. The student then drops a steel paper clip into water and reaches for a magnet. Another magnet has a white dot and blue paint on its ends. Before storing the magnets, the student checks their poles and arranges them safely.
activities.prompt: Which arrangement follows the rules for storing the magnets safely?
options: Put magnets in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, place wood between each pair, and place two pieces of soft iron across the ends.
Put magnets in pairs with like poles on the same side, place wood between each pair, and place two pieces of soft iron across the ends.
Put magnets in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, keep each pair together without wood, and place two pieces of soft iron across the ends.
Put magnets in pairs with unlike poles on the same side, place wood between each pair, and leave the ends without soft iron.

why.Put magnets in pairs with like poles on: Like poles on the same side do not follow the storage rule.
why.Put magnets in pairs with unlike poles o: A piece of wood must be placed between each pair.
Two pieces of soft iron must be placed across the ends.

activities.explanation: Unlike poles belong on the same side of stored pairs.

activities.prompt: Explain how a magnet can move the steel balls and the paper clip without touching them.
activities.answer: Magnets can move some objects without touching them. Thus, a magnet below the cardboard tray can move the steel balls through the maze. This also lets a magnet pick up the steel paper clip after it falls into water, without the magnet and clip touching first.
points: Magnets can move some objects without touching them.
A magnet below cardboard can move steel balls through a maze.
A magnet can pick up a steel paper clip from water.
The movement does not require the magnet and object to touch first.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

chapters.title: Measurement of Length and Motion
chapters.summary: In this chapter: 5.1 measuring with body parts; 5.2 standard units of length; 5.3 measuring length correctly; 5.4 curved lines and 5.5 describing position.

lessons.title: 5.1 Measuring with Body Parts

activities.prompt: Why might your body be useful for measuring?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Body Measures
activities.body:
You visit Deepa's grandmother. She measures cloth using the length of her arm. You wonder how her arm helps her measure the cloth.

Next, you meet a farmer. He can measure land by walking and counting his strides. Farmers may also use the length of their feet. You consider two ways to measure.

Then you visit Deepa's mother. She calls a handspan a balisht. Soon, five friends test their handspans. You find that their handspans have different lengths. The number of handspans needed for the table is different for everyone.

Now you learn how to describe a measured length. It needs a number and a unit. In 13 handspans, 13 is the number and handspan is the unit. A standard unit should give the same measurement for everyone measuring the same length.

Finally, you see scales and measuring tapes. These tools are useful because body-based units can differ between people. A standard unit helps everyone measure the same length consistently.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Measuring with Your Body
activities.body: Body-based measurements use a person’s body as a unit. A handspan is one such unit, and Deepa’s mother calls it a balisht. People can have different handspan lengths, so the same length may need different numbers of handspans. Every measured length has a number and a unit. A standard unit should give everyone the same measurement for the same length. Scales and measuring tapes are useful because body-based units can differ between people.
keyPoints: Arms, feet, strides and handspans can measure length.
A measured length has a number and a unit.
A standard unit gives the same measurement for everyone.
activities.explanation: Different handspan lengths can give different measurements.

activities.prompt: Two friends measure the same table using their own handspans. Why might their results differ, and what should be used when everyone must get the same result?
steps: The friends' handspans have different lengths, as five friends found.
Different handspan lengths can make the same table need different numbers of handspans.
A standard unit is useful for shared measuring because it should give everyone the same measurement.
Therefore, body-based measures may differ between people, while scales and measuring tapes can help people agree on a measurement.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Walking Across Land
activities.prompt: A farmer can measure land by walking and counting his steps.
activities.explanation: Yes. Walking and counting steps is one way to measure land.

activities.title: Another Word for Handspan
activities.prompt: Deepa’s mother says ______ for a handspan.
activities.hint: This word means handspan in Deepa’s home.
activities.explanation: Deepa’s mother says balisht for a handspan.

activities.title: Number and Unit
activities.prompt: Which word is the unit in “13 handspans”?
options: handspan
length
table
activities.explanation: The number is 13. The unit is handspan.

activities.title: Measuring the Table
activities.prompt: All five friends needed the same number of handspans to measure the table.
activities.explanation: Their handspans had different lengths. So the numbers were different.

activities.title: Why Are Answers Different?
activities.prompt: Two friends measure the same table. They use their handspans. Why can their answers be different?
options: Their handspans can have different lengths.
Handspans have the same length for everyone.
Only one handspan can measure a table.
A handspan measurement has no unit.
activities.explanation: Different handspans can give different numbers for one table.

activities.title: Using a Standard Unit
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order. Show how a standard unit helps.
items: Choose a standard unit
Measure the same length
Everyone gets the same measurement
activities.explanation: A standard unit gives everyone the same measurement.

activities.prompt: Two friends measure the same table by placing their own handspans end to end. What will likely happen?
options: They will likely count different numbers of handspans.
They must count exactly the same number of handspans.
The longer handspan will need more repeats.
Each friend will use the same standard unit.

why.They must count exactly the same number: This wrongly assumes that every person's handspan has the same length.
why.The longer handspan will need more repea: This reverses the idea that a longer handspan needs fewer repeats.
why.Each friend will use the same standard u: This mistakes a body-based unit for one that gives the same result for everyone.

activities.explanation: Their handspans have different lengths, so the counts can differ.

activities.prompt: Two friends say, 'A handspan is a standard unit to measure a table.' What mistake are they making?
options: They think a table cannot be measured with handspans.
They think the number of handspans never changes.
They think a length does not need a unit.
They ignore that people's handspans can be different sizes.

why.They think a table cannot be measured wi: A table can be measured with handspans. So this is wrong.
why.They think the number of handspans never: The number of handspans can change if people's handspans differ.
why.They think a length does not need a unit: A length needs a unit and a number.

activities.explanation: Their mistake is ignoring that handspans differ between people.

activities.prompt: A child writes a table's length as "13 handspans." What does this show? Why can others not compare it fairly?
options: It shows 13 handspans. But people's hands can be different sizes.
It shows 13 standard units. So all people will agree.
It shows a unit but no number. So nobody can read it.
It shows a number but no unit. So the table size is unknown.

why.It shows 13 standard units. So all peopl: A handspan is a body unit. It is not the same for everyone.
why.It shows a unit but no number. So nobody: The record has 13 and handspans. So it does have a number.
why.It shows a number but no unit. So the ta: The record has handspans and 13. So it does have a unit.

activities.explanation: The number is 13. The unit is handspan. People's handspans can be different lengths.

funFacts: Ancient Egyptians measured with the cubit, the length from their elbow to their middle fingertip.
Horses are still measured in hands today. One hand is 4 inches, a unit based on a human hand.
Long before rulers, people used their hands, feet and fingers to measure things.

lessons.title: 5.2 Standard Units of Length

activities.prompt: How do people agree on how to measure length?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Length Units
activities.body:
Your tour begins with three curious words: angula, dhanusa and yojana. These were units named in ancient Indian literature. You pause to notice that traditional carpenters and tailors still use the angula.

You now travel between countries and wonder why everyone measures alike. Travel had caused confusion about measurements, so different countries adopted shared standard units. The system used now is called the International System of Units, or SI units. Its unit of length is the metre, and its symbol is m.

You hold a metre scale and look closely. It is divided into 100 equal divisions. Each division on the scale is called a centimetre. This also shows that one metre equals 100 centimetres. Looking closer still, you find that one centimetre equals 10 millimetres.

Your tour now moves towards longer distances. One kilometre equals 1000 metres. Finally, you meet the inch and learn that one inch equals 2.54 centimetres. You finish with a clearer picture of how these units compare.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Our shared standard units
activities.body: Different countries agreed on shared standard units. This was because travel had caused confusion about measurements. The system we use now is the International System of Units. It is called SI units for short. Its unit of length is the metre. It is written as m. A metre has 100 equal parts. Each part is called a centimetre.
keyPoints: Shared units reduce confusion when people travel.
The SI unit of length is the metre.
Each part of a metre is called a centimetre.
activities.explanation: Shared units help people everywhere measure length clearly.

activities.prompt: A carpenter uses the angula. A traveller uses a measure from another country. Why can this cause confusion? Which shared unit should they use for length?
steps: The angula is an old Indian unit of length.
Some carpenters and tailors still use the angula today.
Travel caused confusion about measurements. So countries chose shared standard units.
The system used now is SI. Its unit of length is the metre. So the metre is the shared length unit.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: An old measuring unit
