lessons.title: 5.3 Measuring Length Correctly

activities.prompt: What helps you measure each object accurately?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your Measuring Tour
activities.body:
You begin by choosing a scale suitable for the length you need to measure. A 15-cm scale can be used to measure a pencil.

A metre scale or measuring tape may be needed to measure a room’s height. A flexible measuring tape is more suitable for measuring a tree’s girth or chest size. You match the scale to each length before you begin measuring.

You place the scale beside the object so it touches the object along its length. You keep your eye directly above the tip of the object while reading the scale. If the zero mark is unclear, you use another full mark on the scale.

You use a flexible measuring tape or thread to measure a curved line. If you use thread, you straighten it before measuring its length with a metre scale.

Finally, you write down the measurement. A written measurement must include both a number and its unit. Your tour ends with a measurement that includes its unit.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Measuring Length Correctly
activities.body: Choose a scale that is right for the length. Use a 15-cm scale for a pencil. You may need a metre scale for a room's height. Use a flexible tape to measure a tree's girth (distance around it). Put the scale beside the object. Keep it touching the object along its length. Keep your eye right above the end. If the zero mark is not clear, use another whole number mark. A measurement needs a number and a unit. A unit is like cm or m. For curved lines, use a flexible tape or thread.
keyPoints: Choose the right scale.
Put the scale in the right place.
Measure curved lines with flexible tape or thread.
activities.explanation: The right tool and careful placing help you measure well.

activities.prompt: How can a child measure a pencil the right way and write the answer?
steps: Pick a 15-cm scale. It is good for a pencil.
Put the scale next to the pencil. It must lie along the whole pencil.
Keep your eye right above the pencil's tip. Then read the number.
Write the number and its unit. You need both.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Match the Tool
activities.prompt: Match each tool with what it measures best.
pairs: a tree's girth (distance around it) or chest size
activities.explanation: Each tool fits the thing it measures.

activities.title: A Room's Height
activities.prompt: You may need a metre scale or a measuring tape to measure a room's height.
activities.explanation: You may need a metre scale or measuring tape for a room's height.

activities.title: Put the Scale
activities.prompt: Where should you put the scale when you measure an object?
options: Next to it, touching along its length.
Above it, away from the object.
At one end, without touching it.
Far away, behind the object.
activities.explanation: The scale must touch the object along its length.

activities.title: Write the Measurement
activities.prompt: A written measurement needs a number and its ______.
activities.hint: This tells you what the number measures.
activities.explanation: A written measurement needs both a number and its unit.

activities.title: Measure a Curved Line
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order. Use thread to measure a curved line.
items: Put the thread on the curved line.
Straighten the thread.
Measure the length with a metre scale.
Write the number and its unit.
activities.explanation: Straighten the thread before you measure it with a metre scale.

activities.title: Choose the Correct Setup
activities.prompt: Which measuring setup follows the rules?
options: Measure a pencil with a 15-cm scale touching it along its length.
Measure a tree's girth with flexible tape, reading below the tip.
Measure a curved line with thread, leaving it curved.
Measure a pencil with a 15-cm scale placed far away.
activities.explanation: This choice uses a suitable scale and correct placement.

activities.prompt: A child needs tools for two measurements: a pencil and a tree's girth. Which choice is most suitable?
options: A 15-cm scale for the pencil; flexible measuring tape for the girth.
A 15-cm scale for the girth; flexible measuring tape for the pencil.
A metre scale for the pencil; a 15-cm scale for the girth.
A metre scale for the pencil; thread for the girth.

why.A 15-cm scale for the girth; flexible me: This swaps the tools because the child has mixed up their uses.
why.A metre scale for the pencil; a 15-cm sc: A metre scale can measure a pencil, but a short scale does not suit a tree's girth.
why.A metre scale for the pencil; thread for: The child has confused measuring a tree's girth with measuring a curved line.

activities.explanation: A 15-cm scale suits a pencil, and flexible measuring tape suits a tree's girth.

activities.prompt: A child puts a ruler slanted over a pencil. It touches at one end only. What should the child do next?
options: Put it next to the pencil, along its length.
Keep it slanted, touching at one end only.
Hold it above the pencil with a small gap.
Move the pencil's tip away from the ruler.

why.Keep it slanted, touching at one end onl: This keeps the ruler slanted. It is not along the pencil.
why.Hold it above the pencil with a small ga: A gap means the ruler does not touch the pencil.
why.Move the pencil's tip away from the rule: Moving the tip away does not help.

activities.explanation: The ruler must be next to the pencil and touch it along its length.

activities.prompt: Two children read the same pencil. One looks straight down at the tip. The other looks from the side. Which child has the better reading position?
options: The child looking straight above the pencil's tip.
The child looking from the side of the pencil.
The child standing farther from the pencil.
The child holding the pencil away from the scale.

why.The child looking from the side of the p: This child does not look straight above the tip.
why.The child standing farther from the penc: Standing farther away does not fix where the eye is.
why.The child holding the pencil away from t: Moving the pencil does not fix the reading position.

activities.explanation: The eye must be straight above the tip when reading the scale.

lessons.title: 5.4 Curved Lines and 5.5 Describing Position

activities.prompt: How can we describe someone’s position using a clear starting point?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Reference Points for Distance
activities.body:
You meet friends who compare how far places are from their homes. Their observations differ because each child measures from a different house. Their observations would agree if they measured from the same object or point. You call this fixed object or point a reference point.

Now you help the friends plan a Kabaddi court. They plan to draw its lines with chuna powder. First, they choose one point on the ground. They will measure all distances from this point.

Next, you see kilometre stones while Padma moves closer to Delhi. A kilometre stone shows that Delhi is 70 km away. The next kilometre stone shows that Delhi is 60 km away. The decreasing numbers show that Padma is getting closer to Delhi.

You now describe Padma’s position by using Delhi as the reference point. When the stone reads 70 km, Padma’s position is 70 km from Delhi. When the stone reads 60 km, Padma’s position is 60 km from Delhi.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Measuring from a Reference Point
activities.body: Distance can look different when people measure from different houses. Their results can match if they measure from the same object or point. A starting point that does not move is a reference point. Padma used Delhi as her reference point. The stones on the road showed 70 km, then 60 km. Padma was getting closer to Delhi.
keyPoints: Distance measurements can be different.
A reference point is a starting point that does not move.
Padma measured her distance from Delhi.
activities.explanation: A reference point gives everyone the same starting place for distances.

activities.prompt: Two children measure the distance to one tree. Each child starts from their own house. Why do their answers differ? How can they get the same answer?
steps: One child measures from one house. The other measures from another house.
Their answers can differ. Each child has a different starting point.
If both children start at the same house, their answers will match. They use the same starting point.
The same starting point is the reference point for both. A reference point is where you start measuring.
activities.explanation: Think about it with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why did the children give different distance observations?
options: They all measured from one point.
They measured from different houses.
They used different rulers.
They measured from Padma's position.
activities.explanation: They measured from different houses, so their starting points were different.

activities.prompt: What did the friends choose before they measured for the Kabaddi court?
options: A different point for each line
The first kilometre stone
Every child's house
One point on the ground
activities.explanation: They chose one point on the ground. Then they measured every distance from it.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct fact.
activities.explanation: Delhi was the reference point for both distances.

activities.prompt: The next kilometre stone shows 60 km. Where was Padma?
options: 60 km from the stone
70 km from Delhi
60 km from Delhi
70 km from the stone
activities.explanation: The stone shows how far Padma was from Delhi.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order.
items: The first kilometre stone shows Delhi is 70 km away.
The next kilometre stone shows Delhi is 60 km away.
Padma knows she is getting closer to Delhi.
activities.explanation: The distance went down from 70 km to 60 km. So Padma was closer.

activities.prompt: Two children measure the distance to one object. Each child starts at their own house. Why do their results differ?
options: They use different houses as starting points.
They measure the same house in opposite ways.
They change the reference point between checks.
They add both distances before giving answers.

why.They measure the same house in opposite: This mistake says the measuring direction changed. That is not the cause.
why.They change the reference point between: This mistake says the reference point changed. But the children used different houses.
why.They add both distances before giving an: This mistake says adding distances explains it. That is not true.

activities.explanation: This is right. Each child measures from a different house.

activities.prompt: Two children want to compare how far they are from one object. They want it to be fair. What should they do next?
options: Measure both distances from the same point.
Measure each distance from a different house.
Measure the object once from each side.
Pick the smaller distance.

why.Measure each distance from a different h: This keeps the starting points different. So their results may not match.
This changes the measuring places, so they are not the same.
This picks an answer. It does not measure fairly.

activities.explanation: This is right. Using one same point gives them the same reference point.

activities.prompt: The friends chose one point on the ground. Why did they do this before drawing the Kabaddi court lines?
options: All distances use one reference point.
Every court line ends at the chosen point.
The chuna powder becomes the reference point.
The court lines need no reference point.

why.Every court line ends at the chosen poin: This wrongly says every line must end at the chosen point.
why.The chuna powder becomes the reference p: This mixes up the drawing powder with the measuring point.
This ignores the chosen point, which gives all distances one start.

activities.explanation: This is right. All measurements from the chosen point use one reference point.

activities.prompt: Padma's stones show 70 km, then 60 km, from Delhi. What does this tell us about Padma?
options: She is getting closer to Delhi.
She is getting farther from Delhi.
She has already reached Delhi.
Her distance stays the same.

This would be true if the distance grew. But it went down.
This is wrong. 60 km is still a distance from Delhi.
This is wrong. The distance changed, from 70 km to 60 km.

activities.explanation: This is right. The distance from Delhi went down, from 70 km to 60 km.

activities.prompt: Padma's distance from Delhi changes from 60 km to 70 km. What does this show?
options: She is moving farther from Delhi.
She is moving closer to Delhi.
She has already reached Delhi.
Her distance is not changing.

This fits a distance that gets smaller. But the distance got bigger.
This is wrong. The reading still shows a distance from Delhi.
This is wrong. The distance changes from 60 km to 70 km.

activities.explanation: This is right. Her distance from Delhi gets bigger: 60 km to 70 km.

activities.prompt: A child says, “The 70 km stone means Padma is 70 km from the stone.” What is the best correction?
options: Padma is 70 km from Delhi.
Padma is 70 km from the stone.
Padma is 70 km from her house.
Padma is 70 km from the court.

This repeats the mistake of treating the stone as the reference point.
This assumes her house is the reference point, but Delhi is used.
This assumes the court is the reference point, but Delhi is used.

activities.explanation: This is right because Delhi is the reference point for Padma's distance.

lessons.title: 5.6 Moving Things

activities.prompt: What could change your view about moving things?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Moving Things
activities.body:
You join Deepa as she watches the passengers inside a moving bus. After a minute, the passengers are still in their seats. Their positions are not changing with time, so they seem at rest.

Now you choose the bus as the reference point. This helps you decide whether an object is at rest or in motion. Compared with the bus, the passengers are at rest.

Next, you look towards a building outside the bus. You use its position as the reference point. From the building’s position, both the passengers and the bus are moving.

After this tour, you see that motion depends on your chosen reference point. You also meet objects that may travel in straight lines. A falling eraser may move along a straight line. An orange dropped from a tree may do the same. Students marching in a parade may move on a straight-line path. A heavy box that is pushed may move along a straight line.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Motion and Reference Points
activities.body: Motion depends on the reference point you choose. A reference point is a thing you compare with. A reference point helps us see if something is moving. If it is not moving, it is at rest (still). Use the bus as the reference point. The people on the bus stayed in their seats. So they were at rest. Now use a building outside as the reference point. Then the bus and the people were both moving.
keyPoints: Motion depends on the reference point you choose.
The people were at rest, compared to the bus.
The bus and the people were moving, compared to a building.
activities.explanation: A good reference point helps you see motion clearly.

activities.prompt: A child says: 'The passengers are not moving. But the bus is moving.' How can both be true?
steps: Choose the bus as the reference point. A reference point is what we compare with.
The passengers sit in their seats. Their place does not change. So they are at rest compared to the bus.
Choose a building outside the bus as a new reference point.
Compared to the building, the passengers and the bus are both moving. So both statements can be true.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Moving Along a Straight Line
activities.body: Some moving things may follow a straight-line path. A falling eraser may move along a straight line. An orange dropped from a tree may move in a straight line. Students marching in a parade may move on a straight-line path. A heavy box that is pushed may move along a straight line.
keyPoints: A falling eraser may move along a straight line.
A dropped orange may move in a straight line.
Marching students and a pushed box may also move straight.
activities.explanation: Different moving objects may share a straight-line path.

activities.prompt: The bus was the reference point. The passengers were at ______.
activities.hint: Use the word that means not moving.
activities.explanation: The passengers were at rest. The bus was the reference point.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the correct fact.
activities.explanation: Delhi was the reference point for both distances.

activities.prompt: Put Deepa's observations and conclusion in order.
items: Deepa found the passengers after a minute
The passengers were still in their seats
Their positions did not change with time
Deepa used the bus as the reference point
The passengers were at rest
activities.explanation: Her observations lead to the conclusion. The passengers are at rest compared with the bus.

activities.prompt: A building outside the bus is the reference point. What was true?
options: Both the passengers and the bus were moving.
The passengers were at rest, but the bus was still.
The building was moving, but the passengers were still.
The passengers and the bus were both at rest.
activities.explanation: Seen from the building, both the passengers and the bus were moving.

activities.prompt: When you push a heavy box, it must move in a straight line.
activities.explanation: The box may move in a straight line. But this is not always true.

funFacts: Earth spins around once every day, so you are always moving, even when you sit still.
Our whole solar system moves around the centre of the Milky Way galaxy.
Stars look still, but they are moving very fast through space.

lessons.title: 5.7 Types of Motion

activities.prompt: Ready to explore what helps us tell different kinds of motion apart?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Types of Motion
activities.body:
Imagine a tour of motion. You move along a straight line. This is called linear motion. Soon, you enter a circular path. This is called circular motion. An object in circular motion travels around the circular path again and again.

Here, you meet motion to and fro. This is called oscillatory motion. An object in oscillatory motion repeats its movement to and fro. Oscillatory motion is periodic, just like circular motion.

Periodic motion means an object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. Circular and oscillatory motion are both periodic. They repeat their paths again and again.

Now, you press a metal strip. Its free end moves up and down. You also see an eraser moving on a thread. This movement is similar to a swing. You can classify motion as linear, circular or oscillatory.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Motion has different types
activities.body: Linear motion means moving along a straight line. Circular motion means moving around in a circle. Oscillatory motion means moving back and forth around one place. Periodic motion repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. A fixed interval means the same time gap every time. Both circular and oscillatory motion are periodic.
keyPoints: Linear motion goes along a straight line.
Circular and oscillatory motions repeat their movement.
Periodic motion repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
activities.explanation: You can sort motion by its path or pattern.

activities.title: Explore swinging motion

tasks.say: Make the string longer than 40 cm and watch the swing.
tasks.then: A longer pendulum swings more slowly.

tasks.say: Make the string shorter than 40 cm and watch the swing.
tasks.then: A shorter pendulum swings more quickly.

activities.takeaway: A pendulum shows oscillatory motion: it moves to and fro, repeating its path after a fixed interval of time.
activities.explanation: A pendulum shows oscillatory motion: it moves to and fro, repeating its path after a fixed interval of time.

activities.prompt: One toy moves on a straight track. One toy goes around a circle. One toy moves back and forth around one fixed point. How can you tell their motion types apart? What do they share?
steps: First, watch the first toy's path. A path on one straight line is linear motion.
Next, watch the second toy's path. Going around a circle is circular motion.
Then watch the third toy. Moving back and forth around one point is oscillatory motion.
Last, compare what repeats. Circular and oscillatory motion are both periodic.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Match each description with the right kind of motion.
pairs: Moves back and forth around a fixed place
The free end of a pressed metal strip
activities.explanation: Each description matches the path or movement from the lesson.

activities.prompt: An object moves on the same path again and again. It returns after the same time each time. What is this motion called?
options: Linear motion
Circular motion
Periodic motion
Oscillatory motion
activities.explanation: Periodic motion goes on the same path again after the same time. That matches the clue.

activities.prompt: Both circular motion and oscillatory motion are periodic.
activities.explanation: True! Circular motion repeats around a path. Oscillatory motion also repeats back and forth.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order. They show why circular motion is periodic.
items: The object moves around the circle.
The object goes around the path again and again.
The path repeats after the same amount of time.
activities.explanation: Circular motion goes around the same path again and again. Motion that repeats after the same time is periodic motion.

activities.prompt: Which answer tells what linear motion is, and which motions are periodic?
options: Linear means round motion; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
Linear means oscillatory motion; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
Linear means staying still; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
Linear means straight-line motion; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
activities.explanation: Linear motion goes in a straight line. Circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.

options: Their counts will probably be different.
Their counts must all be the same.
The friend with the longest handspan needs more handspans.

This ignores that the handspans are different lengths.
why.The friend with the longest handspan nee: A longer handspan makes the number needed smaller.

activities.context: Deepa's grandmother measured cloth using the length of her arm. When five friends tried measuring a table with their handspans, they found that their handspans had different lengths, and the number of handspans needed was different for everyone. Deepa's mother calls a handspan a balisht. A farmer can measure land by walking and counting his strides, or by using the length of his feet.
activities.prompt: The friends measure a table. They want the same answer. What should they do?
options: Use a standard unit. Then everyone can get the same answer.
Keep using each person's handspan. Everyone has the same hand length.
Compare only the numbers from handspans. Ignore the units.
Let each person use a different body part. Expect one shared result.

why.Keep using each person's handspan. Every: The friends' handspans did not all have the same length.
A length needs both a number and a unit.
why.Let each person use a different body par: Different body units can give different results.

activities.context: Deepa's grandmother measured cloth using the length of her arm. When five friends tried measuring a table with their handspans, they found that their handspans had different lengths, and the number of handspans needed was different for everyone. Deepa's mother calls a handspan a balisht. A farmer can measure land by walking and counting his strides, or by using the length of his feet.
activities.prompt: Deepa's mother wants to measure the table with a standard instrument. She does not want to use her handspan. What should she do?
options: Use a measuring tape instead of her handspan.
Keep using her handspan and hope all counts match.
Give only the number of handspans, with no unit.
Use each visitor's foot and hope all lengths match.

why.Keep using her handspan and hope all cou: Using a handspan can give different counts.
why.Give only the number of handspans, with: A length needs both a number and a unit.
why.Use each visitor's foot and hope all len: Feet are also different for different people.

activities.explanation: A measuring tape is good. Handspans are different for different people.

activities.prompt: Five friends measure the same table with handspans. Explain why they need different numbers of handspans.
activities.answer: The five friends had handspans of different lengths. Because a handspan is a body-based unit, one person's handspan was not the same size as another's. This difference led to different numbers being needed for the same table.
points: The friends' handspans have different lengths.
A handspan is a unit based on the body.
Different handspan lengths give different counts.
The table was the same length for everyone.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a teacher looks for.

activities.prompt: Why do countries use the same units? What is the SI unit of length?
activities.answer: Different countries use shared standard units because travel had caused confusion about measurements. The system used now is called the International System of Units, or SI units. Its unit of length is the metre, written with the symbol m.
points: Travel caused confusion about measures.
The system used now is called SI units.
The SI unit of length is the metre.
The symbol for metre is m.
activities.explanation: Check your answer with these points.

activities.prompt: How can you measure a curved line with thread?
activities.answer: Use a flexible measuring tape or thread to measure the curved line. If using thread, straighten it before measuring its length with a metre scale. The measurement must then be written with both a number and its unit.
points: Use a soft measuring tape or thread for the curved line.
Straighten the thread before measuring it.
Measure the straight thread with a metre scale.
Write the number and its unit.
activities.explanation: Check your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: While planning a kabaddi court with friends, the group prepared to mark its lines using chuna powder. They selected one ground point from which to measure all distances. During Padma’s journey toward Delhi, one kilometre stone showed 70 km and the next showed 60 km. The lower number indicated that she was getting closer to Delhi, so Delhi served as her reference point.
activities.prompt: Friends start measuring distances from their own houses. What should they do so their results agree?
options: Use one shared reference point for every measurement.
Keep measuring from each friend's own house.
Change the reference point after each distance.
Measure once from each house. Join the numbers together.

why.Keep measuring from each friend's own ho: Different houses make different starting points.
why.Change the reference point after each di: Changing the point each time means no shared reference point.
why.Measure once from each house. Join the n: Joining separate results does not make them agree.

activities.explanation: A shared reference point gives everyone the same starting point.

activities.context: While planning a kabaddi court with friends, the group prepared to mark its lines using chuna powder. They selected one ground point from which to measure all distances. During Padma’s journey toward Delhi, one kilometre stone showed 70 km and the next showed 60 km. The lower number indicated that she was getting closer to Delhi, so Delhi served as her reference point.
activities.prompt: Padma sees the first kilometre stone. It shows 70 km. What can she correctly say about where she is?
options: She was 70 km away from Delhi.
She was 60 km away from Delhi.
She was 70 km from a different ground point.
She was 60 km from a different ground point.

The 60 km reading was on the next stone.
why.She was 70 km from a different ground po: Padma measured from Delhi, not from another point.
why.She was 60 km from a different ground po: Neither the distance nor the point matches the first stone.

activities.explanation: Padma measured her distance from Delhi.

activities.prompt: Explain why children can get different distance results. How can they make their results agree?
activities.answer: Different houses serve as different points from which distances are measured, so the observations can differ. The children can make their observations agree by measuring from the same object or point. This common fixed point is called a reference point.
points: Different houses give different starting points.
Different starting points can give different results.
Everyone should use the same object or point.
That shared point is called a reference point.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Deepa found that the passengers were still in their seats after a minute. Their positions were not changing with time, so they were at rest when the bus was used as the reference point. Yet their positions changed relative to things outside the bus. When Deepa used a building outside the bus as the reference point, she saw that both the passengers and the bus were moving.
activities.prompt: What should Deepa use as the reference point to decide whether the passengers are at rest?
options: the bus itself
the building outside the bus
the falling eraser
the orange dropped from a tree

why.the building outside the bus: The building shows that both the bus and the passengers are moving.
why.the falling eraser: The falling eraser is an example of straight-line movement, not the reference point in this case.
why.the orange dropped from a tree: The orange is another straight-line movement example, not the reference point in this case.

activities.explanation: The bus is the reference point used to identify the passengers as at rest.

activities.context: Deepa found that the passengers were still in their seats after a minute. Their positions were not changing with time, so they were at rest when the bus was used as the reference point. Yet their positions changed relative to things outside the bus. When Deepa used a building outside the bus as the reference point, she saw that both the passengers and the bus were moving.
activities.prompt: Why can the same passengers be described as at rest in one comparison and moving in another?
options: The chosen reference point changes how their positions are compared.
Their actual positions change whenever another place is named.
Rest and motion can be decided only after a minute has passed.
Every reference point gives the same comparison of their positions.

why.Their actual positions change whenever a: Naming a place does not change the passengers' actual positions.
why.Rest and motion can be decided only afte: The comparison does not depend on waiting for a particular time.
why.Every reference point gives the same com: Different reference points can give different comparisons.

activities.explanation: The reference point helps decide whether an object is at rest or in motion.

activities.prompt: Explain why the passengers can be at rest relative to the bus but moving relative to the building.
activities.answer: The passengers' positions were not changing with time when the bus was the reference point, so they were at rest. However, their positions changed relative to things outside the bus. From the building's position, both the passengers and the bus were moving.
points: Bus used as the reference point
Passengers' positions did not change with time
Positions changed relative to things outside the bus
Both passengers and bus moved relative to the building
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A learner presses a metal strip and watches its free end move up and down. The learner also watches an eraser on a thread move in a way similar to a swing. An object moves around a circular path again and again. The learner wants to classify each movement and decide which movements repeat after a fixed interval of time.
activities.prompt: How should the learner classify the movement of the metal strip's free end?
options: Oscillatory motion
Linear motion
Circular motion
One-way motion

why.Linear motion: Treating it as one-way travel misses the return movement.
why.Circular motion: The movement does not travel around a circular path.
why.One-way motion: The free end does not continue in one direction; it moves up and down.

activities.explanation: The free end moves up and down, showing movement to and fro about a fixed position.

activities.context: A learner presses a metal strip and watches its free end move up and down. The learner also watches an eraser on a thread move in a way similar to a swing. An object moves around a circular path again and again. The learner wants to classify each movement and decide which movements repeat after a fixed interval of time.
activities.prompt: If the object moving around the circular path were changed so that it moved to and fro about a fixed position, how should its motion be classified?
options: Oscillatory and periodic
Circular and periodic
Linear and non-periodic
Linear and periodic

why.Circular and periodic: The changed movement no longer follows a circular path.
why.Linear and non-periodic: Movement to and fro is not linear motion, and it repeats rather than being non-periodic.
why.Linear and periodic: The motion repeats, but the movement to and fro about a fixed position is not linear motion.

activities.explanation: Movement to and fro about a fixed position is oscillatory motion, and oscillatory motion is periodic.

activities.prompt: Explain why the metal strip and the eraser on the thread are examples of oscillatory motion.
activities.answer: The free end of the pressed metal strip moves up and down, so it moves to and fro about a fixed position. The eraser on a thread moves like a swing and also repeats its movement to and fro. Both are therefore examples of oscillatory motion.
points: The metal strip's free end moves up and down.
Up-and-down movement shows movement to and fro.
The eraser's movement is similar to a swing's movement.
Both movements fit oscillatory motion.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

funFacts: Bees do a special waggle dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
Plants make their own food using sunlight, water and air.
Most of your body is water, which helps carry food and oxygen around.

activities.prompt: Everyone measures the same length. Which unit gives everyone the same answer?
options: metre
handspan
foot
arm length

activities.prompt: A measured length needs a number and a ______.
activities.hint: It tells you the kind of length.

activities.prompt: Put these steps for measuring in the right order.
items: Choose a good scale
Put the scale next to the object
Keep your eye above the tip

activities.prompt: Padma measured her distance from Delhi. What is Delhi called?
options: scale
reference point
unit
handspan
activities.explanation: Delhi was the fixed point Padma measured from.

activities.prompt: The passengers were at rest when a building outside the bus was the reference point.
activities.explanation: From the building, both the passengers and the bus were moving.

activities.prompt: Use a bendy measuring tape or ______ to measure a curved line.
activities.hint: Make it straight before you measure its length.
activities.explanation: Thread can bend to follow a curved line.

activities.prompt: Match each kind of motion with its description.
pairs: motion back and forth around a fixed place
repeating a path after a set time
activities.explanation: Each motion type matches its path or repeated movement.

activities.prompt: Put these observations about Padma's journey in order.
items: Read the first stone: 70 km
Read the next stone: 60 km
Notice the distance has decreased
See that Padma is getting closer to Delhi
activities.explanation: The distance decreased from 70 km to 60 km, so Padma moved closer.

chapters.title: Materials Around Us
chapters.summary: In this chapter: 1. observing objects around us; 2. how to group materials?; 3. appearance, hardness and softness; 4. seeing through and dissolving materials.

lessons.title: 1. Observing Objects Around Us

activities.prompt: What stories are hiding in the materials of objects around you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Materials
activities.body:
Begin your tour by looking at objects around you. Ask what each one is made from. A material is any substance used to create an object. Everyday objects are made from various materials, and paper is one of them.

Next, travel back to early pottery. The earliest pottery found in the Ganga plains dates back to 7,000 to 8,000 years. It was also found in Baluchistan at Mehrgarh.

Now, meet the Sindhu-Sarasvatī people. They developed wheel-turned pottery techniques about 4000 BCE onwards. Their Harappan pottery had a bright red surface painted with black-coloured designs.

Watch the making process with care. Makers carefully selected the clay used for pots, dishes, bowls and other items. The prepared clay was finally baked in a kiln to make terracotta. Each stage helps turn clay into useful objects.

Finish your tour by imagining pots in daily life. Pots were used for cooking and for storing food grains, oil, ghee and other things.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Objects and Materials
activities.body: Materials are the substances used to make objects. Everyday objects are made from different materials. Paper is one such material. People also made pots, dishes and bowls from carefully selected clay. The clay was prepared and baked in a kiln to make terracotta. These pots helped with cooking and storing food.
keyPoints: A material is used to create an object.
Everyday objects are made from various materials.
Paper and clay are materials.
Prepared clay becomes terracotta when baked in a kiln.
activities.explanation: Objects tell us about the materials used to make them.

activities.prompt: How should a potter make a Harappan-style pot for storing food grains?
steps: The potter selects clay carefully because it is used for pots and bowls.
The prepared clay is baked in a kiln because this makes terracotta.
The surface is painted with black designs because Harappan pottery had them.
The result is a bright red, black-decorated terracotta pot for storing grains.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which one is a material used to make everyday objects?
options: Cooking
Paper
Storing
Painting
activities.explanation: Paper is one material used to make everyday things.

activities.prompt: Paper is one of the ______ used to make everyday things.
activities.hint: A substance used to create an object.
activities.explanation: A material is any substance used to create an object.

activities.prompt: All everyday objects are made from paper.
activities.explanation: Everyday objects are made from many materials. Paper is one of them.

activities.prompt: What did people use pots for?
options: Cooking and storing food
Painting black designs
Choosing and preparing clay
Baking clay in a kiln
activities.explanation: Pots were used for cooking and storing food.

activities.prompt: Which order shows how terracotta was made?
options: Pick clay, prepare it, then bake it in a kiln
Pick clay after baking it in a kiln
Use paper, then bake it in a kiln
Store prepared clay in a pot
activities.explanation: First the clay was picked and made ready. Then it was baked in a kiln.

activities.prompt: Which answer is completely correct, based on the lesson?
options: Harappan pots were bright black; they stored oil.
Harappan pots had red and black designs; they stored paper.
Harappan pots had red and black designs; they stored oil.
Harappan pots had red and black designs; they baked clay.
activities.explanation: Harappan pots had a bright red surface with black designs. They stored oil.

activities.prompt: A paper bowl and a clay pot are everyday objects. What links them?
options: Each is made from a material used to create it.
Each is made from paper because paper makes every object.
Each is made without any material because objects need none.
Each is made from clay because clay is the only material.

why.Each is made from paper because paper ma: This wrongly thinks all objects are made from paper.
why.Each is made without any material becaus: This wrongly thinks objects do not need materials.
why.Each is made from clay because clay is t: This wrongly thinks clay is the only material used.

activities.explanation: Both are everyday objects made from substances used to create them.

activities.prompt: A potter prepares clay for bowls. What should come before shaping?
options: Select the clay carefully for the items.
Bake the clay in a kiln before shaping.
Paint the clay black before baking it.
Fill the clay pots with food grains.

This mistakes the final kiln step for the first step.
This mistakes surface decoration for clay preparation.
This mistakes a pot's later use for its making.

activities.explanation: Careful selection is needed before the prepared clay is baked.

activities.prompt: A Harappan pot is painted fully black. What should the maker change?
options: Make the surface bright red and paint only black designs.
Make the surface black and paint only bright red designs.
Make the surface clay-coloured and paint no designs.
Make the surface bright red and paint no black designs.

why.Make the surface black and paint only br: This swaps the surface colour and the design colour.
why.Make the surface clay-coloured and paint: This wrongly leaves out the painted black designs.
why.Make the surface bright red and paint no: This leaves out the black-coloured designs of Harappan pottery.

activities.explanation: Harappan pottery had a bright red surface with black-coloured designs.

activities.prompt: An explorer finds early pottery at Mehrgarh. Which place should the explorer record?
options: Baluchistan, because Mehrgarh is in that region.
The Ganga plains, because early pottery was found there too.
Sindhu-Sarasvatī, because wheel-turning began with those people.
A kiln, because early pottery was baked in kilns there.

why.The Ganga plains, because early pottery: This confuses another place of discovery with the explorer's find.
why.Sindhu-Sarasvatī, because wheel-turning: This confuses a people group with the place where pottery was found.
why.A kiln, because early pottery was baked: This confuses a kiln used for baking with a place of discovery.

activities.explanation: Mehrgarh is in Baluchistan, where early pottery was found.

lessons.title: 2. How to Group Materials?

activities.prompt: How can you decide which objects belong together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sorting Objects and Materials
activities.body:
Imagine you enter a room filled with objects. You want to sort them into groups, but where should you begin? Look for shared properties, such as shape, colour, hardness, softness and shine.

Classification means arranging objects into groups. Objects can be classified according to a common property. Materials can also be classified according to certain properties. You might make one group for shiny objects and another for soft objects.

One object can be made from different materials. One material can be used to make more than one object. You can group both the objects and the materials.

Think about a tumbler. Its material must be capable of holding water. You choose a material according to its properties. The purpose of an object also affects your choice of material.

Different parts of an object may use different materials. A pen may contain plastic, metal and ink. Sports balls are made from specific materials for specific sports.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How We Group Materials
activities.body: You can group objects by their properties. Properties are things like shape, colour, hardness, softness and shine. Grouping is called classification. One object can use many materials. One material can make many objects. The material we pick depends on its properties and its use. Different parts can use different materials. For example, a pen can have plastic, metal and ink.
keyPoints: Classification means putting objects into groups.
We pick materials by their properties and use.
One object can have different materials.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you group things. They also help you pick useful materials.

activities.prompt: How should we choose a material for a tumbler?
steps: A tumbler must be able to hold water.
We choose a material according to its properties.
So we check if the material can hold water before making the tumbler.
The material's properties and the tumbler's purpose guide our choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Meaning of Classification
activities.prompt: What does classification mean?
options: Putting objects into groups
Mixing all objects together
Giving each object a different name
Measuring each object
activities.explanation: Classification means putting objects into groups.

activities.title: Common Property
activities.prompt: We can group objects by a ______ property.
activities.hint: All the objects in a group share this property.
activities.explanation: A common property is shared by objects in the same group.

activities.title: Match Each Idea
activities.prompt: Match each idea with its meaning.
pairs: Makes us ask how and why questions
activities.explanation: Curiosity makes us ask questions. Careful observation notices what is around us. Science helps us find answers.

activities.title: Choosing a Tumbler Material
activities.prompt: What must the material of a tumbler be able to do?
options: Shine brightly
Hold water
Stay soft
Work for every sport
activities.explanation: A tumbler's material must be able to hold water.

activities.title: Protect life
activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order.
items: People cause the loss of natural habitats.
Damage takes away homes, food and other things we need.
We must protect biodiversity.
Our planet stays full of life.
activities.explanation: Losing habitats harms plants and animals. So protecting biodiversity helps life grow.

activities.title: Materials in a Pen
activities.prompt: Which materials can a pen have?
options: Only plastic
Only metal
Plastic, metal and ink
Only ink
activities.explanation: A pen can have plastic, metal and ink.

activities.prompt: Objects can be grouped by shape, colour, hardness, softness and shine. Some objects are blue. Others are red. Which property should the child use?
options: The colour of each object.
The hardness of each object.
The softness of each object.
The shine of each object.

The situation gives no information about hardness.
The situation gives no information about softness.
The situation gives no information about shine.

activities.explanation: Colour is given, so it can divide the objects into two groups.

activities.prompt: One object can be made from different materials. A pen may contain plastic, metal and ink. What should the maker do?
options: Choose a suitable material for each part.
Choose one material for every part.
Choose the softest material for every part.
Choose the shiniest material for every part.

This assumes every part should use one material.
why.Choose the softest material for every pa: This assumes softness is always the best choice.
why.Choose the shiniest material for every p: This assumes shine is always the best choice.

activities.explanation: Different parts may be made from different materials.

activities.prompt: A material for a tumbler must be capable of holding water. The maker has several materials. Which one should the maker choose?
options: A material that can hold water.
A material that shines brightly.
A material that feels very soft.
A material that feels very hard.

Shine does not show that a material can hold water.
Softness does not show that a material can hold water.
Hardness does not show that a material can hold water.

activities.explanation: This choice meets the tumbler's need to hold water.

lessons.title: 3. Appearance, Hardness and Softness

activities.prompt: How can you tell what looks shiny, feels hard, or feels soft?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Materials
activities.body:
Imagine touring wood, paper, rubber, and metals.

Freshly cut, unpolished wood has a distinct appearance.
Iron, copper, zinc, aluminium, and gold are examples of metals.
Shiny surfaces usually give materials a lustrous appearance.

You see that paper, wood, rubber, and jute are non-lustrous.
Some metals lose lustre and look dull because of air and moisture.
Not every material that shines is a metal.
Polishing or a thin coating can make some non-metals look shiny.

Now you press and scratch different materials to compare them.
Materials that are easily compressed or scratched are soft.
Materials that are difficult to compress or scratch are hard.
Rubber gives you an interesting result during this test.

Rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron.
This shows you that hardness and softness are relative properties.
One material can be harder than another but softer than a third.

Before you leave, notice how appearance can offer clues.
Shiny surfaces often look lustrous, but shine does not always mean metal.
Your final reminder is to compare, because relative properties need a comparison.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Comparing How Materials Look
activities.body: Appearance means how a material looks. Freshly cut wood that is not polished has its own look. Lustrous means shiny. Non-lustrous means not shiny. Shiny surfaces are usually lustrous. But not every shiny thing is a metal. Hard materials are not easily squashed or scratched. Soft materials are easily squashed or scratched. We must compare materials to say hard or soft.
keyPoints: Shiny surfaces are usually lustrous.
Hard materials are not easily squashed or scratched.
Hard and soft depend on comparing things.
activities.explanation: Comparing helps you describe how things look and how hard they are.

activities.prompt: A child finds a shiny object and compares rubber with iron.
steps: Shiny surfaces are usually lustrous, so shine gives a useful clue.
Shine alone cannot prove metal, because some non-metals also shine.
Rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron.
Therefore, hardness depends on which materials are compared.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which material is a metal?
options: Copper
Paper
Rubber
Jute
activities.explanation: Copper is a metal. Paper, rubber and jute are non-lustrous (not shiny).

activities.prompt: Match each cause with its effect.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a cause and its effect on how a material looks.

activities.prompt: Rubber is harder than ______. But it is softer than iron.
activities.hint: This material is softer than rubber.
activities.explanation: Rubber is harder than sponge. Rubber is softer than iron.

activities.prompt: A craft item shines after receiving a thin coating. What can we conclude?
options: It must be a metal
It may be a non-metal
It must have lost its lustre
It cannot be scratched
activities.explanation: A thin coating can make some non-metals look shiny. Shining does not prove something is metal.

activities.prompt: Put these materials in order, from softest to hardest.
items: sponge
rubber
iron
activities.explanation: Rubber is harder than sponge. Rubber is softer than iron. So this order is correct.

activities.prompt: Why should you compare materials when you say how hard they are?
options: Hardness and softness are relative properties
Every material is equally hard
Soft materials always look shiny
Iron is the only hard material
activities.explanation: Hardness and softness are relative properties. They show how one material compares with another.

activities.prompt: A child finds a shiny object. What can the child safely conclude?
options: Shine proves that the object is metal.
Shine proves that the object is not metal.
Shine alone cannot tell us for sure.
Every shiny object must be metal.

This wrongly treats shine as proof that a material is metal.
why.Shine proves that the object is not meta: This wrongly treats shine as proof against being metal.
This wrongly assumes that all shiny materials are metals.

activities.explanation: Some non-metals shine too, so shine alone cannot prove metal.

activities.prompt: Rubber and iron are scratched with the same object and force. What is likely?
options: The rubber will scratch more easily.
The iron will scratch more easily.
Both materials will scratch at the same rate.
Neither material will be scratched at all.

Iron is harder than rubber, so it resists scratches better.
why.Both materials will scratch at the same: The facts show that the two materials are not equally hard.
why.Neither material will be scratched at al: This wrongly treats difficult to scratch as impossible to scratch.

activities.explanation: Rubber is softer than iron, so it is easier to scratch.

activities.prompt: Two pieces, rubber and iron, need a fair hardness test. Which action is best?
options: Compare how easily rubber and iron are scratched.
Compare how shiny rubber and iron are.
Compare how much air reaches rubber and iron.
Compare how fresh the cut wood looks.

Shine shows appearance, but it does not show hardness.
why.Compare how much air reaches rubber and: Air exposure can affect lustre, but it does not show hardness.
The appearance of fresh wood does not compare hardness.

activities.explanation: Scratching compares hardness because harder materials are harder to scratch.

lessons.title: 4. Seeing Through and Dissolving Materials

activities.prompt: What can you discover by looking through different materials?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Materials
activities.body:
Imagine glass before your eyes. You can see things clearly through this transparent material. The view remains clear as your eyes look beyond it.

You try air and water next. Both are transparent, and so is cellophane paper. Through each one, you can still see the things behind it clearly.

Now you meet a piece of wood. You cannot see at all through this opaque material. An opaque material stops your view completely. Cardboard and metals are opaque too.

Next, you hold butter paper. You can see objects through it, but not clearly. This material is translucent. Frosted glass is translucent too. Your view stays, but it is not sharp.

Finally, you look at water with some liquids. Some mix completely with it. Others form a separate layer because they do not mix with water. Oxygen gas dissolves in water, which is important for water-living animals and plants.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Three kinds of materials
activities.body: Glass, water, air and cellophane paper are transparent. You can see clearly through transparent materials. Wood, cardboard and metals are opaque. You cannot see through many opaque materials. Butter paper and frosted glass are translucent. You can see objects through them, but not clearly.
keyPoints: Transparent materials let you see clearly.
Opaque materials block your view.
Translucent materials let you see, but not clearly.
activities.explanation: Transparent, opaque and translucent materials help you see in different ways.

activities.prompt: A wooden block is under butter paper. What can a child see?
steps: Butter paper is translucent, so it does not give a clear view.
Wood is opaque, so seeing through the block itself is not possible.
Therefore, she can see the block, but not clearly, through the paper.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A clear window
activities.prompt: Which material is transparent?
options: Glass
Cardboard
Butter paper
Wood
activities.explanation: Glass is transparent. You can see clearly through it.

activities.title: A cloudy pane
activities.prompt: You can see objects through ______ materials. But not clearly.
activities.hint: Butter paper and frosted glass are examples.
activities.explanation: Translucent materials let you see objects. But you cannot see them clearly.

activities.title: Material groups
activities.prompt: Match each kind of material with an example.
activities.explanation: Each example shows how that kind of material lets you see.

activities.title: Oil and water
activities.prompt: What happens when some liquids do not mix with water?
options: They dissolve completely
They make a separate layer
They become opaque
They turn transparent
activities.explanation: Some liquids make a separate layer because they do not mix with water.

activities.title: From clear to blocked
activities.prompt: Put these groups in order. Start with the clearest. End with the one you cannot see through.
items: Transparent materials
Translucent materials
Opaque materials
activities.explanation: You can see clearly through transparent materials. You can see a little through translucent materials. You cannot see through many opaque materials.

activities.title: Choose the right idea
activities.prompt: Which statement is correct?
options: Frosted glass is opaque.
Metals are transparent materials.
Some liquids mix fully with water. Others form a separate layer.
You cannot see objects through translucent materials.
activities.explanation: Some liquids mix fully with water. Others form a separate layer.

activities.prompt: Glass is transparent, while wood is opaque. What will she see through each?
options: She sees clearly through glass, but not through wood.
She sees clearly through wood, but not through glass.
She sees unclearly through both glass and wood.
She sees unclearly through neither glass nor wood.

why.She sees clearly through wood, but not t: This swaps the properties of transparent glass and opaque wood.
why.She sees unclearly through both glass an: This treats opaque wood like translucent material, which gives an unclear view.
why.She sees unclearly through neither glass: This ignores the clear view possible through transparent glass.

activities.explanation: This is right because glass is transparent and wood is opaque.

activities.prompt: Frosted glass is translucent, while clear glass is transparent. What difference should she expect?
options: Frosted glass gives a clearer view than clear glass.
Both materials give exactly the same clear view of objects.
Frosted glass gives a less clear view than clear glass.
Neither material lets an object be seen at all.

why.Frosted glass gives a clearer view than: This reverses the clear and unclear views of the two materials.
why.Both materials give exactly the same cle: This ignores the difference between transparent and translucent materials.
why.Neither material lets an object be seen: This treats both materials as opaque, so neither gives a view.

activities.explanation: Clear glass is transparent, while frosted glass is translucent.

activities.prompt: Oxygen gas dissolves in water. A child says this matters only outside water. What is the best reply?
options: The claim is right because water-living things do not need it.
The claim is wrong because it matters for water-living animals and plants.
The claim is wrong because oxygen makes all liquids mix.
The claim is right because oxygen only affects opaque materials.

why.The claim is right because water-living: This denies the fact's link to water-living animals and plants.
why.The claim is wrong because oxygen makes: This confuses oxygen dissolving with liquids mixing completely.
why.The claim is right because oxygen only a: This confuses dissolving with changing opaque materials.

activities.explanation: This is right because the fact names water-living animals and plants.

Snowflakes are clear like ice, but many snowflakes together look white.

lessons.title: 5. Mass and Volume

activities.prompt: What can you learn by comparing two different tumblers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Mass and Volume
activities.body:
Imagine you are holding two tumblers. Both have the same capacity, but they hold different amounts of water. One holds more, while the other holds less.

Mass helps you describe whether an object is heavier or lighter. The heavier object has more mass, while the lighter object has less mass.

Water also takes up space. The space occupied by water represents its volume. Tumblers with the same capacity can hold different amounts of water, so equal capacity does not always mean equal volume.

Water bottles show another useful clue. The quantity written on each bottle tells you the volume of water it holds. You can also write volume units in a shorter way: litre is written as L, and millilitre as mL.

Mass has its own special unit. The kilogram is the SI unit used for measuring mass. Its symbol is written in lower case as kg. Cubic metre is the SI unit of volume, and one cubic metre equals 1000 litres. As you explore, remember that mass and volume are two properties possessed by all materials.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Mass and Volume
activities.body: Mass tells whether an object is heavier or lighter. More mass means heavier, and less mass means lighter. Volume is the space occupied by water. Two tumblers can have the same capacity but hold different amounts of water. Water bottles show volume in litres or millilitres, written L and mL. Mass uses the kilogram, written kg. The cubic metre is the volume unit. One cubic metre equals 1000 litres.
keyPoints: Heavier means more mass; lighter means less mass.
Volume is the space occupied by water.
Mass uses kilograms; volume uses the cubic metre.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare mass and volume.

activities.prompt: Two tumblers have the same capacity. One holds more water. Do their water volumes match?
steps: The tumblers have equal capacity, yet they hold different amounts of water.
More water occupies more space, so the fuller tumbler has more volume.
Their water volumes differ, because volume is the space occupied by water.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which unit measures mass?
options: L
kg
mL
cubic metre
activities.explanation: Kilogram (kg) is the unit for mass.

activities.prompt: The kilogram is written in small letters as ______.
activities.hint: Use small letters.
activities.explanation: Kilogram is written as kg in small letters.

activities.prompt: Two tumblers have the same capacity. One has more water in it. What is greater?
options: Volume of water in the fuller tumbler
Capacity of the fuller tumbler
Capacity of both tumblers
Amount of water in both tumblers
activities.explanation: The water in the fuller tumbler takes up more space. So its volume is greater.

activities.prompt: Match each item to its correct description.
activities.explanation: Each pair links a word with its correct meaning.

activities.prompt: Put these sentences in the right order.
items: Mass tells us if an object is heavy or light.
The heavier object has more mass.
The lighter object has less mass.
activities.explanation: Start with what mass means. Then compare the heavy and light objects.

activities.prompt: Which sentence matches each property with its unit?
options: A kilogram measures mass. A cubic metre measures volume.
A kilogram measures volume. A cubic metre measures mass.
A litre measures mass. A millilitre measures mass.
A cubic metre and a kilogram both measure volume.
activities.explanation: A kilogram measures mass. A cubic metre measures volume.

activities.prompt: Two tumblers have the same capacity. One holds more water. What do their water volumes show?
options: The fuller water has more volume, because it occupies more space.
The less-filled water has more volume, because empty space counts.
Both waters have equal volume, because their capacities match.
Their volumes cannot be compared, because capacity is not volume.

why.The less-filled water has more volume, b: This mistake counts empty space as part of the water volume.
why.Both waters have equal volume, because t: This mistake confuses equal capacity with equal amounts of water.
why.Their volumes cannot be compared, becaus: This mistake treats capacity as different from the space occupied.

activities.explanation: This is right because more water occupies more space.

activities.prompt: Two bags are compared. One bag is heavier than the other. What is the best conclusion?
options: The heavier bag has more mass than the lighter bag.
The heavier bag has less mass than the lighter bag.
The heavier bag has the same mass as the lighter bag.
The two bags cannot be compared using mass.

why.The heavier bag has less mass than the l: This mistake reverses the meaning of heavier and lighter.
why.The heavier bag has the same mass as the: This mistake treats heavier and lighter as if they meant equal mass.
why.The two bags cannot be compared using ma: This mistake thinks mass cannot show which object is heavier.

activities.explanation: This is right because the heavier object has more mass.

activities.prompt: A mass label uses kg. A water bottle label uses mL. What do these labels measure?
options: The first measures mass. The second measures water volume.
The first measures volume. The second measures mass.
The first measures capacity. The second measures mass.
The first measures mass. The second measures empty-bottle mass.

why.The first measures volume. The second me: This mistake swaps the uses of the two units.
why.The first measures capacity. The second: This mistake confuses mass with capacity.
why.The first measures mass. The second meas: This mistake treats the water quantity as the mass of the empty bottle.

activities.explanation: This is right because kg measures mass and mL measures volume.

funFacts: One litre of water weighs about one kilogram.
A balloon full of air is heavier than an empty balloon, because air has mass.
Oil floats on water because it is lighter than water for the same amount of space.

lessons.title: 6. Matter and Classification

activities.prompt: How can we sort the things around us? What is matter?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Matter
activities.body:
You begin your journey by looking around you at everything that takes up space. You soon learn that anything occupying space and having mass is called matter. Mass tells you how much matter there is.

Next, you follow an object through a busy workshop. The space occupied by that matter is its volume. Materials are types of matter used when objects are created. You compare both ideas as you explore.

Then, you enter a room where things are grouped by shared properties. Grouping helps you study and observe patterns in the properties of things. The non-living world is also classified according to properties.

You also find that Ayurveda has its own system for grouping things. The Ayurvedic shloka describes twenty properties. These properties form ten pairs of opposite qualities. You now recognise these pairs as you compare different things.

At the end, you see that these properties describe all physical matter. They can also describe living systems, the environment, and food. You leave ready to explore how matter can be understood and organised.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Matter and Classification
activities.body: Matter is anything that takes up space and has mass. Mass shows how much matter there is. Volume is the space it takes up. Materials are kinds of matter used to make things. Properties are features we use to group and describe things. Grouping helps us see patterns. Ayurveda also groups things. Its twenty properties make ten pairs of opposite qualities. These properties describe physical matter, living things, the environment and food.
keyPoints: Matter takes up space and has mass.
Mass shows the amount. Volume shows the space.
Twenty properties make ten pairs of opposite qualities.
activities.explanation: This card joins the main ideas about matter and grouping.

activities.prompt: A child finds two objects at home and wants to sort them. How should the child think?
steps: Both objects occupy space and have mass, so both are matter.
Mass gives the quantity of matter, so it helps compare how much matter is present.
Volume gives occupied space, so it helps compare how much space is taken.
Grouping objects by properties helps us study patterns, so sorting helps us understand them.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is Matter?
activities.prompt: Which pair is part of the definition of matter?
options: takes up space and has mass
has mass and moves
takes up space and can be seen
has volume and is a material
activities.explanation: Matter must have mass and take up space. You found the full definition!

activities.title: What Does Mass Tell Us?
activities.prompt: Mass tells us the ______ of matter.
activities.hint: Think about how much matter there is.
activities.explanation: Mass tells us the quantity of matter. The blank asks for this word.

activities.title: Match Each Term
activities.prompt: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: kinds of matter used to make objects
activities.explanation: Each term matches its meaning. Matching helps you remember.

activities.title: Why Group Things?
activities.prompt: What does grouping help us do?
options: Study patterns in properties.
Change the mass and volume.
Make new matter from materials.
Stop the need to look at things.
activities.explanation: Grouping makes patterns easier to study. Well done!

activities.title: Classification Systems
activities.prompt: Which two facts are true?
options: Ayurveda groups things. The non-living world uses properties.
Ayurveda cannot group things. But the non-living world uses properties.
Ayurveda groups things. But the non-living world ignores properties.
Ayurveda does not group things. The non-living world does not either.
activities.explanation: Ayurveda groups things. The non-living world uses properties. Good work!

activities.title: Opposite Property Pairs
activities.prompt: The Ayurvedic shloka describes twenty properties. What do these properties form?
options: Ten pairs of same qualities
Ten pairs of opposite qualities
Twenty pairs of opposite qualities
One pair of changing qualities
activities.explanation: The twenty properties make ten pairs of opposite qualities. Great memory!

activities.prompt: Matter occupies space and has mass. If two blocks have equal mass, what follows?
options: They have the same quantity of matter.
They occupy the same amount of space.
One must contain more matter than the other.
Their materials must be exactly the same.

This confuses equal mass with equal occupied space.
why.One must contain more matter than the ot: This wrongly assumes different quantities despite equal mass.
why.Their materials must be exactly the same: Equal quantity does not mean the materials must be identical.

activities.explanation: Equal mass means equal quantity of matter, because mass gives quantity.

activities.prompt: The Ayurvedic properties can describe living systems, the environment and food. Which plan uses them correctly?
options: Use them for the plant, meal, surroundings, and nearby matter.
Use them only for the plant, meal, and nearby matter.
Use them only for the plant and nearby surroundings.
Use them only for the meal and nearby matter.

why.Use them only for the plant, meal, and n: It wrongly limits the properties to only some uses.
why.Use them only for the plant and nearby s: It leaves out food and physical matter.
why.Use them only for the meal and nearby ma: It leaves out living systems and the environment.

activities.explanation: It includes living systems, environment, food, and physical matter.

activities.prompt: The non-living world is classified according to properties. Which plan is fairest for studying patterns?
options: Choose one property, sort by it, then compare the groups.
Choose one property, sort by it, then change the other properties.
Use a different property for each group, then compare the results.
Sort by object names, then treat the groups as property groups.

why.Choose one property, sort by it, then ch: Changing other properties stops the groups from being a fair comparison.
why.Use a different property for each group,: Different sorting rules make the groups hard to compare fairly.
why.Sort by object names, then treat the gro: Names do not show patterns in the properties being studied.

activities.explanation: It keeps one property as the sorting rule and checks patterns.

activities.prompt: Matter occupies space and has mass. Grouping studies property patterns. Which plan is correct?
options: Choose a material, then group objects by properties.
Choose a volume, then group objects by mass.
Choose a mass, then group objects by names.
Choose a group, then group objects randomly.

why.Choose a volume, then group objects by m: Volume is occupied space, not a type of matter used to create objects.
why.Choose a mass, then group objects by nam: Mass gives quantity, but it is not the type of matter called material.
why.Choose a group, then group objects rando: A property group classifies objects, but it is not matter used to create them.

activities.explanation: A material is matter used to create objects, and grouping uses properties.

Scientists have found about 118 elements, the simplest kinds of matter.
Water can be ice, liquid or steam. It is the same stuff in three forms.

lessons.sceneAlt: An Indus ceramic bowl features painted decoration.
