lessons.title: Cooling, Clouds and the Water Cycle

activities.prompt: What makes clouds, rain and snow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Water
activities.body:
You arrive at a pot-in-pot cooler. You find sand inside it. You must keep this sand moist. As you continue your tour, you look closely at the air around you. Tiny droplets form around dust particles. Some small droplets float in the air and form clouds.

You meet clouds during your journey. You remember that burnt newspaper can provide tiny dust particles. Water vapour can form clouds around these particles. Now you understand why dust matters.

You watch water drops in a cloud. When the water drops become heavy, they fall as rain. Under special conditions, water may fall as hail or snow. Your tour shows you several kinds of falling water.

At the end of your journey, you look back at the whole movement. The movement of water between the Earth's surface and atmosphere is called the water cycle. You also remember that we must use water wisely and avoid wasting it. You leave ready to use water wisely.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Water Moves and Forms Clouds
activities.body: Water moves between the Earth's surface and the atmosphere. This movement is called the water cycle. Water vapour is water in the air that can form clouds around tiny dust particles. Burnt newspaper provides tiny dust particles. Small droplets float in the air and form clouds. Moist sand has water in it. Water drops that become heavy fall as rain. Under special conditions, water may fall as hail or snow.
keyPoints: The water cycle moves water between Earth's surface and atmosphere.
Tiny droplets form around dust; small droplets float and form clouds.
Heavy drops fall as rain; special conditions can cause hail or snow.
activities.explanation: These facts connect moving water with cloud formation and falling water.

activities.title: Follow a drop of water

tasks.say: Go to the clouds.
tasks.then: Vapour cools high up and condenses.

tasks.say: Make it rain.
tasks.then: Heavy drops fall.

tasks.say: Bring it back to the sea.
tasks.then: Then the cycle begins again.

activities.takeaway: Water keeps moving between the sea, the air and the land.
activities.explanation: Water keeps moving between the sea, the air and the land.

activities.prompt: Why can burnt newspaper help make a cloud?
steps: Burnt newspaper provides tiny dust particles for cloud formation.
Water vapour forms around those particles, so tiny droplets appear.
Small droplets float in the air, so they can form clouds.
Thus, burnt newspaper can help form a cloud.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where Do Droplets Float?
activities.prompt: Which place do small droplets float in?
options: Inside wet sand
Inside the air
Inside burnt newspaper
Inside a heavy drop
activities.explanation: Clouds form when small droplets float in the air.

activities.title: Match Each Part
activities.prompt: Match each part with what it does.
activities.explanation: Each part has a job in clouds, rain, or cooling.

activities.title: Keep the Sand Moist
activities.prompt: A pot-in-pot cooler has sand. The sand must be kept ______.
activities.hint: Moist means having water in it.
activities.explanation: The sand in a pot-in-pot cooler must be kept moist.

activities.title: What Happens to Heavy Drops?
activities.prompt: What happens when water drops get heavy?
options: They float higher.
They fall as rain.
They dry the sand.
They form dust.
activities.explanation: Heavy water drops fall as rain.

activities.title: Cloud Formation Steps
activities.prompt: Put the cloud and rain steps in the right order.
items: Tiny droplets form around dust particles.
Small droplets float in the air.
Clouds form.
Heavy water drops fall as rain.
activities.explanation: Droplets form first. Then they float and make clouds. Then they fall as rain.

activities.title: Why Burnt Newspaper?
activities.prompt: Why can burnt newspaper help make clouds?
options: It gives tiny dust particles.
It holds heavy water drops.
It makes the sand wet.
It stops water moving.
activities.explanation: Burnt newspaper gives tiny dust particles. Water vapour forms clouds around them.

activities.prompt: A child finds dry sand in a pot-in-pot cooler. What should the child do?
options: Add water and keep the sand moist.
Add more dry sand to the cooler.
Put the dry sand near a cloud.
Wait for rain to wet the sand.

This mistake thinks dry sand needs more sand.
This mistake mixes sand with cloud formation.
This mistake expects rain to water the sand.

activities.explanation: This is right because the cooler requires moist sand.

activities.prompt: Tiny droplets have formed around dust particles in the air. What happens next?
options: They float in the air and form clouds.
They fall as rain before clouds form.
They change into heavier drops at once.
They stay beside the dust particles.

This mistake reverses cloud formation and rain.
This mistake predicts heavy drops before cloud formation.
This mistake thinks droplets stay beside dust.

activities.explanation: Small droplets float in the air and form clouds.

activities.prompt: The small droplets in a cloud have become heavy. What will happen next?
options: They will fall to the ground as rain.
They will float higher and form more clouds.
They will change back into dust particles.
They will stay still inside the cloud.

why.They will float higher and form more clo: This mistake thinks heavy drops keep floating.
why.They will change back into dust particle: This mistake confuses water droplets with dust.
This mistake ignores that heavy drops fall.

activities.explanation: Heavy water drops fall as rain, so this is correct.

activities.prompt: Someone says snow may fall, but hail never may. What is wrong?
options: Hail may also fall under special conditions.
Snow may also fall during normal rain.
Rain may also fall as tiny dust.
Clouds may also fall as heavy snow.

This mistake treats snow as an ordinary rain condition.
This mistake confuses rain with dust.
This mistake confuses clouds with falling water.

activities.explanation: Hail, like snow, may fall under special conditions.

activities.prompt: Burnt newspaper is used to make a cloud. Why can it work?
options: The newspaper dust helps water vapour form clouds.
The newspaper smoke traps heavy rain drops.
The newspaper heat turns droplets into sand.
The newspaper drops gather into a cloud.

why.The newspaper smoke traps heavy rain dro: This mistake confuses dust particles with smoke.
why.The newspaper heat turns droplets into s: This mistake invents a heat and sand change.
This mistake treats the newspaper itself as water drops.

activities.explanation: Burnt newspaper dust lets water vapour form clouds.

activities.prompt: During the water cycle, water moves between Earth's surface and atmosphere. What should people do?
options: Use water wisely and avoid wasting it.
Use water quickly and waste some.
Use water only when clouds appear.
Use water only when rain is falling.

This mistake treats wasting water as harmless.
This mistake links water use to cloud watching.
This mistake thinks water is unavailable without rain.

activities.explanation: Using water wisely and avoiding waste protects water.

activities.context: An ice cube was left on a table during the day. Some water that had splashed formed a playground puddle, and water was left on a utensil nearby. By evening, the ice had become water, some water in the puddle had disappeared, and the water on the utensil had dried up. The ice and water were forms of the same substance, while the disappearing water had changed into water vapour.
activities.prompt: What would have happened if the ice cube had been left in a freezer instead of on the table?
options: It would be converted into ice.
It would change into water that flows and splashes.
It would turn into visible water vapour.
It would stay hard and begin to flow.

why.It would change into water that flows an: Water in a freezer becomes ice, not flowing water.
The gaseous state is water vapour, which is invisible.
Ice does not flow or splash.

activities.explanation: Water left in a freezer is converted into ice.

activities.context: An ice cube was left on a table during the day. Some water that had splashed formed a playground puddle, and water was left on a utensil nearby. By evening, the ice had become water, some water in the puddle had disappeared, and the water on the utensil had dried up. The ice and water were forms of the same substance, while the disappearing water had changed into water vapour.
activities.prompt: Why did the puddle lose some water and the water on the utensil dry up?
options: Liquid water changed into water vapour through evaporation.
The water changed into ice and then disappeared.
Visible water vapour settled onto the utensil.
The water changed into a different substance.

why.The water changed into ice and then disa: This change of water into vapour is called evaporation.
why.Visible water vapour settled onto the ut: Water vapour is invisible, and steam is visible because of tiny droplets.
why.The water changed into a different subst: Evaporation changes the state of water without changing the substance.

activities.explanation: Water can change into the gaseous state called water vapour.

activities.context: An ice cube was left on a table during the day. Some water that had splashed formed a playground puddle, and water was left on a utensil nearby. By evening, the ice had become water, some water in the puddle had disappeared, and the water on the utensil had dried up. The ice and water were forms of the same substance, while the disappearing water had changed into water vapour.
activities.prompt: A classmate says that the water vapour from the drying puddle can be seen directly. Which reply uses the facts correctly?
options: Water vapour is invisible, though steam can be visible because of tiny droplets.
Water vapour is visible, and steam is visible for the same reason.
Water vapour becomes visible after changing into ice.
Water vapour can be seen whenever liquid water disappears.

why.Water vapour is visible, and steam is vi: Tiny water droplets make steam visible.
why.Water vapour becomes visible after chang: Ice is not the gaseous state of water.
why.Water vapour can be seen whenever liquid: Disappearing water changes into invisible water vapour.

activities.explanation: Water vapour itself cannot be seen.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between ice and water as states of the same substance.
activities.answer: Water and ice are two forms of the same substance, so a change between them is a change of state. Ice feels hard when touched and does not flow or splash. Water can flow and splash. Since different forms of a substance are called states, ice and water show different states of the same substance.
points: Ice and water are forms of the same substance.
Different forms of a substance are called states.
Ice feels hard and does not flow or splash.
Water flows and splashes.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A child filled a glass tumbler with cold water and ice and noticed tiny water droplets on the outside. The small droplets combined to form bigger drops. One possible reason was that some ice had melted outside the tumbler, although the children argued that the water level did not go down. Dew drops could also be seen on plants. Later, water drops gathered on the inner side of a steel plate covering boiling water.
activities.prompt: Which explanation could apply to the drops on the outside of the tumbler and the drops on the inner side of the steel plate?
options: Water vapour can change into liquid water on both surfaces; this change is condensation.
Liquid water passes through both surfaces and collects on their other sides.
The tumbler drops come only from melting ice, while the plate drops come only from boiling water.
Water vapour changes into ice before becoming the liquid drops.

why.Liquid water passes through both surface: The activity shows that water does not seep through the tumbler.
why.The tumbler drops come only from melting: This overlooks condensation as an explanation for both sets of drops.
why.Water vapour changes into ice before bec: This replaces condensation with a change into ice.

activities.explanation: Correct: this is the stated meaning of condensation.

activities.context: A child filled a glass tumbler with cold water and ice and noticed tiny water droplets on the outside. The small droplets combined to form bigger drops. One possible reason was that some ice had melted outside the tumbler, although the children argued that the water level did not go down. Dew drops could also be seen on plants. Later, water drops gathered on the inner side of a steel plate covering boiling water.
activities.prompt: What should the children consider when explaining all the water outside the tumbler?
options: Consider condensation and the possible melting of ice outside the tumbler.
Consider condensation only, because it is always the sole cause.
Reject condensation because the water level did not go down.
Consider melting ice outside as the only possible cause.

why.Consider condensation only, because it i: This wrongly treats condensation as the only source.
why.Reject condensation because the water le: The unchanged level shows no seepage, not that condensation is impossible.

activities.explanation: Correct: the activity alone cannot rule out either possibility.

activities.prompt: Explain how condensation can be connected with the drops on the tumbler and the steel plate.
activities.answer: The outside drops of the tumbler and the drops on the inner side of the steel plate can both involve water vapour changing into liquid water. This change is called condensation. Condensation can therefore help explain drops appearing in different places, although the activity does not prove that it explains every outside drop.
points: Condensation is water vapour changing into liquid water.
The tumbler has drops on its outside.
The steel plate has drops on its inner side.
Condensation may not be the only source of the outside drops.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Someone places ice in a container and heats it. At first, the ice keeps its own shape and cannot flow or spread. As heating continues, the ice melts and becomes liquid water. The liquid water flows and changes its shape to match the container. With further heating, the liquid changes into water vapour, which spreads throughout the available space.
activities.prompt: If heating continues after the ice has melted, what will happen next?
options: It will enter the gaseous state and spread through the space.
It will stay liquid because the earlier heating had already melted it.
It will return to solid form because the container cannot hold it.
It will remain solid because further heating will have no effect.

why.It will stay liquid because the earlier: Further heating does more than melting; it changes liquid water into a gas.
why.It will return to solid form because the: The ice has already melted, and further heating changes the liquid into a gas.
why.It will remain solid because further hea: Further heating can change liquid water into its gaseous state.

activities.explanation: Further heating changes liquid water into its gaseous state.

activities.context: Someone places ice in a container and heats it. At first, the ice keeps its own shape and cannot flow or spread. As heating continues, the ice melts and becomes liquid water. The liquid water flows and changes its shape to match the container. With further heating, the liquid changes into water vapour, which spreads throughout the available space.
activities.prompt: If the liquid water is moved into another container, what can be expected?
options: It will flow, change shape, and keep the same volume.
It will keep its old shape because it is already water.
It will spread as water vapour and keep the same volume.
It will become solid and keep the shape of the first container.

why.It will keep its old shape because it is: Keeping the old shape is the behaviour of solid ice.
why.It will spread as water vapour and keep: Water vapour is produced only after further heating of the liquid.
why.It will become solid and keep the shape: Freezing, not moving the water, changes liquid water into a solid.

activities.explanation: Liquid water flows, changes shape, and retains its volume.

activities.context: Someone places ice in a container and heats it. At first, the ice keeps its own shape and cannot flow or spread. As heating continues, the ice melts and becomes liquid water. The liquid water flows and changes its shape to match the container. With further heating, the liquid changes into water vapour, which spreads throughout the available space.
activities.prompt: Why did the ice keep its original shape at the beginning of the case?
options: Because the water was still in its solid form.
Because it had already melted and become liquid.
Because it had already changed into water vapour.
Because heating always makes water keep its original shape.

why.Because it had already melted and become: The melting stage had not happened when the ice kept its shape.
why.Because it had already changed into wate: Water vapour spreads through space rather than keeping the shape of ice.
why.Because heating always makes water keep: Heating causes melting and then changes the liquid into gaseous water.

activities.explanation: At the beginning, the ice was solid and had not yet melted.

activities.prompt: Explain how heating changes water from ice into water vapour.
activities.answer: Heating first melts the solid ice into liquid water. The liquid flows and changes shape to fit its container, but its volume remains constant. If heating continues, the liquid changes into gaseous water, which spreads throughout the available space.
points: Heating causes ice to melt.
Liquid water flows and changes shape.
The volume of liquid water stays constant when its shape changes.
Further heating produces water vapour, which spreads.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student puts water in a capped bottle and also spreads some water on a plate. The student leaves both in sunlight and records how long each amount takes to evaporate completely, changing one condition while keeping the others the same. The cap has less exposed area, while the plate exposes more water to air. The student then notices that the water on the plate has disappeared sooner.
activities.prompt: Why did the water on the plate evaporate completely before the water in the capped bottle?
options: More of its surface was exposed to air, allowing it to disappear sooner.
Less of its surface was exposed to air, so it disappeared sooner.
It contained less water, so less time was needed to evaporate.
It was protected from moving air, so its water disappeared sooner.

why.Less of its surface was exposed to air,: A smaller exposed area does not explain faster evaporation.
why.It contained less water, so less time wa: The amount of water was not the condition being compared.
why.It was protected from moving air, so its: Protection from moving air would not explain the result.

activities.explanation: A larger exposed area makes evaporation faster.

activities.context: A student puts water in a capped bottle and also spreads some water on a plate. The student leaves both in sunlight and records how long each amount takes to evaporate completely, changing one condition while keeping the others the same. The cap has less exposed area, while the plate exposes more water to air. The student then notices that the water on the plate has disappeared sooner.
activities.prompt: If the investigation is repeated when the air has more humidity and the other conditions remain the same, what should happen?
options: The water should take more time to evaporate completely.
The water should take less time to evaporate completely.
The water should take the same time because the containers have different exposed areas.
The water should take less time because sunlight makes evaporation faster regardless of humidity.

why.The water should take less time to evapo: Faster evaporation would not agree with the effect of humidity.
why.The water should take the same time beca: Different exposed areas do not remove the effect of humidity.
why.The water should take less time because: Sunlight does not remove the effect of humidity.

activities.explanation: More humidity makes water evaporate slowly.

activities.prompt: Explain why the water spread on the plate should evaporate completely before the water in the capped bottle when the other conditions stay the same.
activities.answer: The water spread on the plate had a larger exposed area than the water in the capped bottle. Water evaporates faster when its exposed area is larger. Therefore, the water on the plate should evaporate completely in less time when the other conditions remain the same.
points: The plate had a larger exposed area.
Water evaporates faster with a larger exposed area.
Other conditions remained the same.
The plate's water should disappear sooner.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A family uses a pot-in-pot cooler for its food. The space between the pots is filled with sand, and the sand is kept moist. Leave the sand dry until it is needed.

why.Mix burnt-newspaper dust into the dry sa: Burnt-newspaper dust is used for cloud formation, not moistening the sand.

chapters.title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
chapters.summary: In this chapter: handpicking and threshing; winnowing, threshers and sieving; making salt and evaporation; decantation, sedimentation and filtration.

lessons.title: Handpicking and Threshing

activities.prompt: How do farmers separate unwanted pieces and grains from their plants?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Handpicking and Threshing
activities.body:
You begin with handpicking. It means removing unwanted pieces from a mixture by hand. You look for particles that differ in size, colour and shape.

Handpicking is convenient when unwanted particles are few and easy to pick. It is useful when you can easily remove the unwanted pieces by hand.

Malli shows you whole black peppers. He picked them from the pulao with his fingers. This is handpicking because he uses his fingers.

Next, you visit harvested stalks spread in the sun to dry. Farmers then beat the stalks on a large wooden log. Beating stalks to separate their grains is called threshing. You watch the threshing separate grains from the stalks.

Many grains remain attached to each wheat stalk before threshing. After beating, the separated grains get mixed with piles of husk.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Handpicking and Threshing
activities.body: Handpicking is removing unwanted pieces from a mixture by hand. It works when particles differ in size, colour and shape. It is convenient when the unwanted particles are few and easy to pick. Malli used his fingers to pick whole black peppers from pulao. To separate grains from stalks, farmers may dry stalks, then beat them on a large wooden log. This beating is called threshing.
keyPoints: Handpicking removes unwanted pieces by hand.
It suits few unwanted particles that are easy to pick.
Threshing separates grains by beating stalks.
activities.explanation: These steps show handpicking and threshing at work.

activities.prompt: Why can Malli remove black peppers from the pulao by hand?
steps: The black peppers differ in colour, so they can be spotted.
They are whole, so Malli's fingers can grasp them.
Handpicking fits because the unwanted pieces are easy to pick.
Therefore, Malli should handpick them from the pulao.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which mixture is best for handpicking?
options: Whole black peppers mixed with pulao
Many grains stuck to one wheat stalk
Cut stalks spread in the sun
Grains mixed with piles of husk
activities.explanation: Whole black peppers can be picked out by hand.

activities.prompt: Match each sentence with the right word or action.
pairs: Taking out unwanted pieces by hand
Farmers did this on a wooden log
activities.explanation: Each word matches taking out unwanted pieces or separating grains.

activities.prompt: When is handpicking easiest?
options: When there are many unwanted particles, hard to pick.
When particles differ in only one way.
When there are few unwanted particles, easy to pick.
When grains stay stuck to each stalk.
activities.explanation: Handpicking is easiest when there are few unwanted particles, and they are easy to pick.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Break a magnet into smaller pieces.
Each piece becomes a smaller magnet.
Each smaller magnet has a North pole and a South pole.
activities.explanation: Breaking makes smaller magnets. Each has a North pole and a South pole.

activities.prompt: Which method separates grains from stalks?
options: Handpicking unwanted pieces from a mixture
Beating stalks on a big wooden log
Spreading cut stalks in the sun
Mixing separated grains with piles of husk
activities.explanation: Beating stalks to separate grains is called threshing.

activities.prompt: Handpicking removes unwanted pieces from a mixture. A bowl has large red beads among small blue beads. The blue beads are wanted. What will handpicking remove?
options: The large red beads will be picked out.
The small blue beads will be picked out.
Both kinds of beads will be picked out.
No beads will be picked from the bowl.

This mistake treats the wanted blue beads as unwanted pieces.
This mistake assumes that handpicking cannot choose what to remove.
This mistake assumes that picking a mixture removes nothing.

activities.explanation: This is right because the red beads are the unwanted pieces.

activities.prompt: Handpicking is convenient when unwanted pieces are few and easy to pick. A tray has one unwanted piece that is easy to grasp. What should someone do?
options: Pick out the unwanted piece by hand.
Wait for the wanted pieces to dry.
Beat the mixture on a large wooden log.
Pick out every wanted piece by hand.

This mistake confuses handpicking with drying.
This mistake confuses handpicking with threshing.
This mistake ignores the one piece that can be picked directly.

activities.explanation: This is right because one easy piece can be picked by hand.

activities.prompt: Beating stalks to separate grains is called threshing. Some harvested stalks are spread in the sun for drying. What should farmers do later to separate the grains?
options: Beat the stalks on a large wooden log.
Pick out all the grains with fingers.
Spread the stalks in the sun again.
Leave all the stalks gathered without beating.

This mistake assumes fingers can remove all attached grains.
This mistake confuses drying with threshing.
why.Leave all the stalks gathered without be: This mistake thinks drying alone separates the grains.

activities.explanation: This is right because beating stalks separates their grains.

activities.prompt: Handpicking removes unwanted pieces from a mixture. After threshing, loose grains are mixed with piles of husk. The husk pieces are few and easy to grasp. What should someone do next?
options: Handpick the husk out of the loose grains.
Handpick the grains out of the husk piles.
Beat the grains again to remove the husk.
Spread the grains back onto the dry stalks.

why.Handpick the grains out of the husk pile: This mistake reverses the wanted and unwanted pieces.
why.Beat the grains again to remove the husk: This mistake confuses handpicking with threshing.
why.Spread the grains back onto the dry stal: This mistake tries to undo the grain separation.

activities.explanation: This is right because the unwanted husk is few and easy to grasp.

lessons.title: Winnowing, Threshers and Sieving

activities.prompt: What can air, threshers and sieves help separate?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Separating Grains and Flour
activities.body:
You arrive at a farm, ready to see how wheat is separated. A farmer shows you a bamboo tray, called a soop. The tray holds threshed wheat. He moves it in the direction of the wind.

As the air blows, heavier and lighter components become separated. You watch carefully as the moving air sorts the mixture. This separation by wind or blown air is called winnowing.

Next, you see a modern thresher. It separates grains from stalks and husk. A thresher performs threshing and winnowing at the same time. Modern technology has led to the development of these machines.

Afterwards, you see a sieve used to remove bran from flour. Fine flour particles pass through its holes. Bran and small stones remain on the sieve. You notice how the small flour travels, while larger pieces stay above.

Sieving is used for solid mixtures with components of different sizes. It separates solids according to differences in particle size. You finish your tour understanding three separation methods.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Three Ways to Separate Mixtures
activities.body: Winnowing uses wind or blown air to separate a mixture. Farmers use a soop. A soop is a bamboo tray. They move it with the wind or air. Threshers separate grains from stalks and husk. A thresher does both threshing and winnowing at once. Sieving separates solids by particle size. A sieve takes bran out of flour. Fine flour goes through the holes. Bran and small stones stay behind.
keyPoints: Winnowing uses wind or blown air.
Threshers separate grains from stalks and husk.
Sieving separates solids by particle size.
activities.explanation: These ways separate mixtures using air, moving parts, or size.

activities.prompt: A farmer has threshed wheat in a bamboo tray. Air blows across the tray. What will happen to the lighter and heavier parts?
steps: The farmer moves the tray toward the blowing air because moving air separates mixed parts.
Lighter parts travel with air, while heavier parts stay nearer the tray.
This happens because the parts have different weights.
So the farmer is winnowing the threshed wheat with wind.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Threshers and Sieves Help
activities.body: Threshing machines separate grains from stalks and husk. A thresher performs threshing and winnowing at the same time. Winnowing uses wind or blown air to separate parts of a mixture. Sieving separates solids when their components have different sizes. During sieving, fine flour particles pass through the holes of a sieve. Bran and small stones remain on the sieve.
keyPoints: A thresher threshes and winnows together.
Fine flour particles pass through sieve holes.
Bran and small stones remain on the sieve.
activities.explanation: Threshers handle grain mixtures, while sieves separate flour by particle size.

activities.title: Choose the Separation Method
activities.prompt: Which method uses wind or blown air to separate a mixture?
options: Winnowing
Sieving
Using a sieve
Moving a bamboo tray
activities.explanation: Winnowing uses wind or blown air to separate a mixture.

activities.title: Know the Soop
activities.prompt: A soop is a bamboo tray. People use it for separation.
activities.explanation: Soop is another name for an old bamboo tray.

activities.title: Match the Methods and Results
activities.prompt: Match each method or material with its correct use or result.
pairs: Separates grains from stalks and husk
activities.explanation: Each pair shows the correct separation method or result.

activities.title: What Does a Thresher Do at Once?
activities.prompt: What can a thresher do at the same time?
options: Threshing and winnowing
Moving a bamboo tray
Passing fine flour through holes
Removing bran with a sieve
activities.explanation: A thresher does threshing and winnowing at the same time.

activities.title: Finish the Kitchen Sentence
activities.prompt: A ______ is used to take bran out of flour.
activities.hint: It has holes. It keeps bran and small stones.
activities.explanation: A sieve takes bran out of flour. Fine flour goes through its holes.

activities.title: Where Does Fine Flour Go?
activities.prompt: Fine flour bits stay on the sieve.
activities.explanation: Fine flour bits go through the holes. Bran and small stones stay on the sieve.

activities.prompt: Blowing air can separate heavier and lighter parts. A tray holds both kinds. What will happen?
options: Light parts move with the air, while heavy parts stay lower.

activities.prompt: A solid mixture has two kinds of small solid pieces. Their sizes are different. Which method is best?

Winnowing, because its holes use the difference in particle size.
Winnowing, because blown air sorts pieces by their size.
Sieving, because blown air sorts pieces by their size.

why.Winnowing, because its holes use the dif: This mistake gives sieving's size rule to winnowing.
why.Winnowing, because blown air sorts piece: This mistake gives sieving's job to wind separation.
why.Sieving, because blown air sorts pieces: This mistake gives wind separation the job of sieving.

lessons.title: Making Salt and Evaporation

activities.prompt: What can you discover when sunlight and air meet seawater?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Making Salt and Drying Plants
activities.body:
You begin beside the sea, where seawater carries salts and other substances dissolved in water. This is the start of your search for salt.

First, you follow seawater into shallow pits. The water rests there while sunlight and air reach it. Slowly, the water evaporates. The pits help you obtain the salt you want.

That evaporation leaves a solid mixture behind. You look closely and discover common salt within this mixture. It has been obtained from what the sea left in the shallow pits.

Now, you visit an Ayurveda garden. Plant parts serve as remedies here. Roots, leaves, flowers, and seeds may become ingredients. You watch medicinal plants dry in the shade.

Drying helps excess water evaporate from the medicinal ingredients. The important part of the medicine remains after drying. You finish by comparing both journeys. Seawater loses water, leaving the mixture. From this mixture, common salt is obtained. Medicinal ingredients also lose excess water, but keep their important part.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Salt Is Made
activities.body: Seawater contains salts and other substances dissolved in water. To obtain salt, seawater is kept in shallow pits. The pits are exposed to sunlight and air. Water evaporates and leaves a solid mixture. Common salt is obtained from the solid mixture left behind.
keyPoints: Seawater contains dissolved salts and other substances.
Shallow pits are exposed to sunlight and air.
Water evaporates, leaving a solid mixture for common salt.
activities.explanation: Salt is obtained after water evaporates from seawater.

activities.title: Heat the water

tasks.say: Freeze the water.
tasks.then: Below 0 degrees water is ice: its particles can only jiggle in place.

tasks.say: Boil it.
tasks.then: At 100 degrees water boils and its particles fly apart as steam.

activities.takeaway: Heating gives particles more energy: held in place in ice, sliding in water, flying apart as steam.
activities.explanation: Heating gives particles more energy: held in place in ice, sliding in water, flying apart as steam.

activities.prompt: How can salt be obtained from seawater?
steps: Seawater contains salts and other substances dissolved in water.
Seawater is kept in shallow pits exposed to sunlight and air.
The water evaporates because the pits are exposed to sunlight and air.
A solid mixture remains, and common salt is obtained from it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: To get salt, seawater is kept in shallow ______.
activities.hint: These are shallow holes. They hold seawater.
activities.explanation: Seawater is kept in shallow pits to get salt.

activities.prompt: Match each part of the process with its description.
pairs: has salt and other things dissolved in water
is taken from the solid mix
activities.explanation: Each pair shows one step in making salt from seawater.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the correct order.
items: Break a magnet into smaller pieces.
Each piece becomes a smaller magnet.
Each smaller magnet has a North pole and a South pole.
activities.explanation: Breaking makes smaller magnets. Each has a North pole and a South pole.

activities.prompt: What happens when water evaporates from seawater?
options: The seawater becomes deeper
A solid mixture remains
The salt becomes water
The pits become dry
activities.explanation: When water evaporates, a solid mixture is left behind.

activities.prompt: Common salt comes from the ______ mixture left behind.
activities.hint: This mixture is left after water evaporates.
activities.explanation: The solid mixture left behind gives common salt.

activities.prompt: A child wants salt from seawater. Which method follows the process?
options: Keep seawater in a deep covered jar.
Keep seawater in a shallow open pit.
Keep seawater in a closed bottle.
Keep seawater in a shaded closed pot.

This is wrong because the pit is not shallow and exposed.
This is wrong because the bottle is closed and not a shallow pit.
This is wrong because the pot is closed and kept in shade.

activities.explanation: This is right because shallow pits are exposed to sunlight and air.

activities.prompt: A child says the solid mixture is already common salt. What is the best correction?
options: Common salt comes from the solid mixture.
Common salt is only the water in the mixture.
Common salt forms before the water evaporates.
Common salt is found only in seawater.

why.Common salt is only the water in the mix: This is wrong because water is not obtained as common salt.
why.Common salt forms before the water evapo: This is wrong because common salt is obtained after water evaporates.
This is wrong because the mixture left behind gives common salt.

activities.explanation: This is right because common salt is obtained from the solid mixture.

activities.prompt: Medicinal plant parts are often dried in the shade. Why is drying useful?
options: It helps excess water evaporate from the ingredients.
It adds more water to the ingredients.
It turns every ingredient into common salt.
It removes all substances from the ingredients.

This is wrong because drying removes water rather than adding it.
why.It turns every ingredient into common sa: This is wrong because drying plant parts does not make common salt.
why.It removes all substances from the ingre: This is wrong because the important part remains after drying.

activities.explanation: This is right because drying helps excess water evaporate.

lessons.title: Decantation, Sedimentation and Filtration

activities.prompt: What will you discover about tea leaves, muddy water, and rice?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Tea, Mud and Pulses
activities.body:
Imagine a cup of tea, with tea leaves resting at the bottom of the vessel. You leave the tea undisturbed, giving the tea leaves time to settle. Now tilt the vessel and pour off the clear liquid. This removal of liquid by tilting is called decantation.

Pour the tea through a strainer, and the tea leaves separate from the tea. Decantation has not removed every tea leaf from it. Filter paper has very fine pores for trapping tiny particles. Cloth also has very small holes between its woven threads.

Picture muddy liquid passing through filter paper. The mud is left on the paper as a residue. The clear liquid that passes through your filter is called the filtrate.

Next, watch a heavier insoluble component settling in a liquid. This process is called sedimentation, and it takes place at the bottom. After the solid settles, tilt the vessel and decant the liquid. Decantation is also used to wash and clean rice and pulses.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Separating tea and other mixtures
activities.body: Decantation means removing liquid by tilting a container. Sedimentation means a heavy part settles at the bottom. This part does not dissolve in the liquid. Tea leaves settle when the tea is left still. Decanting does not remove every tea leaf. Filtering tea through a strainer separates the leaves. Cloth has very small holes. Filter paper has tiny pores. They trap very small particles. Mud stays behind as residue. The clear liquid that passes through is filtrate.
keyPoints: Sedimentation makes heavy insoluble parts sink to the bottom.
Decantation removes liquid by tilting a container.
A strainer separates tea leaves from tea.
activities.explanation: These methods separate the tea leaves from the tea.

activities.prompt: After making tea, someone wants clear tea without any tea leaves. What should they do?
steps: Tea leaves are heavier and insoluble, so they settle at the bottom.
They should tilt the vessel because this removes the clear liquid by decantation.
Decantation may leave some leaves because it does not remove every tea leaf.
They should pass the tea through a strainer to separate the remaining leaves.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is sedimentation?
options: Heavy bits that do not dissolve sink in a liquid
Pouring off liquid by tilting a container
Catching tiny bits in very small holes
Separating tea leaves with a strainer
activities.explanation: Heavy bits that do not dissolve settle at the bottom of a liquid.

activities.prompt: In decantation, you remove the liquid by ______ the container.
activities.hint: You slant the container so the liquid can flow out.
activities.explanation: Decantation means taking out the liquid by tilting the container.

activities.prompt: Which material has tiny holes between its woven threads?
options: Filter paper
Cloth
Tea leaves
Mud
activities.explanation: Cloth has tiny holes between its woven threads.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its right description.
activities.explanation: Lodestones are natural magnets. Pencil box magnets are artificial. Iron is magnetic.

activities.prompt: A clear liquid goes through a filter. We call this liquid the ______.
activities.hint: This word names the clear liquid.
activities.explanation: The clear liquid is called the filtrate.

activities.prompt: Put these tea steps in the right order.
items: Leave the tea still
The leaves sink to the bottom
Tilt the pot and pour out the liquid
Filter the tea through a strainer
activities.explanation: Decanting removes some settled leaves. Then the strainer takes out the rest.

activities.prompt: Tea has settled. A person tilts the vessel. What is removed first?
options: The clear liquid above the settled leaves.
The settled tea leaves from the bottom.
The tea leaves caught by a strainer.
The mud from a filter paper.

This mistake thinks decantation removes settled leaves first.
This mistake confuses decantation with filtering tea through a strainer.
This mistake mixes filtering muddy water with tea decantation.

activities.explanation: This is right because tilting the vessel removes the liquid.

activities.prompt: Which test best compares cloth and filter paper for trapping tiny mud?
options: Pass muddy water through each, then check the mud left.
Leave each material in muddy water without filtering it.
Fill each material with tea, then compare the settled leaves.
Wash rice and pulses with each, then compare the grains.

why.Leave each material in muddy water witho: This mistake confuses settling with passing liquid through a filter.
why.Fill each material with tea, then compar: This mistake uses tea instead of muddy water in the test.
why.Wash rice and pulses with each, then com: This mistake changes the material being tested instead of holding it steady.

activities.explanation: This is right because the same muddy water tests both materials.

activities.prompt: A child claims that decanting tea removes every tea leaf. What shows the claim is wrong?
options: Some leaves remain after the liquid is tilted out.
The tea leaves settle before the liquid is tilted.
The clear liquid is removed by tilting the vessel.
The tea leaves rest at the bottom of the vessel.

why.The tea leaves settle before the liquid: This fact only shows settling, not that leaves remain after tilting.
why.The clear liquid is removed by tilting t: This fact only shows how liquid is removed, not that every leaf goes.
why.The tea leaves rest at the bottom of the: This fact only shows where leaves settle, not that all are removed.

activities.explanation: This is right because decantation does not remove every tea leaf.

lessons.title: Churning and Magnetic Separation

activities.prompt: What wonders can you uncover through churning and magnetic separation?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Churning and Magnetic Separation
activities.body:
You begin by watching curd being churned with a churner called a mathni. You watch until butter is obtained from the curd. You remember the tool's name and the process. You now know what churning produces.

Next, you meet sawdust containing iron nails. You watch a magnet attract all the nails. You learn that substances attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic substances. Iron is a common magnetic substance. That is why you see the iron nails moving towards the magnet.

Then you watch a magnetic separation demonstration. A magnet separates magnetic and non-magnetic substances. You compare the iron nails with the sawdust around them. You see the magnetic part move towards the magnet. You now understand how this separation works.

Finally, you visit a waste sorting place. Recyclers use magnets to separate iron articles from waste. You then see a crane-mounted magnet at work. It separates scrap iron from waste materials. You connect this scene with the sawdust demonstration. You now know why magnets help separate iron from waste.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Churning and magnets
activities.body: Curd is churned with a mathni, and churning gives butter. A magnet attracts iron nails in sawdust. Substances attracted towards a magnet are magnetic substances. Iron is a common magnetic substance. Magnetic separation uses a magnet to separate magnetic and non-magnetic substances. Recyclers use magnets to separate iron from waste. Crane-mounted magnets separate scrap iron from waste materials.
keyPoints: Curd is churned with a mathni to obtain butter.
Iron is a common magnetic substance.
Magnets separate magnetic substances from other materials.
activities.explanation: These facts show two useful processes involving churners and magnets.

activities.title: Push and pull

tasks.say: Make the magnets push each other away.
tasks.then: Like poles facing each other repel.

tasks.say: Bring them very close.
tasks.then: Closer magnets pull or push much harder.

activities.takeaway: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel, and both get stronger when the magnets are close.
activities.explanation: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel, and both get stronger when the magnets are close.

activities.prompt: A recycler has iron articles mixed with waste. How can the iron articles be separated?
steps: Iron is magnetic, so a magnet attracts it.
The magnet therefore pulls iron articles away from the waste.
Recyclers use magnets to separate iron from waste.
Thus, iron articles are separated from the waste materials.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is a mathni?
options: A churner used for curd
A magnet used for waste
A crane used for iron
A nail used in sawdust
activities.explanation: A mathni is the churner used to churn curd.

activities.prompt: Substances that a magnet pulls are called ______ substances.
activities.hint: The name tells how they act with a magnet.
activities.explanation: These substances are called magnetic substances.

activities.prompt: Match each item with its partner.
activities.explanation: Churning makes butter. Iron is magnetic. Magnets help with magnetic separation.

activities.prompt: Why do recycling workers use magnets?
options: To churn curd into butter
To make iron things into sawdust
To separate iron things from waste
To turn waste into iron
activities.explanation: Magnets help recycling workers separate iron things from waste.

activities.prompt: Magnets on a crane separate what?
options: Curd from butter
Butter from a mathni
Sawdust from iron nails
Scrap iron from waste
activities.explanation: Crane magnets separate scrap iron from waste.

activities.prompt: Iron nails are mixed with sawdust. A magnet moves close. What will happen?
options: All the sawdust will move toward the magnet.
The iron nails will move away from the magnet.
Only the iron nails will move toward the magnet.
Both the nails and sawdust will stay still.

why.All the sawdust will move toward the mag: This mistakes sawdust for a magnetic substance.
why.The iron nails will move away from the m: This wrongly thinks a magnet pushes iron away.
why.Both the nails and sawdust will stay sti: This wrongly thinks the magnet attracts nothing here.

activities.explanation: The magnet attracts the iron nails in the sawdust.

activities.prompt: A recycler wants iron articles separated from waste. Which test is fair?
options: Use a magnet and observe what it attracts.
Use a magnet after removing every iron article.
Check whether all the waste sticks to a magnet.
Use two magnets and count all the waste.

why.Use a magnet after removing every iron a: This removes the iron before the test can show it.
why.Check whether all the waste sticks to a: This checks the waste instead of separating iron articles.
This measures the magnets, not magnetic attraction.

activities.explanation: This directly tests what the magnet can attract.

activities.prompt: A claim says sawdust is magnetic. Why is the claim wrong?
options: The sawdust is magnetic, so the magnet attracts it.
The magnet attracts iron nails, not the sawdust.
Iron nails are non-magnetic, so the magnet avoids them.
The magnet attracts sawdust but leaves every nail behind.

why.The sawdust is magnetic, so the magnet a: This wrongly treats sawdust as a magnetic substance.
why.The magnet attracts sawdust but leaves e: This reverses what the magnet attracts and leaves.

activities.explanation: The magnet attracts the iron nails in the sawdust.

activities.prompt: A magnet pulls iron nails from sawdust. Which explanation fits best?
options: Iron is non-magnetic, so the magnet attracts the nails.
The nails attract the magnet because they are non-magnetic.
Iron is magnetic, so the magnet attracts the nails.
All sawdust is magnetic, so the magnet attracts it.

why.Iron is non-magnetic, so the magnet attr: This wrongly says iron is non-magnetic.
why.The nails attract the magnet because the: This wrongly uses non-magnetic iron to explain attraction.
why.All sawdust is magnetic, so the magnet a: This wrongly treats all sawdust as magnetic.

activities.explanation: Iron is a common magnetic substance, so the magnet attracts nails.

activities.prompt: Iron nails and curd need different tools. Which tools should be used?
options: Use a mathni for nails and a magnet for curd.
Use a magnet for nails and a magnet for curd.
Use a mathni for nails and a mathni for curd.
Use a magnet for nails and a mathni for curd.

why.Use a mathni for nails and a magnet for: This swaps the jobs of the magnet and mathni.
why.Use a magnet for nails and a magnet for: This wrongly uses a magnet for churning curd.
why.Use a mathni for nails and a mathni for: This wrongly uses a mathni for separating iron nails.

activities.explanation: A magnet separates nails, and a mathni churns curd into butter.

lessons.sceneAlt: Farmers thresh grain manually.
lessons.sceneCaption: Farmers work together to thresh grain manually.

sceneCredit.creator: Drashokk

activities.context: Malli found whole black peppers mixed with the grains in the pulao. He picked out the black peppers with his fingers because they were easy to remove and did not look like the grains. The unwanted pieces were few, and their colour and shape were different from the other grains. This made handpicking a convenient way to separate them.
activities.prompt: If Malli had harvested stalks with many grains still attached, what should he do to separate the grains?
options: Beat the stalks on a large wooden log.
Spread the stalks in the sun and leave them without beating.
Pick the grains from the stalks one by one by hand.
Remove only the black peppers and leave the stalks unchanged.

why.Spread the stalks in the sun and leave t: Drying stalks in the sun does not separate the attached grains.
why.Pick the grains from the stalks one by o: Handpicking removes unwanted pieces from a mixture.
why.Remove only the black peppers and leave: Removing black peppers would not separate grains from stalks.

activities.explanation: Beating stalks to separate grains is called threshing.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between handpicking and threshing.
activities.answer: Handpicking means removing unwanted pieces from a mixture by hand. Threshing means beating stalks to separate the grains from them. Handpicking is convenient when the unwanted pieces are few, easy to pick, and different in size, colour, and shape. Threshing is useful when many grains remain attached to harvested stalks.
points: Handpicking removes unwanted pieces by hand.
Threshing separates grains by beating stalks.
Handpicking suits mixtures with few, distinct, easy-to-pick pieces.
Threshing suits stalks with many attached grains.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After wheat has been threshed, a farmer places the threshed wheat on a traditional bamboo soop. The farmer carries the tray to a place where air is moving, then moves it in the direction of the wind. The moving air separates the lighter and heavier parts of the mixture. Later, flour is placed in a sieve so that fine flour particles pass through its holes, while bran and small stones remain on top.
activities.prompt: The farmer has filled the soop with threshed wheat, and the air is blowing. What should the farmer do next to winnow the wheat?
options: Take the loaded tray along the airflow.
Take the loaded tray against the airflow.
Keep the loaded tray completely still.
Hold a sieve above the loaded tray.

why.Take the loaded tray against the airflow: Working against the airflow does not follow the winnowing method.
Winnowing requires the loaded tray to move in the wind's direction.
A sieve separates solids by particle size and is not used to winnow wheat.

activities.explanation: Moving the tray with the airflow allows winnowing to separate the mixture.

activities.context: After wheat has been threshed, a farmer places the threshed wheat on a traditional bamboo soop. The farmer carries the tray to a place where air is moving, then moves it in the direction of the wind. The moving air separates the lighter and heavier parts of the mixture. Later, flour is placed in a sieve so that fine flour particles pass through its holes, while bran and small stones remain on top.
activities.prompt: If the farmer replaces the manual winnowing work with a modern thresher, what result should the farmer expect?
options: It will separate the grains from stalks and husk while carrying out winnowing at the same time.
It will separate the grain from the stalk but leave winnowing for a later step.
It will sieve bran from flour while also threshing the wheat.
It will remove small stones from flour but will not separate wheat from stalks or husk.

why.It will separate the grain from the stal: A modern thresher does not leave winnowing for a later separate step.
why.It will sieve bran from flour while also: Removing bran from flour is sieving, not threshing.
why.It will remove small stones from flour b: Separating grain from stalks and husk is the role of a thresher.

activities.explanation: A thresher performs threshing and winnowing together.

activities.prompt: Explain how winnowing separates the components of the wheat mixture in the case.
activities.answer: Winnowing uses wind or blown air to separate parts of a mixture. Heavier and lighter components are separated because the moving air affects them differently. The farmer therefore moves the bamboo tray in the direction of the wind while it holds the threshed wheat.
points: Winnowing uses wind or blown air.
Heavier and lighter components are separated.
The bamboo tray is moved in the wind's direction.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Seawater was poured into shallow pits and left where sunlight and air could reach it. As time passed, water evaporated from the pits. A solid mixture was left behind. The people collected this mixture and obtained common salt from it. Nearby, medicinal plant parts had been gathered as ingredients. Some ingredients were dried in the shade so that excess water could evaporate, leaving the important part of the medicine.
activities.prompt: Why should the shallow pits remain exposed to sunlight and air?
options: This helps water evaporate from the seawater.
This makes seawater dissolve more salt.
This changes plant roots into common salt.
This allows common salt to form before the water evaporates.

Wrong: seawater already contains dissolved salt and other substances.
why.This changes plant roots into common sal: Wrong: plant roots do not become common salt.
why.This allows common salt to form before t: Wrong: common salt is obtained after water has evaporated and a solid mixture remains.

activities.explanation: Correct: exposure supports the evaporation of water.

activities.context: Seawater was poured into shallow pits and left where sunlight and air could reach it. As time passed, water evaporated from the pits. A solid mixture was left behind. The people collected this mixture and obtained common salt from it. Nearby, medicinal plant parts had been gathered as ingredients. Some ingredients were dried in the shade so that excess water could evaporate, leaving the important part of the medicine.
activities.prompt: Why are some medicinal plant parts dried in the shade?
options: To keep extra water inside the plant parts.
To turn the plant parts into common salt.
To remove excess water while keeping the important medicinal part.
To change roots, leaves, flowers, and seeds into one another.

why.To keep extra water inside the plant par: Wrong: drying helps excess water escape rather than remain.
why.To turn the plant parts into common salt: Wrong: plant parts do not become common salt.
why.To change roots, leaves, flowers, and se: Wrong: drying does not change one type of plant part into another.

activities.explanation: Correct: drying removes excess water while the important part remains.

activities.prompt: How does making salt from seawater involve evaporation?
activities.answer: Seawater is kept in shallow pits exposed to sunlight and air. Water evaporates, but the dissolved salts and other substances remain as a solid mixture. Common salt is then obtained from this solid mixture. Thus, evaporation removes the water that allowed the substances to stay dissolved.
points: Seawater is placed in shallow pits.
The pits are exposed to sunlight and air.
Water evaporates and leaves a solid mixture.
Common salt is obtained from the mixture.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Tea is left undisturbed so the tea leaves settle at the bottom of the vessel. The person tilts the vessel to remove the tea by decantation. Some leaves remain, so the tea is also passed through a strainer to separate the leaves from the tea. Separately, a liquid containing mud is passed through filter paper. Mud remains as a residue, while the clear liquid passing through is the filtrate. Decantation is also used to wash and clean rice and pulses.
activities.prompt: After the tea leaves have settled, what should the person do next to carry out decantation?
options: Tilt the vessel so that the liquid can be removed while the settled leaves stay behind.
Keep the vessel level and wait for the liquid to disappear on its own.
Pass the tea through a strainer and call this step decantation.
Stir the tea so that the leaves move upward with the liquid.

why.Keep the vessel level and wait for the l: A level vessel does not remove the settled liquid.
why.Pass the tea through a strainer and call: Using a strainer is filtration, not decantation.
why.Stir the tea so that the leaves move upw: Stirring would disturb the settled tea leaves.

activities.explanation: Correct: decantation removes liquid by tilting the vessel.

activities.context: Tea is left undisturbed so the tea leaves settle at the bottom of the vessel. The person tilts the vessel to remove the tea by decantation. Some leaves remain, so the tea is also passed through a strainer to separate the leaves from the tea. Separately, a liquid containing mud is passed through filter paper. Mud remains as a residue, while the clear liquid passing through is the filtrate. Decantation is also used to wash and clean rice and pulses.
activities.prompt: Why does filter paper collect the mud as a residue while the clear liquid passes through?
options: Filter paper has very fine pores that trap the tiny particles.
Filter paper has large pores, so the tiny mud particles pass through.
Cloth has smaller openings than filter paper, so the paper lets the mud pass.
The mud particles are lighter than the liquid and rise above the filter.

why.Filter paper has large pores, so the tin: Large pores would allow tiny particles to pass through.
why.Cloth has smaller openings than filter p: Filter paper has finer pores than the small holes in cloth.
why.The mud particles are lighter than the l: Sediment is heavier, not lighter, and settles at the bottom.

activities.explanation: Correct: the very fine pores trap tiny particles.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between decantation and filtration?
activities.answer: Decantation removes liquid by tilting the vessel, leaving settled solid behind. Filtration separates solids from liquids by passing them through a filter. A strainer separates tea leaves from tea, while filter paper has fine pores that trap tiny particles and let the clear filtrate pass through.
points: Decantation involves tilting the vessel to remove liquid.
Filtration involves passing a mixture through a filter.
A strainer separates tea leaves from tea.
Filter paper traps tiny particles, and the filtrate passes through.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a dairy stall, a worker churns curd using a churner called a mathni to obtain butter. Nearby, a recycler sorts waste containing sawdust and iron nails. A magnet attracts all the iron nails in the sawdust. At another waste site, a crane-mounted magnet separates scrap iron from waste materials. These activities show how churning and magnetic separation are used for different purposes.
activities.prompt: What is the next result after the worker churns the curd with the mathni?
options: Butter will form from the churned curd.
The mathni will pull iron nails out of the curd.
A magnet will separate the butter from the curd.
A crane-mounted magnet will obtain the butter.

why.The mathni will pull iron nails out of t: A mathni is used for churning, not for attracting nails.
why.A magnet will separate the butter from t: Magnets separate magnetic substances, not butter.
why.A crane-mounted magnet will obtain the b: Crane-mounted magnets separate scrap iron from waste materials.

activities.explanation: This is the stated purpose of churning.

activities.context: At a dairy stall, a worker churns curd using a churner called a mathni to obtain butter. Nearby, a recycler sorts waste containing sawdust and iron nails. A magnet attracts all the iron nails in the sawdust. At another waste site, a crane-mounted magnet separates scrap iron from waste materials. These activities show how churning and magnetic separation are used for different purposes.
activities.prompt: Why does the crane-mounted magnet lift scrap iron from the waste materials?
options: Iron is a common magnetic substance.
All waste materials are magnetic substances.
The magnet attracts sawdust instead of iron.
Iron articles in waste are non-magnetic.

why.All waste materials are magnetic substan: Magnetic attraction does not mean that all waste is magnetic.
why.The magnet attracts sawdust instead of i: The magnet attracts iron, not sawdust.
Iron articles are attracted towards magnets.

activities.explanation: Iron is attracted towards a magnet.

activities.prompt: Explain why churning curd with a mathni is used to obtain butter.
activities.answer: Churning is used to obtain butter from curd. The mathni is the churner used for this purpose. Therefore, when the worker churns the curd with the mathni, the desired product is butter. A magnet is not needed for this step.
points: Churning obtains butter from curd.
The mathni is used as the churner.
The worker churns curd with the mathni.
Magnetic separation is not required.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

Separating parts using wind or blowing air

The pits get sun and air
The water evaporates
We get common salt from the solid mixture

The leaves settle at the bottom
Tilt the pot to pour out the clear tea

chapters.title: Living Creatures: Exploring their Characteristics
chapters.summary: In this chapter: what makes the living apart from non-living?; essential conditions for germination of a seed; growth and movement in plants; life cycle of a plant.

lessons.title: What Makes the Living Apart from Non-living?

activities.prompt: How can you tell whether something is alive?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Living Things
activities.body:
You begin your tour by meeting a plant. Its flowers open, showing movement. It does not move from one place to another.

You watch living beings grow larger during their lives. They need food for their growth and development. Every living being respires. Breathing is part of this process, called respiration.

You also watch living beings remove waste from their bodies. This process is called excretion.

During your tour, you learn about stimuli. A stimulus is anything or any event that makes a living being respond. Plants also respond to stimuli. When you touch a touch-me-not plant, it folds its leaves.

You learn that reproduction produces new living beings of the same kind. A living being is dead when it cannot show all life characteristics. This remains true even when it has the needed resources. Anything without any life characteristics is classified as non-living.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Signs of Life
activities.body: Living beings show several signs of life. They grow bigger as they live. They need food. Respiration is the process that includes breathing. Excretion removes waste from the body. A stimulus is something that makes a living being respond. Reproduction makes new living beings of the same kind. Plants also respond. Their flowers open. Touch-me-not leaves fold when touched. A thing with none of these signs is non-living.
keyPoints: Living beings grow, need food, respire and remove waste.
They respond to stimuli and reproduce.
Plants can move parts but stay in one place.
A thing with no sign of life is non-living.
activities.explanation: These signs help you tell living beings from non-living things.

activities.prompt: A child touches a touch-me-not plant. Its leaves fold. Why does this happen?
steps: The touch is a stimulus because it makes the plant respond.
The plant responds by folding its leaves.
This shows that plants can respond to stimuli.
So the leaves fold because touch causes a response.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which action shows the plant movement described in this lesson?
options: Opening its flowers
Moving to another place
Making new plants of the same kind
Removing waste from its body
activities.explanation: A plant's flowers can open. The plant still stays in the same place.

activities.prompt: Living beings need ______ to grow and develop.
activities.hint: Living beings need this to grow and develop.
activities.explanation: Food helps living beings grow and develop.

activities.prompt: What is a stimulus?
options: Anything that makes a living thing respond
Only something that moves from one place to another
The removal of waste products
The process of making new living things
activities.explanation: A stimulus is anything that makes a living thing respond.

activities.prompt: Match each life characteristic with its meaning.
pairs: Removing waste products from the body
Producing new living beings of the same kind
activities.explanation: Each pair names a life characteristic and explains what it means.

activities.prompt: Put the touch-me-not plant's steps in order.
items: A living thing is touched.
The touch is a stimulus.
The touch-me-not plant folds its leaves.
activities.explanation: The touch is a stimulus because it makes the plant respond. Then the plant folds its leaves.

activities.prompt: A child can use two touch-me-not plants. The child wants to test if they respond to touch. What should the child do?
options: Touch one plant's leaves, leave the other's untouched, then compare them.
Touch one plant's leaves twice, leave the other's untouched, then compare them.
Touch both plants' leaves once, then compare them with each other.
Touch neither plant's leaves, then decide that touch has no effect.

why.Touch one plant's leaves twice, leave th: Different amounts of touch make the two plants unfair to compare.
why.Touch both plants' leaves once, then com: Both plants receive touch, so there is no untouched plant for comparison.
why.Touch neither plant's leaves, then decid: Neither plant receives touch, so the test cannot show a response.

activities.explanation: It compares one touched plant with one untouched plant.

activities.prompt: A flower opens, but the plant stays in one place. What does the opening show?
options: The plant shows movement without moving from one place to another.
The plant has reproduced by making new living beings of its kind.
The plant has excreted waste products through its open flower.
The plant has stopped responding to all stimuli.

why.The plant has reproduced by making new l: Reproduction makes new living beings, but opening a flower is movement.
why.The plant has excreted waste products th: Excretion removes waste, while flower opening is a plant movement.
why.The plant has stopped responding to all: Opening a flower does not mean the plant stops responding.

activities.explanation: Flowers can open as movement, while the plant stays in one place.

activities.prompt: A child gives no food to a living being during its life. What happens to its growth and development?
options: They cannot happen properly because food is needed for them.
They happen properly because food is only needed for reproduction.
They happen faster because missing food makes the body work harder.
They stop because every living being must move to find food.

why.They happen properly because food is onl: Food is needed for growth, not only for reproduction.
why.They happen faster because missing food: Missing food does not make growth happen faster.
why.They stop because every living being mus: This confuses the need for food with a need to move.

activities.explanation: Food is needed for growth and development, so missing food prevents them.

activities.prompt: A living being breathes, and waste products leave its body. Which two processes are happening?
options: Respiration and excretion, because breathing is part of respiration.
Respiration and growth, because breathing is part of growth.
Movement and excretion, because breathing causes the body to move.
Reproduction and excretion, because breathing produces new living beings.

why.Respiration and growth, because breathin: Breathing is part of respiration, not part of growth.
why.Movement and excretion, because breathin: Breathing is part of respiration, not a cause of movement.
why.Reproduction and excretion, because brea: Breathing is part of respiration, not the production of new beings.

activities.explanation: Breathing belongs to respiration, and excretion removes waste from the body.

activities.prompt: A mother animal gives birth to a young animal. The young animal is the same kind as its mother. What process has happened?
options: It reproduced because it made a new living being like itself.
It grew because the young animal is becoming larger.
It responded because the young animal answers a sound.
It excreted because the mother removed waste from her body.

why.It grew because the young animal is beco: Growth makes a living being larger, not a new one.
why.It responded because the young animal an: Responding means answering a stimulus, not making a new being.
why.It excreted because the mother removed w: Excretion removes waste, while reproduction makes a new living being.

activities.explanation: Reproduction produces new living beings of the same kind.
