lessons.title: Essential Conditions for Germination of a Seed

activities.prompt: What does a seed need to turn into a little plant?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Starting a Seed
activities.body:
Imagine that you are holding a bean seed and wondering what it needs next. You place it in soil, but the seed is not a sprout yet. A seed has germinated when it turns into a sprout.

First, give it water. Seeds require water for germination. Water helps the seed carry out the processes needed for growth. It also softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo inside. You have learned why water matters.

Next, check the air around it. Seeds use the air found in the spaces between soil particles. These spaces also help roots grow easily. Bean seeds need the right amounts of both water and air to germinate.

Should you put the seed in sunlight? Light is not essential for bean seeds to germinate. Most seeds do not need light either. After germination, sunlight is needed for further growth. Some seeds, such as Coleus and Petunia, need light to germinate. Others, such as Calendula and Zinnia, need darkness. You can now check each seed’s needs before you plant it.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Does a Seed Need?
activities.body: A seed germinates when it turns into a sprout. Seeds need water and air. Water softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo. Seeds use air found in spaces between soil particles. These spaces also help roots grow easily. Most seeds do not need light to germinate. Sunlight helps further growth after germination. Some seeds, such as Coleus and Petunia, need light. Others, such as Calendula and Zinnia, need darkness.
keyPoints: Water softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo.
Seeds need air found between soil particles.
Most seeds do not need light to germinate.
activities.explanation: Water and air help a seed become a sprout.

activities.prompt: A bean seed sits in dry soil with air. Will it germinate? Why?
steps: Bean seeds need water and air to germinate.
Air can enter the spaces between soil particles.
Dry soil does not supply the water needed for growth processes.
Without water, the seed will not germinate into a sprout.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Is Germination?
activities.prompt: What happens when a seed germinates?
options: It stays unchanged.
It grows into a sprout.
It becomes soil.
It grows more leaves.
activities.explanation: A seed has germinated when it grows into a sprout.

activities.title: Water and Germination
activities.prompt: Seeds need water for germination.
activities.explanation: Seeds need water to germinate.

activities.title: Air in the Soil
activities.prompt: Seeds use ______ found in the spaces between soil particles.
activities.hint: This gas is needed for germination.
activities.explanation: Seeds use air found in the spaces between soil particles.

activities.title: Match Each Thing
activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it does.
activities.explanation: Water softens the seed coat. Air is needed for germination. Sunlight helps growth after germination.

activities.title: Light and Germination
activities.prompt: Most seeds need light for germination.
activities.explanation: Most seeds do not need light for germination. Some seeds do.

activities.title: Seeds That Need Light
activities.prompt: Which seeds need light to germinate?
options: Coleus and Petunia need darkness.
Calendula and Zinnia need light.
Calendula and Petunia need darkness.
Coleus and Petunia need light.
activities.explanation: Coleus and Petunia need light, while Calendula and Zinnia need darkness.

activities.prompt: Bean seeds need the right amounts of water and air. Maya gives her seeds both. What will happen next?
options: The seeds will germinate and become small sprouts.
The seeds will stay still because sunlight is missing.
The seeds will soften but cannot help their embryo.
The seeds will wait for sunlight before starting growth.

why.The seeds will stay still because sunlig: This mistakes sunlight, which is not essential for bean seeds.
why.The seeds will soften but cannot help th: This wrongly says water cannot help the tiny embryo.
why.The seeds will wait for sunlight before: This confuses sunlight for later growth with germination.

activities.explanation: Water and air let the bean seeds germinate into sprouts.

activities.prompt: Water helps seeds carry out growth processes. It also softens the seed coat. What can the bean seed do?
options: It can begin the growth processes needed to germinate.
It can germinate without carrying out any growth processes.
It must wait for sunlight before its coat softens.
It can soften its coat without helping the embryo.

why.It can germinate without carrying out an: This wrongly separates germination from the growth processes it needs.
why.It must wait for sunlight before its coa: This wrongly makes sunlight a requirement for softening the coat.
why.It can soften its coat without helping t: This forgets that water also helps the tiny embryo inside.

activities.explanation: The water supports growth and helps the embryo, so germination can begin.

activities.prompt: Some seeds need light to germinate. Coleus and Petunia are among them. Where should their seeds be planted?
options: In light-exposed soil so they can receive light.
In dark soil so their seed coats can soften.
In watered soil so sunlight can reach their roots.
In dry soil so their embryos grow more easily.

why.In dark soil so their seed coats can sof: This wrongly gives them darkness, which they do not need.
why.In watered soil so sunlight can reach th: This wrongly focuses on roots and sunlight after germination.
why.In dry soil so their embryos grow more e: This wrongly treats dryness as helping the embryo.

activities.explanation: Coleus and Petunia need light to germinate.

activities.prompt: Bean seeds can germinate without light. A gardener says every seed needs sunlight first. Why is this claim flawed?
options: Bean seeds need no light; sunlight helps their later growth.
Bean seeds need darkness before their seed coats soften.
Bean seeds use sunlight to soften their seed coats.
Bean seeds need no air to begin their growth.

why.Bean seeds need darkness before their se: This confuses darkness with water, which softens the seed coat.
why.Bean seeds use sunlight to soften their: This wrongly makes sunlight soften the coat instead of water.
why.Bean seeds need no air to begin their gr: This wrongly says air is unnecessary, but seeds need air to germinate.

activities.explanation: Light is not essential for beans; sunlight supports growth after germination.

lessons.title: Growth and Movement in Plants

activities.prompt: What helps a plant know which way to grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Grow and Move
activities.body:
You begin with a germinated seed. It develops into a seedling with a small root and shoot. Now you visit three beakers, labelled A, B and C. In beaker A, a seedling stands upright. Wet blotting paper gives moisture to the seedling.

Next, you look at beaker B. The seedling in beaker B is inverted. Its shoot points downwards. Its root points upwards. The root bends and grows downwards. The shoot bends and grows upwards.

Then you visit beaker C. The seedling here receives light from only one direction. Its shoot grows towards the light. The root keeps growing downwards. You watch the shoot change its direction.

Finally, you compare the plants. In an upright plant, the root grows downwards and the shoot grows upwards. In an inverted plant, both parts bend towards their usual directions. With light from one side, the shoot grows towards it. Plant shoots grow upwards and show movement towards sunlight. You have watched growth and movement.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Plants Grow and Move
activities.body: A seed that has germinated (started to sprout) grows into a seedling. A seedling has a small root and shoot. In an upright plant, roots grow down and shoots grow up. If you turn a plant upside down, its parts bend. Each part grows in its normal direction. Roots bend down. Shoots bend up. When light comes from one side, the shoot grows towards it. The root keeps growing down.
keyPoints: A seed that germinates becomes a seedling.
Roots grow down and shoots grow up.
Shoots grow towards light from one side.
activities.explanation: Plants change how they grow, so they grow correctly.

activities.prompt: You turn a seedling upside down. What will its root and shoot do?
steps: The root points up and the shoot down because it is inverted.
The root bends and grows down, because inverted roots grow downwards.
The shoot bends and grows up, because inverted shoots grow upwards.
So the root ends downwards and the shoot ends upwards, despite the start.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does a germinated seed grow into?
options: A seedling with only a root
A seedling with only a shoot
A seedling with a small root and shoot
A seedling without a root or shoot
activities.explanation: A germinated seed grows into a seedling with a small root and shoot.

activities.prompt: In an upright plant, the shoot grows ______.
activities.hint: This is the opposite direction to the root.
activities.explanation: Well done! The shoot grows upwards, while the root grows downwards.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its right description.
activities.explanation: Lodestones are natural magnets. Pencil box magnets are artificial. Iron is magnetic.

activities.prompt: The seedling in beaker C receives light from one direction. How does its shoot grow?
options: It grows away from the light
It grows towards the light
It grows straight downwards
It stops growing
activities.explanation: Correct! The shoot grows towards the light while the root keeps growing downwards.

activities.prompt: Put these in order, from the start of growth.
items: A germinated seed
A seedling with a small root and shoot
A plant standing up, with roots down and shoot up
activities.explanation: Well done! A seed grows into a seedling. Its parts grow in opposite directions.

activities.prompt: A plant is turned upside down. Which statement describes what happens next?
options: The root bends and grows downwards
The root bends and grows upwards
The shoot bends and grows downwards
Neither the root nor the shoot bends
activities.explanation: Exactly! The root bends and grows downwards, while the shoot bends and grows upwards.

activities.prompt: In beaker B, the shoot points down and the root points up. Where will they grow next?
options: The root will grow down, and the shoot will grow up.
The root will grow up, and the shoot will grow down.
The root will grow down, and the shoot will grow sideways.
The root will grow up, and the shoot will grow sideways.

why.The root will grow up, and the shoot wil: This wrongly assumes the root keeps its first upward direction.
why.The root will grow down, and the shoot w: This wrongly makes the shoot grow sideways instead of upwards.
why.The root will grow up, and the shoot wil: This wrongly keeps the root upwards and makes the shoot sideways.

activities.explanation: This matches the growth directions of an inverted plant.

activities.prompt: A seedling rests on wet blotting paper. Light comes from only one side. Where will its root and shoot grow?
options: The root grows towards the light; the shoot grows down.
The root grows up; the shoot grows towards the light.
The root grows down; the shoot grows away from the light.
The root grows down; the shoot grows towards the light.

why.The root grows towards the light; the sh: This wrongly swaps the root and shoot directions.
why.The root grows up; the shoot grows towar: This wrongly makes the root grow upwards.
why.The root grows down; the shoot grows awa: This wrongly makes the shoot grow away from light.

activities.explanation: The root grows down, while the shoot grows towards the light.

activities.prompt: Beaker A stays upright, but beaker B is turned upside down. How will their roots grow differently?
options: B's root grows up; A's root grows down.
B's root bends down; A's root grows down.
B's shoot bends down; A's shoot grows up.
B's shoot stays down; A's shoot grows up.

This wrongly assumes an inverted root keeps growing upwards.
why.B's shoot bends down; A's shoot grows up: This confuses the shoot's bending with the root's bending.
why.B's shoot stays down; A's shoot grows up: This wrongly assumes an inverted shoot cannot bend upwards.

activities.explanation: Both roots grow down, but only B's root must bend.

activities.prompt: Light comes from one side. The child says the root should bend towards it. What is wrong?
options: The root keeps growing down, not towards the light.
The shoot stops growing when the root bends towards light.
The root grows up, so it cannot bend down.
The shoot grows down, so light has no effect.

why.The shoot stops growing when the root be: This wrongly makes the shoot stop growing.
why.The root grows up, so it cannot bend dow: This wrongly says the root grows upwards.
why.The shoot grows down, so light has no ef: This wrongly makes the shoot grow downwards and ignore light.

activities.explanation: One-sided light bends the shoot; the root keeps growing down.

lessons.sceneCaption: Plants grow shoots up and roots down, even when inverted or lit from one side.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Plant

activities.prompt: How does a tiny seed become the next generation of plants?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Bean’s Life Cycle
activities.body:
You begin your journey with a bean seed. It needs suitable conditions if it is to grow. Soon, you watch germination happen. A young plant appears, and you see leaves as it grows.

Next, you follow the plant towards its flowers. You can record how long the first flower takes to appear. This time belongs in your observation notes.

After flowering, you notice that some flower parts may dry. The plant may still grow further. Other parts of the flower can develop into a pod or fruit.

You look inside the bean plant’s fruit. It is a pod, and it holds seeds. The plant may also turn yellow and dry. This happens even when it continues to receive water.

Finally, you consider what happens next. The seeds can grow into a new generation of bean plants. Your journey from seed to plant and next seeds is a plant’s life cycle. A plant is considered dead when its growth and life activities gradually stop. This can happen even when necessary conditions remain available.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Plant's Life Cycle
activities.body: A bean plant starts as a seed. With the right conditions, it germinates and grows into a young plant. Germination means beginning to grow. The young plant grows leaves, flowers and fruit. Then the plant dies. Its flowers can dry up. Other flower parts can become a pod. A pod holds seeds. These seeds can grow into new bean plants. This whole journey is the plant's life cycle.
keyPoints: A seed grows into a young plant with leaves.
A pod has seeds for new plants.
The whole journey is the plant's life cycle.
activities.explanation: A seed starts the cycle, and new seeds continue it.

activities.prompt: A child plants a bean seed and watches it grow. What journey will the plant follow?
steps: Suitable conditions let the bean seed grow into a young plant.
The young plant later produces flowers and fruit.
Some flower parts may dry while the plant continues to grow further.
The remaining flower parts can form a pod with seeds, and those seeds can grow into the next generation; this whole journey is a plant's life cycle.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where Does the Life Cycle Begin?
activities.prompt: Which part begins a plant's life cycle?
options: Flower
Pod
Seed
Death
activities.explanation: The life cycle begins with a seed. It later grows into a plant that makes more seeds.

activities.title: The Bean Plant's Fruit
activities.prompt: The fruit of a bean plant is a ______. It has seeds inside.
activities.hint: Look at the bean plant's fruit.
activities.explanation: A bean plant's fruit is a pod. The pod has seeds in it.

activities.title: Match the Life Cycle
activities.prompt: Match each plant part or stage with what happens next.
pairs: Can develop into a pod or fruit
activities.explanation: These pairs follow the bean plant's life cycle. A seed grows, flowers form, and fruits hold new seeds.

activities.title: Put the Stages in Order
activities.prompt: Put these parts of a plant's life cycle in order.
items: Seed
Germination
Leaves
Flowers
Fruit
activities.explanation: This order follows the listed life cycle: seed, germination, leaves, flowers and fruits. Death comes later.

activities.title: Recording What You Watch
activities.prompt: What can you record when you watch a bean plant?
options: The time for a pod to become a young plant
The time for a dead plant to grow again
The time for the first flower to appear
The time for new seeds to die before they sprout
activities.explanation: You can record the time for the first flower to appear.

activities.title: After Flower Parts Dry
activities.prompt: What can happen after some parts of a flower have dried?
options: The plant must die as soon as a flower dries.
The plant may grow more, and other parts may form a pod or fruit.
The other flower parts must become new seeds.
The pod must form before any flower dries.
activities.explanation: Some flower parts can dry while the plant keeps growing. Other parts can grow into a pod or fruit.

activities.prompt: A bean seed has suitable conditions for growth. What is most likely to happen next?
options: It will grow into a young plant.
It will remain only a seed.
It will become yellow and dry.
It will make a pod first.

This mistake thinks a seed never changes when conditions are suitable.
This mistake mixes the seed stage with the later yellow, dry stage.
This mistake puts the pod stage before the young plant stage.

activities.explanation: This is right because a seed can grow into a young plant.

activities.prompt: Some flower parts on a bean plant have dried. What may happen next?
options: The plant may show further growth.
The plant must die at once.
The dried parts become new seeds.
The plant can grow without flowers.

This mistake thinks drying flower parts always mean death.
This mistake thinks dried flower parts can become seeds.
This mistake thinks flowers are not needed for later growth.

activities.explanation: This is right because a plant may grow after some flower parts dry.

activities.prompt: A bean plant is yellow and dry, but it still receives water. Is it certainly dead?
options: No, it may still be alive.
Yes, yellow means it is dead.
Yes, dry means it is dead.
No, water keeps it young forever.

This mistake thinks yellow colour alone proves death.
This mistake thinks dryness alone proves death.
This mistake thinks water can stop all life-cycle changes forever.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Mosquito and Silk Moth

activities.prompt: How do mosquitoes and silk moths grow and change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Life Journeys
activities.body:
Imagine you are taking a tour of two life cycles. First, you meet a female mosquito. She can spread diseases such as malaria, dengue and chikungunya.

You follow her to water, where she lays her eggs on or near it. The cycle continues. Next, you see a larva and a pupa. These are two different stages in mosquito development.

Both larvae and pupae live in water and need air for respiration. You watch them come to the water surface to get air. Then the pupa changes into an adult mosquito.

Now you tour the silk moth’s life cycle. It passes through the egg, larva, pupa and adult stages. During the larva stage, it makes a thread-like material. People use this material to make silk fabric.

Finally, you learn that mosquito breeding should be prevented. You should not allow water to stagnate around you. Kerosene oil forms a thin layer over the surface of water.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Mosquitoes and Silk Moths
activities.body: Female mosquitoes can spread malaria, dengue and chikungunya. So, stop mosquitoes from breeding. Do not let water stay still around you. Mosquito larvae and pupae live in water. They need air. They come up to the surface to breathe. The pupa changes into an adult. The female lays eggs on or near water. Silk moths go through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult.
keyPoints: Female mosquitoes can spread diseases.
Mosquito larvae and pupae live in water.
Silk moths pass through four stages.
activities.explanation: Good learning! These stages and habitats help you understand both life cycles.

Prevent breeding because female mosquitoes can spread diseases such as malaria.

activities.body: The larva and the pupa are two mosquito stages. Both live in water. Both need air for respiration. That means breathing. They come up to the water surface to get air. Kerosene oil makes a thin layer on the water's surface. The pupa later changes into an adult mosquito. An adult female lays eggs on or near water. This continues the cycle.
keyPoints: Mosquito larvae and pupae need air.
They come to the water surface for air.
A pupa changes into an adult mosquito.
activities.explanation: You found what young mosquitoes need!

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Frog

activities.prompt: What might you discover while following a frog's life?

activities.title: A Frog's Life Cycle
activities.body:
You begin your journey beside water, where you notice jelly-like eggs. These eggs are called spawn. You follow a frog through its four-stage life cycle.

First, you see the egg stage. It develops into the embryo stage. The early tadpole has a tail but no legs. Its tail helps it swim in water.

Next, you meet a later tadpole. It now has hind legs. Its tail still helps it swim in water. You notice that its habitat has changed.

Now, you follow the froglet. This stage comes between the tadpole and adult frog. You see it living in water. You also see it spending some time on land. Its habitat changes during this part of its life.

Finally, you watch the growing frog lose its tail completely. Its legs become strong enough for jumping and landing. The adult frog can live both in water and on land. Your journey ends as you watch the adult frog.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How a Frog Changes
activities.body: A frog goes through four life stages. Its jelly-like eggs are called spawn. Spawn grows into an embryo. A tadpole has a tail but no legs. Later, the tadpole grows hind legs (back legs). A froglet lives in water and on land. The growing frog loses its tail. Its strong legs help it jump. So an adult frog can live in water and on land.

A frog's habitat changes as it grows.

lessons.title: Air and Wind

activities.prompt: What is wind, and how does it make windmills turn?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Air and Wind
activities.body:
Imagine taking a deep breath. Fresh air fills your lungs and helps you stay healthy. That air carries oxygen, which your body needs for its activities. Without it, you cannot live for even a few minutes without oxygen.

Now look around you. Air is a mixture of several gases. It contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. Percentage shows how many parts are in one hundred. You can use percentage to compare these parts of air.

Next, meet the moving part. Moving air is called wind. You see a firki spinning because the wind pushes its blades. Windmills can also draw water from wells. Some can generate electricity for people to use. Would you like to visit a place with many windmills?

A windmill farm contains many windmills. In India, Muppandal, Jaisalmer and Brahmanvel are among the leading windmill farms. Stand safely nearby and watch each firki rotate. You can now see how air, oxygen and wind work together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Air, Breathing and Wind
activities.body: Air around the Earth is a mixture of gases. It has nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. The air we breathe in has oxygen. Our body needs oxygen to do its work. Deep breaths bring more fresh air into your lungs. This helps us stay healthy. Moving air is called wind. Wind makes a firki turn. Windmills can draw water from wells and make electricity.
keyPoints: Air has several gases, including oxygen.
Our body needs oxygen to do its work.
Moving air is called wind.
Wind can help useful machines work.
activities.explanation: These facts connect breathing, gases, wind and windmill uses.

activities.prompt: Air moves around a windmill. What will happen to its firki?
steps: Moving air is called wind, and the windmill is in that air.
Wind makes a firki rotate, so the windmill's firki will turn.
A turning windmill can draw water from wells and generate electricity.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Gas Our Body Needs
activities.prompt: Which gas does our body need to do its activities?
options: Oxygen
Nitrogen
Argon
Carbon dioxide
activities.explanation: Our body needs oxygen to do its activities. Oxygen is in the air we breathe in.

activities.title: Fresh Air and Your Lungs
activities.prompt: Taking deep breaths brings more fresh air into the ______.
activities.hint: This is where air enters your body.
activities.explanation: Deep breaths bring more fresh air into your lungs. This helps you stay healthy.

activities.title: Make the Correct Links
activities.prompt: Match each thing with its correct link.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows how air, oxygen and wind are connected. Your lungs and body both need oxygen.

activities.title: Gases Around Earth
activities.prompt: Which statement about gases around Earth is true?
options: Air around Earth has only one gas.
Air has no carbon dioxide.
Air contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide.
Moving air is another gas around Earth.
activities.explanation: Air around Earth is a mixture of several gases. It contains the gases listed here.

activities.title: Wind at Work
activities.prompt: Which sentence about wind, firki and windmills is correct?
options: Wind makes a firki turn. Windmills only bring fresh air into lungs.
Wind brings fresh air into lungs. Windmills can only draw water from wells.
Wind makes a firki stay still. Windmills can only make electricity.
Wind makes a firki turn. Windmills can draw water or make electricity.
activities.explanation: Wind makes a firki turn. Windmills can draw water from wells and make electricity.

activities.prompt: A child feels out of breath after running. She takes deep breaths. Why will this help?
options: Deep breaths bring fresh air and oxygen into her lungs.
Deep breaths bring nitrogen into her lungs for energy.
Deep breaths push used air deep into her body.
Deep breaths make her body need less oxygen.

why.Deep breaths bring nitrogen into her lun: The body needs oxygen for activities, not nitrogen for energy.
why.Deep breaths push used air deep into her: Fresh air enters the lungs; it does not push used air deeper.
why.Deep breaths make her body need less oxy: This is backwards: the body needs oxygen, and deep breaths supply more.

activities.explanation: Deep breaths bring fresh air, including oxygen, into the lungs.

activities.prompt: A person enters a room with no oxygen. What will happen next?
options: The person will not be able to stay alive.
The body will need less oxygen for its activities.
The body will get more energy from nitrogen.
The body will stay active because oxygen is not needed.

why.The body will need less oxygen for its a: The body needs oxygen to carry out its activities.
why.The body will get more energy from nitro: Nitrogen is in air, but the body needs oxygen for activities.
why.The body will stay active because oxygen: This wrongly treats oxygen as unnecessary for body activities.

activities.explanation: We cannot live for even a few minutes without oxygen.

activities.prompt: A child says, "Air is only oxygen." Air has several gases. What is wrong with the claim?
options: Air is a mixture, so oxygen is not all of it.
Air is a mixture, so oxygen is the only useful gas.
Air has just oxygen, so nitrogen and argon are not real.
Air is a mixture, so carbon dioxide is the only other gas.

why.Air is a mixture, so oxygen is the only: Oxygen is needed, but several other gases are present too.
why.Air has just oxygen, so nitrogen and arg: Nitrogen and argon are both present in the air mixture.
why.Air is a mixture, so carbon dioxide is t: Air has other gases besides carbon dioxide and oxygen.

activities.explanation: Air contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, and other gases.

activities.prompt: A firki hangs outside on a windy day. What will happen next?
options: The firki will turn because moving air makes it rotate.
The firki will stay still because wind cannot move it.
The firki will turn because nitrogen pushes its blades.
The firki will stay still because only oxygen can move it.

why.The firki will stay still because wind c: This mistake treats wind as still air, which cannot turn the firki.
why.The firki will turn because nitrogen pus: Wind acts on the firki; nitrogen is not what makes it rotate.
why.The firki will stay still because only o: This mistake treats oxygen as the moving air that turns the firki.

activities.explanation: Moving air is wind, and wind makes a firki rotate.

activities.prompt: We want to test wind on a windmill. Which setup is fairest?
options: Keep the windmill the same, but change the air from moving to still.
Keep the windmill the same, but use only moving air.
Change the windmill and the air at the same time.
Keep the windmill the same, but use only still air.

why.Keep the windmill the same, but use only: Without still air, the test cannot compare wind with no wind.
why.Change the windmill and the air at the s: Changing the windmill as well makes the test unfair.
why.Keep the windmill the same, but use only: Without moving air, the test cannot show wind turning it.

activities.explanation: Only the air changes, so the test can show wind's effect.

lessons.title: Water and Its Careful Use

activities.prompt: How can your family use water wisely every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Water
activities.body:
Imagine starting your day with a glass of water. You need it for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and cleaning.

You also see water helping plants grow. Farmers use it for crops, and industries use it too. From above, water covers about two-thirds of the Earth’s surface. Most of it lies in oceans and seas. This ocean water is saline, which means it is salty.

Visit freshwater places. You find it as ice, snow, rivers, lakes and underground water. Only a small part of this freshwater is easily accessible.

At home, care for every drop. Turning off taps and repairing leaks can reduce water wastage.

Polluted water cannot be consumed by living beings. Many parts of India face water shortages because freshwater sources are limited. Rainwater harvesting collects and stores rainwater for later use. You can help by saving water and harvesting rainwater.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Why Water Matters
activities.body: Water is needed for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and cleaning. It also helps grow crops and supports industries. Most Earth's water lies in oceans and seas. This salt water is not the easily accessible freshwater we use. Only a small part of freshwater is easily accessible. Careful use and rainwater harvesting can help us.
keyPoints: Water has many everyday uses.
Most water is salty ocean water.
Only a small part of freshwater is easily accessible.
activities.explanation: Water is useful, but easy freshwater is limited.

activities.prompt: Rain is falling, and a family wants water for later. What can they do?
steps: They should use rainwater harvesting because it stores rain for later use.
Stored rain can help because only a small freshwater part is usable.
This helps many parts of India because their freshwater sources are limited.
Collecting rainwater is a careful way to meet later water needs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Protecting Our Water
activities.body: Most water on Earth is in oceans and seas. This water is salty. Fresh water is in ice, snow, rivers, lakes, and under the ground. Only a small part is easy to use. Polluted water is dirty. We cannot drink it. Turning off taps and fixing leaks saves water. Rainwater harvesting means saving rain for later.
keyPoints: Polluted water cannot be drunk.
Leaks and running taps waste water.
Rainwater can be collected and saved.
activities.explanation: Careful habits help us keep fresh water safe.

activities.title: Match Water Facts
activities.prompt: Match each thing with its right description.
activities.explanation: Lodestones are natural magnets. Pencil box magnets are artificial. Iron is magnetic.

activities.title: Saving Rainwater
activities.prompt: Why is rainwater harvesting useful?
options: It makes dirty water clean to drink.
It collects rainwater and keeps it for later.
It makes all underground water easy to reach.
It means no need to fix leaking taps.
activities.explanation: Rainwater harvesting collects rainwater and keeps it for later use.

activities.title: Fill the Space
activities.prompt: Rainwater harvesting collects and ______ rainwater for later use.
activities.hint: This word tells us what happens to the collected rainwater.
activities.explanation: The harvested rainwater is stored, so it can be used later.

activities.title: Harvesting Rainwater
activities.prompt: Put these rainwater harvesting steps in the correct order.
items: Collect rainwater
Store rainwater
Use stored rainwater later
activities.explanation: Rainwater must be collected, stored and then used when needed.

activities.title: Why Does Water Run Short?
activities.prompt: Why do many parts of India face a water shortage?
options: Most rivers and lakes contain salty water.
People never use water for cooking or cleaning.
Freshwater sources are limited in many parts.
Rainwater harvesting prevents every water shortage.
activities.explanation: Many parts of India have limited freshwater sources, so water shortages occur.

activities.prompt: Ocean water is saline, meaning it is salty. A child tastes both bowls. One tastes salty. Which bowl did the child taste?
options: The bowl holding river water.
The bowl holding lake water.
The bowl holding underground water.
The bowl holding ocean water.

This mistake treats freshwater as if it were ocean water.
This mistake treats freshwater as if it were ocean water.
This mistake treats freshwater as if it were ocean water.

activities.explanation: This is right because ocean water is salty.

activities.prompt: Water covers about two-thirds of Earth's surface. Most water is in oceans and seas. Only a small freshwater part is easy to use. What is the fair choice?
options: Treat all freshwater as equally easy to use.
Leave taps open because freshwater is easy to find.
Use accessible freshwater carefully and repair leaks.
Choose ocean water because most water is there.

why.Treat all freshwater as equally easy to: This mistake assumes every freshwater source is easy to access.
why.Leave taps open because freshwater is ea: This mistake ignores leaks and the limited easy freshwater supply.
why.Choose ocean water because most water is: This mistake ignores that ocean water is salty.

activities.explanation: This is right because only a small freshwater part is easily accessible.

activities.prompt: Polluted water cannot be consumed by living beings. A pond has polluted water. What should people and animals do?
options: They should drink it because water is needed for living.
They should give it only to animals because animals can drink it.
They should not let people or animals drink the pond water.
They should mix it with clean water before drinking it.

why.They should drink it because water is ne: This mistake confuses needing water with being able to drink polluted water.
why.They should give it only to animals beca: This mistake thinks animals are not living beings.
why.They should mix it with clean water befo: This mistake assumes mixing makes polluted water safe.

activities.explanation: This is right because polluted water cannot be consumed by living beings.

activities.prompt: Freshwater is found as ice, snow, rivers, lakes and underground water. Which claim about these sources is fair?
options: Only ice and snow count, because other forms are not freshwater.
They are all freshwater, but only a small part is easily accessible.
All freshwater forms are equally easy for people to access.
Only rivers and lakes hold freshwater, while ice and snow do not.

why.Only ice and snow count, because other f: This mistake denies that rivers, lakes and underground water are freshwater.
why.All freshwater forms are equally easy fo: This mistake assumes all freshwater forms are easy to access.
why.Only rivers and lakes hold freshwater, w: This mistake leaves out ice, snow and underground water.

activities.explanation: Freshwater has many forms, but only a small part is easily accessible.

lessons.title: Energy from the Sun and Forests

activities.prompt: How does sunlight help forests grow and power your home?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sunlight and Forest Life
activities.body:
Begin your visit in a forest. You look around a large area and see many kinds of plants growing close together. The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth. This forest is a natural home for wild animals, birds and insects.

Now follow the sunlight to the leaves. Plants use it to prepare their food. Grass also needs sunlight to grow. All plants and animals here depend on the Sun.

Next, imagine an animal taking a bite of grass. It gains energy by eating plants, and that energy helps it grow. This is a simple journey of energy through the forest.

Now step towards a house. Solar panels capture the Sun's energy and make electricity. In another place, sunlight can be used directly for cooking. We use the Sun's heat and light in many ways.

Finally, remember what happens when too many trees are cut down. Large-scale cutting has reduced forest cover. A new forest takes many years to grow. Restoring a lost forest also takes many years.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Sun Power and Forest Life
activities.body: The Sun is the main energy source for Earth. Its heat and light help us and living things. Sunlight helps plants make food. Grass needs sunlight to grow. Animals get energy by eating plants. Solar panels catch sunlight and make electricity. Forests have many plants. Forests give homes to wild animals, birds and insects. Cutting trees makes the forest cover smaller. Growing back a forest takes many years.
keyPoints: The Sun is Earth's main energy source.
Plants need sunlight. Animals get energy from eating plants.
Forests give homes to wildlife. Cutting trees makes forest cover smaller.
activities.explanation: The Sun gives power to living things. Forests give homes to wild animals.

activities.prompt: A child wants a plant to grow well in a room. What should the child check first?
steps: Check for sunlight, because sunlight helps plants prepare their food.
Keep the plant in sunlight, because all plants depend on the Sun.
The plant can then use the Sun's energy to grow well.
Therefore, sunlight is needed for the plant to grow well.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which is the main source of energy on Earth?
options: the Sun
a solar panel
a forest
grass
activities.explanation: The Sun supplies Earth's main energy. Solar panels capture this energy.

activities.prompt: Solar panels take energy from the Sun to make electricity.
activities.explanation: Solar panels take energy from the Sun. They turn it into electricity.

activities.prompt: Match each action or event with its result.
activities.explanation: Sunlight supports plants, while tree cutting reduces forest cover.

activities.prompt: What happens when trees are cut on a large scale?
options: Forest cover stays the same.
Grass no longer needs sunlight.
Animals stop depending on the Sun.
Forest cover is reduced.
activities.explanation: Large-scale cutting of trees has reduced the forest cover.

activities.prompt: A new forest can grow in a very short time.
activities.explanation: It takes many years to grow a new forest or restore a lost one.

activities.prompt: Many trees are cut down. What happens to forest cover? How long does a new forest take to grow?
options: Forest cover goes up. A new forest grows fast.
Forest cover goes down. A new forest grows fast.
Forest cover stays the same. A new forest takes many years.
Forest cover goes down. A new forest takes many years.
activities.explanation: Cutting trees lowers forest cover. Growing a forest back takes many years.

activities.prompt: A patch of grass stays in darkness. What will happen to its growth?
options: It will grow even faster.
It will not grow well.
It will need less sunlight.
It will grow very large.

This mistake thinks darkness makes grass grow faster.
This mistake thinks grass needs less sunlight.
This mistake thinks too little sunlight causes larger grass.

activities.explanation: Grass needs sunlight to grow, so darkness causes poor growth.

activities.prompt: An animal has eaten no food. Where can it get energy?
options: By eating forest plants
By taking in sunlight
By breathing forest air
By resting under trees

why.By taking in sunlight: This mistake thinks animals can take energy from sunlight.
why.By breathing forest air: This mistake thinks forest air gives animals energy.
why.By resting under trees: This mistake thinks resting gives animals the needed energy.

activities.explanation: Animals get energy by eating plants, so grass gives energy.

activities.prompt: A cooking device has no solar panel. It is placed in sunlight. How can it cook?
options: It uses a solar panel.
It eats plants for energy.
It uses energy from trees.
It uses Sun energy directly.

This mistake thinks cooking needs electricity from a panel.
This mistake thinks cooking devices eat plants.
This mistake thinks cooking uses energy from trees.

activities.explanation: The Sun's energy can be used directly for cooking.

activities.prompt: Trees are cut from a forest. What is needed to restore it?
options: Many years of forest growth
Less sunlight and no trees
More trees and less time
More animals and no plants

why.Less sunlight and no trees: This mistake thinks less sunlight and no trees help restoration.
why.More trees and less time: This mistake thinks more trees can restore a forest in less time.
why.More animals and no plants: This mistake thinks animals, not plants, can restore a forest.

activities.explanation: Growing or restoring a forest takes many years.

activities.prompt: Forest cover shrinks. What may happen to wild animals?
options: They may grow more trees.
They may make more sunlight.
They may need no plants.
They may lose forest homes.

This mistake thinks animals can grow trees.
This mistake thinks animals can make sunlight.
This mistake thinks animals no longer need plants.

activities.explanation: Forests are natural homes, so less forest cover can remove homes.

lessons.title: Soil, Rocks and Minerals

activities.prompt: What wonders hide beneath your feet, and how were they made?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Soil and Rocks
activities.body:
You begin your journey in a forest. You lift a fallen leaf and look at the soil. Around you, the forest contains different types of soil.

Earthworms wriggle through the ground. They help turn and loosen the soil. Spaces between soil particles hold air. They also give roots room to grow. Fallen leaves decay and add nutrients to the soil.

Here, your guide explains that soil forms slowly. Rocks break apart over a long time. The Sun, water and living organisms help this process. Even rocks take thousands to millions of years to form.

You then visit a rocky hillside. Each rock is made up of minerals. Important metals can be obtained from minerals. Rocks are useful. People use them to build houses, roads, dams and other structures.

Finally, you think about protecting nature's treasures. Soil supports biodiversity. That makes soil precious. We must conserve and use rocks responsibly. Your tour ends, but your care can continue.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Soil Helps Living Things
activities.body: Rocks break into small bits over a long time. The Sun, water and living things break rocks. This is how soil is made. Spaces between soil bits give air and room for roots. Earthworms help turn and loosen soil. Fallen leaves decay (break down) and add nutrients (food) to soil. Soil helps biodiversity. Biodiversity means the variety of living things.
keyPoints: Soil forms as rocks break into small bits.
Earthworms and fallen leaves help soil.
Spaces between soil bits give air and room for roots.
activities.explanation: Soil helps many living things. It is very valuable.

activities.prompt: Why can fallen leaves and earthworms both help a garden's soil?
steps: Fallen leaves decay, so they add nutrients to the soil.
Earthworms turn and loosen the soil, so roots have more room.
Soil spaces provide air and room for roots to grow.
So fallen leaves and earthworms both help soil support plant growth.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Rocks and Their Uses
activities.body: People use rocks to build houses, roads, dams and more. Minerals make up rocks. Important metals come from minerals. Rocks take thousands to millions of years to form. We must conserve rocks and use them with care. Forests have many kinds of soil.
keyPoints: Rocks have many uses in building.
Minerals make up rocks.
Rocks need careful use.
activities.explanation: Rocks are useful, but they take a very long time to form.

activities.prompt: Which part of soil helps roots grow?
options: Spaces between particles
Earthworms only
Rocks and minerals
Fallen leaves only
activities.explanation: Spaces between soil particles provide air and room for roots.

activities.prompt: Fallen leaves ______ and add nutrients to the soil.
activities.hint: They break down over time.
activities.explanation: Decaying leaves return nutrients to the soil.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with its correct connection.
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a connection explained in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Why is soil valuable?
options: It supports biodiversity.
It is used to build dams.
It has important metals.
It is used to make houses and roads.
activities.explanation: Soil supports biodiversity. That means many kinds of living things.

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order described.
items: A long time passes
Sun, water and living organisms help break rocks apart
Soil forms
activities.explanation: Rocks break apart over a long time before soil forms.

activities.prompt: A builder wants to use many rocks fast. Which advice matches the lesson?
options: Use rocks carefully. They take thousands to millions of years to form.
Use rocks freely. They form in a moment.
Never use rocks. They contain no useful materials.
Use only soil. Rocks cannot help build structures.
activities.explanation: We must save rocks and use them carefully. They take a long time to form.

activities.prompt: Fallen leaves stay under a tree. What will happen to the soil?
options: The soil will gain nutrients while the leaves decay.
The soil will lose nutrients while the leaves decay.
The soil will gain more air while the leaves decay.
The soil will turn to rock while the leaves decay.

why.The soil will lose nutrients while the l: This mistake thinks decay takes nutrients away.
why.The soil will gain more air while the le: This mistake thinks decay adds air to soil.
why.The soil will turn to rock while the lea: This mistake confuses soil with slowly formed rock.

activities.explanation: The leaves decay and add nutrients to the soil.

activities.prompt: A child tests earthworms. Which comparison is fair?
options: Same soil in two pots, with worms in only one.
Same soil in two pots, with worms in both.
Different soil in two pots, with worms in one.
One pot with worms and one pot without soil.

why.Same soil in two pots, with worms in bot: This mistake gives both pots earthworms, so there is no test.
why.Different soil in two pots, with worms i: This mistake changes the soil as well as the earthworms.
why.One pot with worms and one pot without s: This mistake changes both soil and earthworm conditions.

activities.explanation: It changes the earthworms while keeping the soil the same.

activities.prompt: One pot has loose soil. Another is packed. How will roots grow?
options: The root in loose soil will have more room.
The root in packed soil will have more room.
Both roots will have exactly the same room.
The root in loose soil will have less air.

why.The root in packed soil will have more r: This mistake thinks packed soil has more spaces.
why.Both roots will have exactly the same ro: This mistake ignores the spaces between loose particles.
why.The root in loose soil will have less ai: This mistake reverses the air provided by spaces.

activities.explanation: Loose soil has spaces that give roots room.

activities.prompt: Small rock pieces lie in soil. How could that soil have formed?
options: Sun, water and living things broke rock over time.
People collected finished soil and placed it there.
Roots pulled up all the broken rock in one day.
Fallen leaves hardened the broken rock into soil.

why.People collected finished soil and place: This mistake thinks people form soil.
why.Roots pulled up all the broken rock in o: This mistake makes rock breaking quick and only root-driven.
why.Fallen leaves hardened the broken rock i: This mistake confuses leaf decay with rock breaking.

activities.explanation: Over time, the Sun, water and living things break rocks apart.

activities.prompt: A town needs rocks for a road. How should it use them?
options: The town should use them carefully and avoid waste.
The town should use every loose rock it can find.
The town should use all rocks as quickly as possible.
The town should ignore future needs for building materials.

why.The town should use every loose rock it: This mistake treats all unused rocks as useless.
why.The town should use all rocks as quickly: This mistake thinks using every rock now is responsible.
why.The town should ignore future needs for: This mistake ignores the duty to use rocks responsibly.

activities.explanation: Careful use and avoiding waste show responsible use.

lessons.title: Fossil Fuels

activities.prompt: What might you find underground in fossil fuels?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Fossil Fuels
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a journey underground, following fuels that power our daily lives. First, you meet petroleum, from which we obtain petrol, diesel and kerosene. These fuels, together with natural gas and coal, are called fossil fuels.

Next, you travel back through time as plants and tiny organisms are buried. You wait millions of years while their buried remains slowly form fossil fuels.

You learn that the most widely used vehicle fuels are petrol and diesel.

You visit a kitchen, where natural gas helps cook food. At a power station, you see coal used mainly to produce electricity. You also see natural gas used to generate electricity. Natural gas is cleaner than petrol or diesel.

Outside, you watch smoke and carbon dioxide rise as fossil fuels burn. They pollute the air when we use too much fossil fuel for transport and cooking. Finally, you walk or cycle to a nearby place and conserve fossil fuels. Remember, these fuels are available only in limited quantities.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What are fossil fuels?
activities.body: Petroleum, natural gas, and coal are fossil fuels. They form from the buried remains of plants and tiny organisms. This process takes millions of years. Fossil fuels are available only in limited quantities. Burning them releases smoke and carbon dioxide, which pollute the air. Walking or cycling nearby helps conserve fossil fuels.
keyPoints: Petroleum, natural gas, and coal are fossil fuels.
Fossil fuels take millions of years to form.
Burning fossil fuels can pollute the air.
activities.explanation: Fossil fuels are useful, but they are limited and can harm the air.

activities.prompt: A family often drives to a nearby shop even though they can walk. How can they save fossil fuel?
steps: A nearby shop is close, so the family can walk there.
Walking replaces a car trip, so petrol and diesel are not needed.
This conserves fossil fuels, because they are available only in limited quantities.
Therefore, walking helps save fuel and reduce pollution from transport.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which fuels do most vehicles use?
options: Petrol and diesel
Natural gas and coal
Petroleum and kerosene
Cooking and electricity
activities.explanation: Most vehicles use petrol and diesel.

activities.prompt: Coal is mainly used to produce ______.
activities.hint: Think of the power used in homes and factories.
activities.explanation: Coal is mainly used to produce electricity.

activities.prompt: Match each fuel with its main use.
activities.explanation: Natural gas serves cooking and electricity needs. Coal mainly produces electricity. Vehicles use petrol and diesel.

activities.prompt: When fossil fuels burn, what goes into the air?
options: Smoke and carbon dioxide
Water and electricity
Plants and tiny living things
Petrol and diesel
activities.explanation: Burning fossil fuels gives off smoke and carbon dioxide. These make the air dirty.

lessons.title: Renewable and Non-renewable Resources

activities.prompt: How can we use natural resources in a caring way?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Natural Resources
activities.body:
You begin a journey through a forest beside flowing water and under the bright Sun. Nature supplies natural resources. People also make human-made resources to meet their needs.

As you walk, you see air, water and forests around you. These renewable natural resources can be renewed or restored within a reasonable time. The Sun’s energy is also an important natural resource.

Then you visit a place filled with soil, rocks and minerals. These resources do not get replenished within a reasonable time. They are non-renewable resources. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are also non-renewable.

Your tour shows how important natural resources are. You use air, water, soil, and food from plants and animals every day. Careful use today can meet our present needs while saving resources for the future.

Outside, you notice vehicles passing through the city. Smoke from vehicles can make city air polluted. Electric vehicles do not release smoke. You can help by conserving natural resources and using them responsibly.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Kinds of natural resources
activities.body: Natural resources come from nature. People also make human-made resources to meet their needs. Renewable resources come back again in a reasonable time. Air, water and forests are renewable natural resources. Minerals, soil, rocks, coal, petroleum and natural gas are non-renewable resources. We must save natural resources. We must use them well for the future.
keyPoints: Renewable resources come back within a reasonable time.
Air, water and forests are renewable natural resources.
Coal and petroleum are non-renewable resources.
activities.explanation: This helps you know the difference between natural, renewable and non-renewable resources.

activities.title: Follow water as it is renewed

activities.takeaway: Water is a renewable resource because it is naturally replenished through the water cycle.
activities.explanation: Water is a renewable resource because it is naturally replenished through the water cycle.

This can meet present needs while saving resources for the future.

activities.prompt: A town burns coal for years. What is the most reasonable prediction?

why.The coal will become water after it is u: This wrongly imagines that coal can turn into another natural resource.
why.The coal will be restored whenever the t: This wrongly thinks resources return whenever people need them.

activities.explanation: This is right because coal is not replenished within a reasonable time.

activities.prompt: A forest is a renewable natural resource. What can careful use allow?
options: The forest can be replenished within a reasonable time.

why.The forest will stay unchanged no matter: This wrongly thinks natural resources stay unchanged after people use them.
why.The forest will disappear because all na: This wrongly thinks all natural resources soon disappear completely.
why.The forest can renew only after every us: This wrongly thinks any use stops a renewable resource from renewing.

activities.explanation: This is right because forests can be replenished within a reasonable time.

activities.prompt: An electric vehicle does not release smoke. Another vehicle releases smoke. Which helps reduce city air pollution?

why.Choose both vehicles for regular city tr: This wrongly keeps a smoke source in regular city travel.
why.Choose the electric vehicle only outside: This wrongly thinks pollution only matters outside the city.

activities.prompt: A family uses water carefully today. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Present needs are met and resources are saved for the future.

activities.context: At a windmill farm near Muppandal, a visitor noticed that the blades of a windmill were turning. The moving air was pushing the blades, so the windmill could work. The air contained oxygen, which the body needed to carry out its activities.
activities.prompt: Why does the visitor's taking of deep breaths help the visitor stay healthy?
options: It helps the body receive the oxygen needed to carry out its activities.
It increases the amount of oxygen in the mixture of gases around the Earth.
It makes the body carry out activities without needing oxygen.
It changes moving air into wind inside the lungs.

why.It increases the amount of oxygen in the: Breathing does not change the mixture of gases around the Earth.
why.It makes the body carry out activities w: The body still needs oxygen to carry out its activities.
why.It changes moving air into wind inside t: Wind is moving air outside; breathing does not turn air into wind.

activities.context: At a windmill farm near Muppandal, a visitor noticed that the blades of a windmill were turning. The moving air was pushing the blades, so the windmill could work. Farther away, another windmill turned to draw water from a well, while another was used to generate electricity. The visitor took several deep breaths and felt fresh air enter the lungs. The air contained oxygen, which the body needed to carry out its activities.
activities.prompt: A student says, “After one deep breath, I will never need oxygen again.” How should the student be corrected?
options: The body needs oxygen for its activities and cannot live for even a few minutes without oxygen.
One deep breath is enough because the lungs store all the oxygen the body will ever need.
Oxygen is only needed when the air is moving, so still air is useless.

why.One deep breath is enough because the lu: The body cannot live for even a few minutes without oxygen.
why.Oxygen is only needed when the air is mo: Air contains oxygen whether the air is moving or still.
why.The body can get oxygen from nitrogen, a: The body needs oxygen; nitrogen, argon, and carbon dioxide cannot replace it.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between air and wind.
activities.answer: Air is the mixture of gases around the Earth. It includes nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide, and other gases. Wind is moving air. Therefore, air can be still, while wind is the same kind of air when it moves.
points: Air surrounds the Earth.
Air is a mixture of several gases.
Wind means moving air.
Still air is not called wind.

activities.context: A family in an area where freshwater sources are limited often sees a water shortage. The family uses water for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and cleaning. activities.context: A family in an area where freshwater sources are limited often sees a water shortage. The family uses water for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and cleaning. One tap was left dripping, so clean water was being wasted. The family also installed a rainwater harvesting system, which collects and stores rainwater for later use. Their neighbors say the tap should be repaired immediately and rainwater should be used wisely.

options: Repair the dripping tap and use stored rainwater for later household needs.

Stop harvesting rainwater because most of Earth's water is freshwater.
Use polluted stored rainwater for drinking because all household uses need water equally.

why.Stop harvesting rainwater because most o: Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water, not freshwater.

activities.context: A home stands beside a large forest where many types of plants grow densely and wild animals, birds, and insects live. activities.prompt: Explain why all plants and animals depend on the Sun.
activities.answer: Plants need sunlight to prepare their food and grow, and grass is an example of a plant that needs sunlight. Animals get energy by eating plants. Since plants provide food and energy to animals, the Sun's energy supports both plants and animals on Earth.

Plants need sunlight to grow.

activities.context: A community is restoring a patch of land beside a forest. The forest contains different types of soil. Earthworms move through the soil, and fallen leaves decay there. They will leave the particles packed exactly as they are.

why.They will remove all the air from the sp: Loosening soil does not remove all the air between particles.
why.They will leave the particles packed exa: Earthworms change the soil by helping loosen it.

activities.context: A community is restoring a patch of land beside a forest. The forest contains different types of soil. Earthworms move through the soil, and fallen leaves decay there. People want to grow plants in the patch and later use nearby rocks to repair a road. The soil particles are packed closely, so there is little air and little room for roots. activities.prompt: Explain why spaces between soil particles are important and how earthworms and fallen leaves help soil.

activities.prompt: Explain how fossil fuels form and why their supplies are limited.
activities.answer: Fossil fuels form from the buried remains of plants and tiny organisms, and the process takes millions of years. lessons.title: Nubra, Stars and Constellations

activities.prompt: What stories do star patterns tell, and how can they guide you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Nubra's Night Sky
activities.body:
You arrive in Nubra, a beautiful region in Ladakh. Yangdol and her twin brother Dorjay live in a village here. They invite you to leave the village after dark and look up.

The night sky is almost cloudless. Thousands of stars light up the whole night. Nubra has very little air or light pollution. So you can see the stars clearly.

Each star produces its own light. As your eyes travel across the sky, groups of stars seem to form patterns. These patterns are called constellations.

Ancient people connected these patterns with animals, things and characters from stories. You might recognise figures that helped them imagine the night sky. Recognising them was useful for finding directions.

Long ago, sailors and travellers used star patterns to find their way. You try their method by turning towards a familiar pattern. There are 88 officially listed constellations, and together they divide the entire sky. Under Nubra's open sky, you see why such patterns mattered.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A sky full of stars
activities.body: Nubra is a beautiful region in Ladakh. Yangdol and her twin brother Dorjay live in a village there. Its weather is almost cloudless. Nubra has very little air or light pollution. Thousands of stars can light up the night sky. Stars produce their own light. Their groups can appear as patterns. Ancient people used these patterns to find directions. There are 88 constellations.
keyPoints: Almost cloudless Nubra has little air or light pollution.
Thousands of stars can light up the night sky.
Star groups can appear as patterns, and 88 constellations divide the sky.
activities.explanation: These ideas link Nubra's skies with patterns people used for directions.

activities.prompt: Why does Yangdol see so many stars during a Nubra night?
steps: Few clouds hide stars, so Nubra's almost cloudless sky reveals them.
Little pollution hides fewer stars, so more remain visible in Nubra.
Stars make their own light, so their glow does not need lamps.
Therefore, thousands of stars can fill the whole night sky.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which place is the beautiful region in this lesson?
options: Nubra
A star pattern
A constellation
The night sky
activities.explanation: Nubra is described as a beautiful region in Ladakh.

activities.prompt: Stars produce ______ light.
activities.hint: Think about where the light comes from.
activities.explanation: the lesson says that stars produce their own light.

activities.prompt: Match each star idea with its meaning.
pairs: Connected patterns with animals, things and characters
activities.explanation: Each pair shows a fact about stars, patterns, stories or directions.

activities.prompt: Put these facts in order. Start with stars making light. End with travellers finding their way.
items: Stars make their own light.
Groups of stars can look like patterns.
Long ago, people linked patterns to animals, things and characters.
Knowing star patterns helped people find directions.
Sailors and travellers once used star patterns to find their way.
activities.explanation: The order goes from stars making light to travellers finding their way.

activities.prompt: Why can Nubra's night sky look filled with stars?
options: Clouds cover most of Nubra's stars.
Light pollution hides Nubra's stars.
Thousands of stars light up the sky.
Stars stop shining at night.
activities.explanation: Thousands of stars can light up the entire night sky.

activities.prompt: Why is Nubra good for seeing many stars?
options: It is cloudy, and light pollution is high.
Stars make their own light, and clouds hide them.
The village has many lights inside houses.
It is almost cloudless, with little air or light pollution.
activities.explanation: Nubra is almost cloudless. It has very little air or light pollution.

activities.prompt: Nubra is almost cloudless and has little air or light pollution. Why can thousands of stars be seen?
options: Village lamps make every star disappear when they are switched on.
Little air and light pollution let many stars remain visible.
Village lamps make stars shine even through thick clouds.
Stars make their own light, so pollution cannot hide them.

why.Village lamps make every star disappear: This mistake assumes switching on lamps makes every star disappear.
why.Village lamps make stars shine even thro: This mistake treats village lamps as the source of starlight.
why.Stars make their own light, so pollution: This mistake thinks stars' own light stops pollution from hiding them.

activities.explanation: Little air and light pollution let many stars stay visible.

activities.prompt: Sailors and travellers once used star patterns to find their way. What can a familiar star pattern help a sailor do?
options: It can help the sailor choose the correct direction.
It can show the sailor the exact spot on Earth.
It can tell the sailor the exact distance home.
It can tell the sailor how far away each star is.

why.It can show the sailor the exact spot on: This mistake thinks directions reveal an exact location.
why.It can tell the sailor the exact distanc: This mistake confuses direction with the distance travelled.
why.It can tell the sailor how far away each: This mistake confuses star patterns with measuring distances to stars.

activities.explanation: Star patterns helped sailors and travellers find their direction.

activities.prompt: Groups of stars can appear as patterns. One group joins them into an animal. Another joins them into a story character. Why can both groups do this?
options: The same stars can appear as different patterns to people.
Each star group can show only one pattern forever.
Story characters can move the stars into new places.
Animal patterns can appear only on cloudless nights.

why.Each star group can show only one patter: This mistake assumes a pattern has only one possible shape.
why.Story characters can move the stars into: This mistake believes story characters can move real stars.
why.Animal patterns can appear only on cloud: This mistake limits star patterns to clear nights in Nubra.

activities.explanation: People can connect one star pattern with different animals or characters.

activities.prompt: Stars produce their own light. Yangdol switches off every lamp at home. What should happen to the stars outside?
options: The stars keep shining because they produce their own light.
The stars go out because their light comes from the lamps.
The stars grow dimmer because the lamps used their light.
The stars change shape because the lamps moved their light.

why.The stars go out because their light com: This mistake treats lamps as the source of starlight.
why.The stars grow dimmer because the lamps: This mistake thinks lamps take light from the stars.
why.The stars change shape because the lamps: This mistake thinks lamps can change the stars' shapes.

activities.explanation: Stars produce their own light, so switching off lamps does not stop them.

activities.prompt: Nubra is almost cloudless and has very little air or light pollution. Yangdol wants to test the pollution idea. Which comparison is fairest?
options: Compare Nubra with a clear place having much more pollution.
Compare Nubra with a cloudy place having much less pollution.
Compare Nubra with a clear place having much less pollution.
Compare Nubra with a cloudy place having much more pollution.

why.Compare Nubra with a cloudy place having: Cloudiness also changes, so pollution cannot be judged alone.
why.Compare Nubra with a clear place having: Less pollution does not test the claim that pollution hides stars.
why.Compare Nubra with a cloudy place having: Clouds and pollution both change, so the cause is unclear.

activities.explanation: This changes pollution while keeping the sky clear, so the test is fairer.

lessons.title: Watching the Night Sky

activities.prompt: What will you discover while exploring the night sky?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of the Night Sky
activities.body:
You step outside on a clear, cloudless night, ready to explore the sky. Many stars may greet you, but some places hide them well. Smoke, dust and bright lights can hide many stars. Excessive artificial light at night is called light pollution.

Light pollution is growing quickly around the world. Tall buildings and trees may block your view of the sky. The best place for night-sky watching is an open, dark area. Ask an adult to help you choose a dark, open place. Never go to a dark open place at night without an adult.

Once you are safely there, wait about half an hour. Your eyes adjust to the darkness during that time. You can download a sky-mapping app on a mobile phone.

You cannot see every constellation from every place on Earth. Your place on Earth affects which constellations you can see.

Now you are ready to explore the stars with your app. You have planned a safe visit to a dark, open place.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Clear and Dark Night Sky
activities.body: On a clear, cloudless night, many stars may be visible. Smoke, dust and light pollution can hide many stars. Light pollution means excessive artificial light at night. It is growing quickly. We cannot see every constellation from every place on Earth. Tall buildings and trees may block the view. The best place is open and dark. Ask an adult. Never go alone. Wait about half an hour so your eyes adjust.
keyPoints: Clear, cloudless nights may show many stars.
Light pollution can hide stars and is growing quickly.
Choose a dark, open place with an adult.
Wait about half an hour so your eyes adjust.
activities.explanation: Clear, dark viewing conditions help you see stars.

activities.prompt: A child at home sees few stars and asks an adult where to watch the night sky.
steps: Smoke, dust, and light pollution can hide many stars, so the home sky may look empty.
Tall buildings and trees may block the sky, so an open place gives a better view.
An adult should help choose it, because the child must never go there alone at night.
After waiting about half an hour, the eyes adjust, making a dark, open place best for watching.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where is the best place for night-sky watching?
options: An open, dark area
A smoky, dusty place
A place beside tall buildings and trees
An area with excessive artificial light
activities.explanation: An open, dark area gives you the best chance to watch stars.

activities.prompt: On a clear, cloudless night, ______ stars may be visible.
activities.hint: Use the word for a large number.
activities.explanation: A clear, cloudless night may allow you to see many stars.

activities.prompt: Match each sky condition with its effect.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects a sky condition with its effect on your view.

activities.prompt: Where can a sky-mapping app be downloaded?
options: Inside a tall building
Under a dark cloud
On a mobile phone
Inside a dusty cloud
activities.explanation: Sky-mapping apps can be downloaded on a mobile phone.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order for watching the night sky.
items: Ask an adult to help you pick a dark, open place
Wait about half an hour
Let your eyes get used to the dark
activities.explanation: An adult helps keep you safe. Your eyes need time in the dark to see well.

activities.prompt: Which statement about light pollution and constellations is correct?
options: Every constellation appears from every place. Light pollution is growing slowly.
Not every constellation appears from every place. Light pollution is shrinking.
Not every constellation appears from every place. Light pollution is growing quickly.
Every constellation appears from every place. Light pollution is staying the same.
activities.explanation: Not every constellation appears from every place on Earth. Light pollution is growing quickly around the world.

activities.prompt: Smoke, dust, and light pollution can hide many stars. What will a child see in a dark, open area?
options: More stars will be visible because fewer lights hide them.
Fewer stars will be visible because darkness hides their light.
No stars will be visible because the sky is too dark.
The same stars will be visible because the night is clear.

why.Fewer stars will be visible because dark: This mistake thinks darkness itself hides the light from stars.
why.No stars will be visible because the sky: This mistake thinks stars can only be seen in bright places.
why.The same stars will be visible because t: This mistake thinks clear skies look the same from every place.

activities.explanation: This is right because a dark, open area has less light pollution.

activities.prompt: One child sees a constellation from one town. What may a child far away on Earth see?
options: They may see different constellations because the sky differs by place.
They must see exactly the same constellations from every single place.
They cannot see any constellation because towns block the whole sky.
They will see only buildings because constellations stay below the ground.

why.They must see exactly the same constella: This mistake assumes every place shows exactly the same sky.
why.They cannot see any constellation becaus: This mistake thinks living in a town hides every constellation.
why.They will see only buildings because con: This mistake confuses buildings on the ground with objects in the sky.

activities.explanation: This is right because we cannot see every constellation from every place.

activities.prompt: Sky-mapping apps can be downloaded on a mobile phone. Does downloading one make a bright, crowded place best for watching?
options: Yes, because the app can remove all light pollution from the sky.
Yes, because the app can move buildings and trees out of view.
No, because bright lights and nearby obstacles can still spoil the view.
No, because a phone screen can show stars better than dark skies.

why.Yes, because the app can remove all ligh: This mistake assumes the app can change the real light pollution.
why.Yes, because the app can move buildings: This mistake assumes the app can move solid objects.
why.No, because a phone screen can show star: This mistake thinks a phone screen improves the real night-sky view.

activities.explanation: This is right because lights and obstacles can still spoil the sky view.

activities.prompt: Light pollution is growing quickly around the world. What may happen to night-sky watching in many places?
options: More artificial light may hide many stars from night-sky watchers.
Fewer stars may turn into planets all around the world.
Smoke and dust may disappear because the world may become darker.
Constellations may all become visible from every place across Earth.

why.Fewer stars may turn into planets all ar: This mistake confuses stars with planets.
why.Smoke and dust may disappear because the: This mistake wrongly expects light pollution to clear smoke and dust.
why.Constellations may all become visible fr: This mistake ignores that not every constellation is visible everywhere.

activities.explanation: This is right because growing light pollution can hide many stars.
