lessons.title: The Sun and the Solar System

activities.prompt: What will you discover about the Sun and our solar system?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Around the Sun
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a journey from the Sun towards Earth. You might first wonder what this glowing centre really is. The Sun is a star, and it is the closest star to us. During your journey, you discover that it gives Earth heat and light. It is also Earth's main source of energy. The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth.

From here, you look back and imagine the huge space between you and the Sun. It is about 150 million kilometres away. One astronomical unit is about the distance between the Sun and Earth. Proxima Centauri is about 269000 astronomical units away.

Now you watch a planet moving around the Sun. This movement is called revolution. A planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun. Earth is one such planet, taking nearly one year to complete one revolution.

Your tour shows that Earth is also rotating about its axis.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Our Bright Neighbour
activities.body: The Sun is a star. It is the closest star to us. It gives Earth heat and light. It is Earth's main source of energy. The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth. Earth is about 150 million kilometres from the Sun. One astronomical unit is the distance from the Sun to Earth. Revolution means an object moves around the Sun. Earth also rotates. This means Earth spins around its axis.
keyPoints: The Sun is the closest star to us.
The Sun gives Earth heat and light.
Revolution means moving around the Sun.
activities.explanation: This card links the Sun, Earth's movement, and distances in space.

activities.prompt: Earth is about 1 astronomical unit from the Sun. Proxima Centauri is about 269000 astronomical units away. How many times farther away is Proxima Centauri?
steps: Earth's distance from the Sun is about 1 astronomical unit.
Proxima Centauri is about 269000 astronomical units away.
Since 269000 is much greater than 1, Proxima Centauri is much farther away.
Therefore, Proxima Centauri is about 269000 times farther away than Earth is.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is the Sun?
options: A star
A planet
An astronomical unit
An axis
activities.explanation: The Sun is a star. It is the closest star to us.

activities.prompt: The movement of an object around the Sun is called ______.
activities.hint: This is the name of the movement around the Sun.
activities.explanation: Revolution means the movement of an object around the Sun.

activities.prompt: What is one astronomical unit?
options: the width of Earth
the energy of the Sun
the distance between the Sun and Earth
the way things move around the Sun
activities.explanation: One astronomical unit is about the distance between the Sun and Earth.

activities.prompt: Match each word with its meaning.
pairs: movement of an object around the Sun
takes almost one year for one revolution
activities.explanation: Each pair joins a thing or movement with its fact.

activities.prompt: Arrange these fact cards to explain the distance.
items: The Sun and Earth are about 150 million kilometres apart.
One astronomical unit is about this distance.
Proxima Centauri is about 269000 astronomical units away.
activities.explanation: Start with the Sun-to-Earth distance. Then define one astronomical unit. Finally, use it for Proxima Centauri.

activities.prompt: Which sentence about Earth is correct?
options: Earth revolves around the Sun and rotates about its axis.
Earth revolves around its axis and rotates around the Sun.
Earth takes one year to make one rotation about its axis.
Earth makes one revolution without moving around the Sun.
activities.explanation: Earth takes almost one year for one revolution. It also rotates about its axis.

activities.prompt: Earth gets heat and light from the Sun. A model Earth stays in a dark box. What happens?
options: The model still receives heat and light from the Sun.
The model receives no heat or light from the Sun.
The model receives heat but no light from the Sun.
The model receives light but no heat from the Sun.

why.The model still receives heat and light: Without sunlight, the model receives neither heat nor light.
why.The model receives heat but no light fro: This wrongly believes heat can arrive without light.
why.The model receives light but no heat fro: This wrongly believes light can arrive without heat.

activities.explanation: This ignores that the model is inside a dark box.

activities.prompt: A ball moves once around a model Sun. Has one revolution happened?
options: Yes, because it moved once around the Sun.
Yes, because the model Sun stayed still.
No, because the ball moved around the Sun.
No, because the ball did not spin on its axis.

Staying still does not decide whether a revolution happened.
why.No, because the ball moved around the Su: This wrongly says motion around the Sun prevents revolution.
why.No, because the ball did not spin on its: This wrongly treats spinning on an axis as necessary for revolution.

activities.explanation: It moved around the Sun, which is exactly one revolution.

activities.prompt: Earth rotates about its axis and revolves around the Sun. Does a globe spinning in place show revolution?
options: No, because spinning about an axis is rotation.
No, because every movement takes nearly one year.
No, because a revolution needs a large sphere.
Yes, because the globe moved around its own axis.

why.No, because every movement takes nearly: This confuses rotation with the yearly journey around the Sun.
why.No, because a revolution needs a large s: It wrongly ties revolution to the object's size.
why.Yes, because the globe moved around its: It mistakes rotation around an axis for revolution around the Sun.

activities.explanation: Spinning about an axis is rotation, not revolution.

activities.prompt: Proxima Centauri is about 269000 astronomical units away. One unit is about the Sun-Earth distance. Which star is closer to us?
options: The Sun is closer to us than Proxima Centauri.
The Sun and Proxima Centauri are equally close.
Proxima Centauri is closer to us than the Sun.
The Sun is farther away than Proxima Centauri.

why.The Sun and Proxima Centauri are equally: Equal distances do not match the given numbers.
why.Proxima Centauri is closer to us than th: This reverses the comparison between 1 and 269000 units.
why.The Sun is farther away than Proxima Cen: It treats Proxima's much larger distance as smaller.

activities.explanation: The Sun is about 1 astronomical unit away, not 269000.

activities.prompt: The Sun gives Earth heat and light. Which test best checks both?
options: Measure both heat and light in sunlight and darkness.
Measure only heat in sunlight and darkness.
Measure only light in sunlight and darkness.
Measure only size in sunlight and darkness.

why.Measure only heat in sunlight and darkne: Checking heat alone cannot show that light is provided.
why.Measure only light in sunlight and darkn: Checking light alone cannot show that heat is provided.
why.Measure only size in sunlight and darkne: Size is not one of the two things the Sun gives.

activities.explanation: Checking heat and light in sunlight and darkness tests both.

lessons.title: Planets, Moons and Craters

activities.prompt: How do planets, moons and craters differ?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Space
activities.body:
You begin among the eight planets. You meet Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

First, you visit the smaller inner planets. They are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. You find that their solid surfaces are covered with rocks. Then, you look towards the four outermost planets. You see that they are much larger than Earth. They are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Venus catches your eye as it shines brightly at dawn and dusk. You learn that it is called the Morning Star or Evening Star. Yet, Venus is not a star.

Mars looks red as you watch it, so it is called the Red Planet. Earth looks blue because much of it is covered with water. You call it the Blue Planet.

Now, you discover moons, which are natural satellites of planets. Earth has one Moon, while Mars has two moons. You watch the Moon take about 27 days to revolve around Earth. On its surface, you see round, bowl-shaped hollows called craters.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Space Neighbours
activities.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the inner planets. They are smaller, with rocky surfaces. The four outer planets are much larger than Earth. Venus shines at dawn and dusk, but it is not a star. Mars looks red. Earth is called the Blue Planet. Moons are natural satellites that travel around planets. The Moon takes about 27 days to circle Earth. Its bowl-shaped hollows are called craters.
keyPoints: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are smaller inner planets with rocky surfaces.
The four outer planets are much larger than Earth.
Moons travel around planets, and craters are bowl-shaped hollows.
activities.explanation: These clues help you identify planets, moons and craters.

activities.prompt: At dawn, you see a bright object in the sky. It is not a star. Which planet could it be?
steps: Venus shines brightly at dawn and dusk.
That brightness makes it stand out in the morning or evening sky.
It is called the Morning Star or Evening Star for this reason.
So the bright object is Venus, not a star.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Choose the Inner Planets
activities.prompt: Which group contains only inner planets?
options: Mercury, Mars and Jupiter
Venus, Earth and Saturn
Mars, Jupiter and Uranus
Earth, Neptune and Venus
activities.explanation: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the inner planets.

activities.title: Rocky Surfaces
activities.prompt: The inner planets have solid surfaces covered with rocks.
activities.explanation: the lesson describes their surfaces as solid and covered with rocks.

activities.title: A Bright Planet
activities.prompt: Venus shines brightly at dawn and ______.
activities.hint: This happens near the end of the day.
activities.explanation: Venus shines brightly at both dawn and dusk.

activities.title: Special Planet Names
activities.prompt: Match each planet with its special name.
activities.explanation: Each name matches the planet's appearance in the lesson.

activities.title: Mars Has Moons
activities.prompt: How many moons does Mars have?
options: One
Two
Three
Four
activities.explanation: Mars has two moons, while Earth has one Moon.

activities.title: Why the Name Needs Care
activities.prompt: Venus is called the Morning Star or the Evening Star. Why must we be careful with this name?
options: It shines in the morning and evening, but it is not a star.
It looks red, so it is called the Red Planet.
It looks blue because water covers much of it.
It is one of the four outer planets.
activities.explanation: The name tells how Venus looks. It does not say what Venus is.

activities.title: Identify Earth's Moon
activities.prompt: Which clues describe Earth's Moon?
options: It is an inner planet with a rocky surface.
It shines brightly at dawn and dusk.
It looks red and has two moons.
It circles Earth and has bowl-shaped hollows.
activities.explanation: Only the Moon is described as circling Earth and having bowl-shaped hollows.

activities.prompt: You make a larger-planet group. Which planets should you use?
options: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune
Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars
Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter
Mercury, Earth, Mars, and Neptune

why.Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars: These are the smaller inner planets, not the larger outer ones.
why.Venus, Earth, Mars, and Jupiter: Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars are the inner planets.
why.Mercury, Earth, Mars, and Neptune: Mercury, Earth, and Mars are inner, while Neptune is outer.

activities.explanation: These are the four outer planets, which are much larger than Earth.

activities.prompt: A claim says Earth's blue colour comes from rocks. What is wrong?
options: Much of Earth is covered with water.
Earth's Moon is covered with blue rocks.
All eight planets are covered with blue water.
Venus has blue hollows on its surface.

This mistake gives Earth's blue rocks to the Moon.
why.All eight planets are covered with blue: This mistake applies Earth's water to all eight planets.
This mistake mixes Venus with the Moon's hollows.

activities.explanation: Much of Earth is covered with water, so Earth is called the Blue Planet.

lessons.title: Asteroids and Comets

activities.prompt: How does a comet change as it travels near the Sun?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Asteroids and Comets
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting the region between Mars and Jupiter. You meet small rocky objects travelling around the Sun. These small rocky objects are called asteroids. Many asteroids travel around the Sun here. This region is called the asteroid belt.

Next, you spot a visitor with a long tail. This is a comet. Comets are made of dust, gases, rocks and ice. Their frozen material starts evaporating when they near the Sun. You follow this icy-rocky visitor on its journey.

During your journey, you watch the comet move away from the Sun. It becomes dim as the distance grows. You still see its long tail. You remember what the comet contains. Dust, gases, rocks and ice make up its mixture. Near the Sun, its frozen material starts evaporating.

Scientists understand comets as icy-rocky visitors travelling near the Sun. You have met one during your tour. You have also seen many rocky asteroids. They travel around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. This region is called the asteroid belt.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet Asteroids and Comets
activities.body: Asteroids are small rocky objects. Many travel around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. This region is called the asteroid belt. Comets are objects with long tails. They are made of dust, gases, rocks and ice. Frozen material in a comet starts evaporating when it nears the Sun. A comet becomes dim as it moves away from the Sun. Scientists understand comets as icy-rocky visitors travelling near the Sun.
keyPoints: Asteroids are small rocky objects.
Comets have long tails and contain ice.
Comets become dim when moving away from the Sun.
activities.explanation: This card introduces asteroids, comets, and how comets change near the Sun.

activities.prompt: A child finds two space objects. One is small and rocky. The other has a long tail. How should the child sort them?
steps: The small object is an asteroid because asteroids are small rocky objects.
Many asteroids travel around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.
That region is the asteroid belt, so the object fits there.
The long-tailed object is a comet because comets have long tails.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which statement describes an asteroid?
options: An asteroid is a small rocky object.
An asteroid is an object with a long tail.
An asteroid is made only of frozen material.
An asteroid always travels between Mars and Jupiter.
activities.explanation: Only the first option matches the definition of an asteroid.

activities.prompt: Many asteroids travel around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.
activities.explanation: The facts say many asteroids travel around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.

activities.prompt: The region between Mars and Jupiter is called the ______ belt.
activities.hint: This region contains many asteroids.
activities.explanation: The region between Mars and Jupiter is called the asteroid belt.

activities.prompt: Match each object with its meaning.
activities.explanation: Each pair joins an object with a fact.

activities.prompt: A comet is near the Sun. What happens to its frozen material?
options: It starts to evaporate.
It becomes solid.
It turns into dust.
It moves farther from the Sun.
activities.explanation: The frozen material starts to evaporate when the comet is near the Sun.

activities.prompt: A comet gets dim as it moves away from the Sun.
activities.explanation: A comet gets dimmer as it moves away from the Sun.

activities.prompt: Put these comet steps in order.
items: A comet nears the Sun.
Frozen material starts evaporating.
A comet becomes dim as it moves away.
activities.explanation: Evaporation happens near the Sun. A comet becomes dim as it moves away.

activities.prompt: A comet is moving away from the Sun. What happens to it?
options: It becomes dim.
It becomes brighter.
It turns into an asteroid.
It becomes an object without a tail.
activities.explanation: A comet becomes dim when it moves away from the Sun. This matches the fact.

activities.prompt: A probe leaves Mars for Jupiter. Where should it find many asteroids?
options: among many small rocks between Mars and Jupiter
in a tight group very close to the Sun
in a rocky band behind Mars alone
in a rocky band beyond Jupiter

why.in a tight group very close to the Sun: This mistake places asteroids close to the Sun, not in the belt.
why.in a rocky band behind Mars alone: This mistake puts the asteroid belt behind Mars instead of between them.
why.in a rocky band beyond Jupiter: This mistake puts the asteroid belt beyond Jupiter instead of between them.

activities.explanation: Many asteroids travel around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.

activities.prompt: Which observation best tests comet brightness at different distances from the Sun?
options: Watch one comet near the Sun, then farther away.
Watch two comets at the same distance from the Sun.
Watch one comet's tail length near and farther from the Sun.
Change one comet's materials, then watch its brightness.

why.Watch two comets at the same distance fr: This mistake keeps the distance the same, so it cannot test distance.
why.Watch one comet's tail length near and f: This mistake measures tail length instead of the brightness asked about.
why.Change one comet's materials, then watch: This mistake changes materials, so the brightness comparison is not fair.

activities.explanation: Watching the same comet at two distances tests brightness fairly.

lessons.title: The Milky Way Galaxy and the Universe

activities.prompt: What is the Milky Way, and could we find life elsewhere?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Beyond Our Galaxy
activities.body:
Imagine you stand in a dark place on a moonless night. You look upward and notice a faint band of light across the sky. The band stretches from near north to south.

Your home galaxy is called the Milky Way Galaxy, or Ākāśha Gangā. Our Solar System is part of it. A galaxy can contain millions to billions of stars.

Now picture yourself visiting other galaxies. Scientists study galaxies to understand stars, galaxies, and the Universe. You might ask whether planets revolve around other stars in our galaxy. Such planets are called exoplanets.

Here is a careful answer to a big question. We do not yet know whether life exists elsewhere in the Universe. Scientists have not yet found any evidence of life elsewhere. Your question remains open, so keep following your curiosity.

End your tour by looking up once more. You now know our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy. You have learned that exoplanets revolve around other stars in our galaxy. What will you explore next?
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Our Home Galaxy
activities.body: Look at the sky on a dark night with no moon. You can see a faint (weak) band of light. The band goes from near north to south across the sky. This band is our home galaxy. It is called the Milky Way Galaxy. It is also called Ākāśha Gangā. A galaxy can have millions to billions of stars. Our Solar System is part of it.
keyPoints: A weak band of light crosses the night sky.
The Milky Way Galaxy is also called Ākāśha Gangā.
Our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy.
activities.explanation: The weak band of light helps us see our home galaxy.

activities.prompt: Why is there a light band? Where is our Solar System?
steps: Dark, moonless nights reveal a faint band because the light is faint.
The band stretches north to south, so the child can follow its direction.
Our Solar System is part of Ākāśha Gangā, the Milky Way Galaxy.
Galaxies can hold millions to billions of stars, so our home is vast.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Faint Band
activities.prompt: On a dark night with no moon, what do you see across the sky?
options: Our Milky Way Galaxy
Our Solar System
A single distant star
An exoplanet
activities.explanation: The Milky Way Galaxy looks like a faint band of light.

activities.title: Another Galaxy Name
activities.prompt: Our home galaxy is called the ______ Galaxy.
activities.hint: It is the name of our home galaxy.
activities.explanation: Our home galaxy is the Milky Way Galaxy, also called Ākāśha Gangā.

activities.title: Galaxy Connections
activities.prompt: Match each space object with the correct fact.
pairs: another name for the Milky Way Galaxy
part of the Milky Way Galaxy
can contain millions to billions of stars
activities.explanation: Ākāśha Gangā is another name for the Milky Way Galaxy. Our Solar System is part of it.

activities.title: Why Study Galaxies?
activities.prompt: Why do scientists study galaxies?
options: To change the position of the Milky Way
To understand stars, galaxies and the Universe
To prove that life exists elsewhere
To name every Solar System in the galaxy
activities.explanation: Scientists study galaxies to understand stars, galaxies and the Universe.

activities.title: Discovering Our Galaxy
activities.prompt: Put these ideas in the correct learning order.
items: A faint band appears across the sky.
The band stretches from near north to south.
The band is our home galaxy.
Our Solar System is part of it.
activities.explanation: We first see the band. Then we learn where it stretches and what it is.

activities.title: Exoplanets and Life
activities.prompt: Which sentence about exoplanets and life is true?
options: Exoplanets go around other stars, and signs of life have been found.
Exoplanets are stars, and no signs of life have been found.
Exoplanets belong to other galaxies, and no signs of life have been found.
Exoplanets go around other stars, and no signs of life have been found.
activities.explanation: Exoplanets go around other stars in our galaxy. No signs of life have been found in other places.

activities.prompt: At night, a child leaves a bright room for a dark place. The night has no moon. What should the child expect?
options: A faint band of light appears across the sky.
A bright band of sunlight appears across the sky.
A large planet appears close above the ground.
A new galaxy appears in one dark place.

why.A bright band of sunlight appears across: This confuses the faint sky band with bright sunlight.
why.A large planet appears close above the g: This invents a nearby planet that the fact does not give.
This confuses a sky-wide band with a galaxy in one place.

activities.explanation: This is right because a dark, moonless night shows the faint band.

activities.prompt: A galaxy is drawn with only a few stars. Does this fit the facts?
options: No, because a galaxy can contain millions to billions of stars.
Yes, because a galaxy can contain only a few stars.
Yes, because the Solar System is part of every galaxy.
No, because a galaxy can contain no stars at all.

why.Yes, because a galaxy can contain only a: This mistakes a few stars for the possible size of a galaxy.
why.Yes, because the Solar System is part of: This confuses galaxy membership with the number of stars.
why.No, because a galaxy can contain no star: This claims galaxies have no stars, but galaxies can contain stars.

activities.explanation: This is right because galaxies can contain millions to billions of stars.

activities.prompt: A planet revolves around a different star in our galaxy. Which claim fits?
options: It is an exoplanet because it revolves around another star.
It is an exoplanet because it belongs to our Solar System.
It is an exoplanet because it does not revolve around a star.
It is an exoplanet because every planet revolves around another star.

why.It is an exoplanet because it belongs to: This confuses Solar System membership with the exoplanet rule.
why.It is an exoplanet because it does not r: This confuses moving around no star with revolving around another.
why.It is an exoplanet because every planet: This applies the exoplanet rule to every planet, not only other stars.

activities.explanation: This is right because it revolves around another star in our galaxy.

activities.prompt: No life has been found elsewhere. Why can’t this prove no life exists elsewhere?
options: We do not yet know whether life exists elsewhere.
Life elsewhere cannot exist because no life was found.
Finding no life elsewhere proves every other place is empty.
Life elsewhere is known not to exist in our galaxy.

why.Life elsewhere cannot exist because no l: This confuses missing evidence with proof that life cannot exist.
why.Finding no life elsewhere proves every o: This treats no evidence as proof that every other place is empty.
why.Life elsewhere is known not to exist in: This turns our uncertainty into a certain claim about our galaxy.

activities.explanation: This is right because life elsewhere is still unknown.

activities.context: Yangdol and her twin brother Dorjay live in a village in Nubra. On an almost cloudless evening, they see thousands of stars across the night sky. Nubra has very little air or light pollution, so the stars can be seen clearly. Yangdol points out a group that appears to form a pattern. She explains that ancient people connected such patterns with animals, things, and story characters, and that sailors and travellers once used them to find their way.
activities.prompt: Why can thousands of stars be seen so clearly from Nubra?
options: Its nearly clear sky and limited pollution make thousands of stars visible.
Its large number of official constellations creates the extra starlight.
Its stories about animals and characters cause new stars to appear.
Its very cloudy weather makes every star easier to see.

why.Its large number of official constellati: Constellations do not create starlight; stars produce their own light.
why.Its stories about animals and characters: Stories do not cause stars to appear in the sky.
why.Its very cloudy weather makes every star: Nubra's weather is almost cloudless, not very cloudy.

activities.explanation: Nubra is almost cloudless and has very little air or light pollution.

activities.context: Yangdol and her twin brother Dorjay live in a village in Nubra. On an almost cloudless evening, they see thousands of stars across the night sky. Nubra has very little air or light pollution, so the stars can be seen clearly. Yangdol points out a group that appears to form a pattern. She explains that ancient people connected such patterns with animals, things, and story characters, and that sailors and travellers once used them to find their way.
activities.prompt: What can travellers do after recognising a star pattern, based on what Yangdol explains?
options: Use it to work out the direction of travel.
Use it to count every star in the whole sky.
Use it to decide which story character the stars represent.
Use it to tell whether the weather in Nubra is cloudy.

why.Use it to count every star in the whole: Finding direction does not involve counting every star in the sky.
why.Use it to decide which story character t: The practical use described to travellers was finding their way.
why.Use it to tell whether the weather in Nu: The cloudless sky and star-pattern navigation are separate ideas.

activities.explanation: Recognising star patterns was useful for finding directions.

activities.prompt: Explain why Nubra's night sky is suitable for seeing stars and star patterns.
activities.answer: Nubra is almost cloudless and has very little air or light pollution. These conditions allow the entire night sky to be lit up with thousands of stars. Groups of these stars can appear as patterns, so people can notice shapes in the sky and recognise star patterns for practical uses such as finding direction.
points: Nubra is almost cloudless.
There is very little air or light pollution.
The night sky can show thousands of stars.
Groups of stars can appear as patterns.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On a clear, cloudless night, a student visits a viewing spot with an adult. Smoke, dust, and excessive artificial light hide many stars, while tall buildings block parts of the sky. The student downloads a sky-mapping app to a mobile phone. After waiting about half an hour, the student still notices only a few stars and wonders whether a darker, open area would give a better view.
activities.prompt: What should the student do next to improve the view?
options: Ask the adult to help choose an open, dark place for watching.
Ask the adult to wait longer beside the bright artificial lights.
Move closer to the artificial lights so that faint stars are easier to see.
Use the app to find a better place and go there alone at night.

why.Ask the adult to wait longer beside the: Extra waiting cannot remove the effects of artificial light.
why.Move closer to the artificial lights so: Bright artificial light can hide many stars.
why.Use the app to find a better place and g: The student must not go to a dark open place alone.

activities.explanation: An open, dark area gives the best viewing conditions.

activities.context: On a clear, cloudless night, a student visits a viewing spot with an adult. Smoke, dust, and excessive artificial light hide many stars, while tall buildings block parts of the sky. The student downloads a sky-mapping app to a mobile phone. After waiting about half an hour, the student still notices only a few stars and wonders whether a darker, open area would give a better view.
activities.prompt: Suppose the smoke and dust are reduced, the excessive artificial light is controlled, and the buildings no longer block the view. What would happen next?
options: Many more stars would likely be visible.
Every constellation would be visible from that place.
The number of visible stars would fall because the sky became darker.
The buildings would make more stars visible once the air was clearer.

why.Every constellation would be visible fro: Not every constellation can be seen from every place.
why.The number of visible stars would fall b: Fewer stars would not result from darker conditions.
why.The buildings would make more stars visi: The buildings are no longer blocking the view in this situation.

activities.explanation: Clearer, darker, unobstructed conditions improve the view.

activities.prompt: Explain why an open, dark place and a wait of about half an hour can improve night-sky watching.
activities.answer: An open, dark area is best because smoke, dust, and light pollution can hide many stars, while tall buildings and trees may block the view. Waiting about half an hour allows the eyes to adjust to darkness, so more stars may become visible.
points: Smoke, dust, and light pollution can hide stars.
Tall buildings and trees may block the sky.
An open, dark area provides better viewing conditions.
The eyes need about half an hour to adjust.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why the Sun is important to Earth.
activities.answer: The Sun is important to Earth because it gives Earth heat and light. It is also Earth's main source of energy. The Sun is a star and the closest star to us, so Earth receives both heat and light from a star.
points: The Sun is a star.
It is the closest star to us.
It gives Earth heat and light.
It is Earth's main energy source.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: At a school space display, a student sees a shining object in the early morning. The display card says the object appears bright at dawn and dusk and is sometimes called the Morning Star or Evening Star, although it is not a star. Elsewhere, the student sees a reddish planet and a blue planet. A photo of Earth’s Moon shows round, bowl-shaped hollows. The student must sort the objects and explain their features to visitors.
activities.prompt: Why should the student identify the shining object as Venus?
options: It is Venus, because its bright dawn-and-dusk appearance gives it the two common names.
It is Mars, because Mars is the reddish planet.
It is Earth, because much of Earth is covered with water.
It is Jupiter, because it is one of the four outermost planets.

why.It is Mars, because Mars is the reddish: Mars looks red, which does not match the brightness clue.
why.It is Earth, because much of Earth is co: Earth is called the Blue Planet because of its water.
why.It is Jupiter, because it is one of the: Jupiter has no described bright appearance at dawn and dusk.

activities.explanation: Venus shines brightly at dawn and dusk.

activities.context: At a school space display, a student sees a shining object in the early morning. The display card says the object appears bright at dawn and dusk and is sometimes called the Morning Star or Evening Star, although it is not a star. Elsewhere, the student sees a reddish planet and a blue planet. A photo of Earth’s Moon shows round, bowl-shaped hollows. The student must sort the objects and explain their features to visitors.
activities.prompt: A visitor asks why the blue object should be labeled Earth. Which explanation is correct?
options: It is Earth, whose water-covered appearance explains the blue color.
It is Mars, because Mars looks red.
It is Venus, because Venus shines brightly at dawn and dusk.
It is Mercury, because it is a smaller inner planet.

Mars is known by its red appearance.
why.It is Venus, because Venus shines bright: Venus is known for its bright appearance at dawn and dusk.
why.It is Mercury, because it is a smaller i: Mercury’s inner-planet status does not explain a blue color.

activities.explanation: Earth is called the Blue Planet because much of it is covered with water.

activities.prompt: Explain the difference between the inner planets and the four outermost planets.
activities.answer: The inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. They are smaller and have solid surfaces covered with rocks. The four outermost planets—Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune—are much larger than Earth.
points: Names Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Says the inner planets are smaller.
Mentions their solid, rock-covered surfaces.
Names the four outermost planets and their large size.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.prompt: Explain why many objects travelling between Mars and Jupiter are called asteroids and why that region is called the asteroid belt.
activities.answer: These travelling objects are small and rocky, so they are called asteroids. Many of them go around the Sun in the space between Mars and Jupiter. That whole region is called the asteroid belt because it is where many asteroids travel.
points: Small rocky objects are asteroids.
Many asteroids travel between Mars and Jupiter.
The region is called the asteroid belt.
The name refers to the many asteroids travelling there.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On a moonless night, a student stood in a dark place and noticed a faint band of light stretching across the sky from near north to south. The student had learned that our home galaxy is called the Milky Way Galaxy or Ākāśha Gangā. The student wondered what the band shows and whether any exoplanets might have life. The student also wanted to know where our Solar System belongs and how scientists investigate such questions.
activities.prompt: The student plans another observation and wants to see the same faint band. Which conditions should the student choose?
options: A moonless night in a place with very little light
A moonless night in a place with bright lighting
A moonlit night in a place with very little light
A moonlit night in a place with bright lighting

why.A moonless night in a place with bright: The bright lighting does not match the stated dark-place condition.
why.A moonlit night in a place with very lit: The moonlit night does not match the stated moonless-night condition.
why.A moonlit night in a place with bright l: Both the lighting and moonlight differ from the stated conditions.

activities.explanation: Correct: this matches both stated conditions: a dark place and no moon.

activities.context: On a moonless night, a student stood in a dark place and noticed a faint band of light stretching across the sky from near north to south. The student had learned that our home galaxy is called the Milky Way Galaxy or Ākāśha Gangā. The student wondered what the band shows and whether any exoplanets might have life. The student also wanted to know where our Solar System belongs and how scientists investigate such questions.
activities.prompt: The student says, “No evidence of life elsewhere has been found, so life definitely does not exist elsewhere.” Which reply correctly applies the facts?
options: We have not found evidence yet, so the existence of life elsewhere remains unknown
We have not found evidence yet, so life definitely does not exist elsewhere
We have not found evidence yet, so life definitely exists elsewhere
We have not found evidence yet, so every exoplanet contains life

why.We have not found evidence yet, so life: This confuses missing evidence with proof that life does not exist.
This confuses missing evidence with proof that life does exist.
why.We have not found evidence yet, so every: This wrongly turns a general search result into a claim about every exoplanet.

activities.explanation: Correct: scientists have not found evidence yet, so existence remains unknown.

activities.prompt: Explain why the student should not claim that the absence of evidence of life elsewhere proves that life exists nowhere else.
activities.answer: No evidence of life elsewhere has been found yet. This means scientists have not confirmed life elsewhere; it does not prove that life cannot exist elsewhere. Therefore, whether life exists elsewhere in the Universe remains unknown.
points: Scientists have not yet found evidence of life elsewhere
Missing evidence is not proof that life does not exist
Whether life exists elsewhere remains unknown
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Beyond Earth

activities.prompt: What makes Nubra good for watching stars?
options: It has almost cloudless weather and very little light pollution.
It has excessive artificial light at night.
Smoke and dust hide many stars there.
Tall buildings block most of the sky there.
activities.explanation: Nubra has almost cloudless weather and very little air or light pollution.

activities.prompt: Sailors once used star patterns to find their way.
activities.explanation: Sailors and travellers once used star patterns to find their way.

activities.prompt: The sky has ______ official constellations.
activities.hint: This asks how many, not how long.
activities.explanation: There are 88 official constellations. They cover the whole sky.

activities.prompt: Match each space object with its meaning.
pairs: Large object that goes around the Sun
Object with a long tail near the Sun
Small rocky object between Mars and Jupiter
activities.explanation: Stars make their own light. Planets go around the Sun. Moons go around planets. Comets have long tails. Many asteroids are between Mars and Jupiter.

activities.prompt: Put these comet events in the correct order.
items: A comet moves nearer the Sun.
Frozen material starts evaporating.
The comet becomes dim farther away.
activities.explanation: Frozen material evaporates when a comet nears the Sun. It grows dim while moving away.

activities.prompt: What is one astronomical unit?
options: The width of the Sun
The gap between Mars and Jupiter
The distance between the Sun and Earth
The distance from the Sun to Proxima Centauri
activities.explanation: One astronomical unit is about the distance between the Sun and Earth.

activities.prompt: Venus is called the Morning Star or Evening Star. But it is not a star.
activities.explanation: Venus shines brightly in the morning and evening. It is one of the eight planets.

activities.prompt: Match each space object with its special name.
pairs: The Morning Star or Evening Star
Part of the Milky Way Galaxy
activities.explanation: You matched five special space names correctly. Our Solar System belongs to the Milky Way Galaxy.

activities.prompt: Put these space objects in order from Earth's moon to our galaxy.
items: Moon
Earth
Solar System
Milky Way Galaxy
activities.explanation: The Moon revolves around Earth. Earth revolves around the Sun, and our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy.
